title: Speaking the Navigator's Language: Trajectory-Grounded Instruction Translation for Frozen Aerial VLN Agents
summary: Aerial vision-and-language navigation (VLN) agents are typically trained on detail-rich, trajectory-aligned commands, whereas users issue short, intent-driven instructions; on a frozen OpenFly navigator, this \emph{instruction gap} drops success rate (SR) from $31.03\%$ to $11.33\%$. To scale translator training, we prompt a language model with human-written style examples to convert original commands into paired, intent-centered Weak commands, which yield $15.27\%$ SR. We introduce the \textbf{Trajectory-Grounded Instruction Translator (TGIT)}, a front-end that keeps the navigator frozen and translates Weak inputs into agent-executable commands by learning from its trajectory outcomes. The resulting Weak-trained translator raises Weak-input SR to $37.93\%$ and transfers zero-shot to real human instructions ($11.33\%{\rightarrow}32.51\%$); it also improves held-out OpenFly ($4.95\%{\rightarrow}20.79\%$) and yields recovery on CityNav and AirVLN.

All navigation policies remain unchanged; only the front-end translator is trained. The translator is Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct with LoRA~ Hu2021LoRALA ( , ) on language modules. For each agent, we build a hard-case pool of original-success / weak-failure instructions, sample cases per round for rounds, and generate candidates with visual frames. DPO starts from and references the round-matched SFT adapter, uses , a learning rate of , and discards pairs with a reward gap below . Adapters carry across rounds; the navigator remains fixed. These settings define the main protocol; Section~ sec:ablation ablates hard-case pool construction, reward ranking, visual frames, and translator backbone as diagnostics. Splits and evaluation. We factor evaluation scenes by two axes used in prior aerial VLN protocol: whether the translator was optimized on that scene (Selected vs.\ Unselected), and whether the frozen agent trained on that scene (Seen vs.\ Unseen)~ gao2025openfly,lee2024citynav,liu2023aerialvln . Selected-Seen / Unselected-Seen / Unseen thus contain OpenFly, CityNav, and AirVLN episodes. Selected-Seen is the pool-construction scene for TGIT; Unselected-Seen is agent-seen but translator-unselected; Unseen is held out for the agent. Each closed-loop rollout lasts at most agent steps, and success requires final distance below \,m. Baselines and Human transfer. We compare Orig, Weak, ICL, and SFT under the Weak protocol; TGIT(W) is the primary result. On OpenFly Selected-Seen, sixteen annotators provide one natural instruction per episode. Human anchors the deployment gap; Weak is the scalable, Human-informed stress protocol. We also report zero-shot TGIT(H), which only reuses the TGIT(W) adapter. Protocol consistency. Within each agent and split, methods use the same episode set, initial conditions, rollout horizon, success threshold, controller, and metric implementation. Only the instruction path and translator update differ. SR is the fraction of episodes that reach the goal. SPL is the mean of over successful episodes only; failed episodes are excluded. Thus SPL measures how efficiently successful trajectories reach the goal and is not upper-bounded by SR. Higher SR/SPL and lower NE are better. Results sec:results The instruction gap is behavioral. On the same OpenFly Selected-Seen episodes and frozen navigator, SR drops from with Orig to with Weak and with Human. Because the route, initial condition, controller, and evaluation remain fixed, this collapse isolates instruction source as the changed interface variable. The lower Human result also shows that the gap is not merely an artifact of LM weakening. Without Human-specific training, the same Weak-trained TGIT adapter raises Human-input SR from to ( ), confirming that interface activation transfers beyond the Weak proxy. Thus the deployment mismatch is behavioral, not only a difference in wording or length. Trajectory grounding recovers the interface. Direct Weak execution reaches SR; prompt-only ICL improves modestly to , and SFT target imitation recovers to but remains below Orig. TGIT reaches , gaining points over Weak, over SFT, and over Orig. The controls identify the missing supervision: ICL rewrites without agent feedback, while SFT learns one executable target without comparing alternative commands under rollout outcomes. TGIT instead executes and ranks candidates before updating only the translator. This pattern is consistent with trajectory-grounded preference learning supplying information beyond prompting and target imitation; Section~ sec:ablation separately tests the hard-case and preference-design mechanisms. Transfer reveals a backbone-bounded regime. Beyond the pool-construction environment, TGIT raises OpenFly SR from to on Unselected-Seen and from to on Unseen. The relative activation also transfers across frozen agents: CityNav improves on Selected-Seen ( ), Unselected-Seen ( ), and Unseen ( ); AirVLN improves on Selected-Seen ( ) and Unselected-Seen ( ). The OpenFly gains outside its -case pool are inconsistent with a pool-memorization-only explanation, while the cross-agent gains show that the activation pattern is not specific to one navigator~ wang2025rethinking,anderson2021sim . TGIT primarily expands success coverage rather than jointly optimizing every navigation metric. Its OpenFly Selected-Seen SPL ( ) remains below Orig and SFT, while the high Human SPL describes only the successful subset. At the agent level, CityNav and AirVLN exhibit relative recovery but low absolute SR, and every AirVLN method remains at on Unseen. This dual pattern---transferable relative activation but backbone-bounded absolute success---defines the claim: TGIT repairs recoverable interface failures but does not supply missing navigation skill.

title: NavGPT-3: Harnessing Context in a Hierarchical Navigation Runtime
summary: Language models trained with long-horizon agentic reinforcement learning can generalize knowledge through reasoning, express precise actions, and pursue goals over many steps, raising the ceiling on what an embodied agent can understand and decide. Physical interaction, however, remains the domain of action policies, which provide dense, low-latency control. We present NavGPT-3, a harness that connects the two models, with an OS-like runtime built above it: reasoning, acting, and monitoring run as threads with their own context, tools, and permissions, while the runtime schedules them and decides which thread controls the robot's motion, so that the robot can react to sudden real-world events through interruption and thread switching. Beneath it, our action policy NavGPT VLA, trained on 19.28M examples, allocates visual tokens using codec allocation, in proportion to scene change; its 8B model alone reaches 74.51 SR on R2R-CE and leads RxR-CE with 78.19 SR. With the complete harness, NavGPT-3 sets the state of the art on R2R-CE (81.51 SR) and, for the first time, brings an autonomous agent to human level: on RxR-CE it matches human followers in success (90.43 vs. 90.4 SR) and path fidelity (78.47 vs. 77.7 nDTW) at 1 min 22 s per episode, versus roughly 3 min for a human. We comprehensively ablate the harness design and the interaction between the two models, showing how tools and the action policy shape the path from language-model reasoning to physical control: when NavGPT VLA executes the route, the reasoning loop shortens and the system's minimum reaction time falls from 3-19 s per language-model decision to 0.5-1 s per action-policy step (1-2 Hz). These results show that designing this embodied interface is central to connecting frontier language-model intelligence with low-level physical control. We will release all models, code, and evaluation records.

The highest-scoring candidate becomes the next harness, while revisits whole categories of changes when progress stalls. Search operates at development time: the chosen interface is fixed during evaluation, without online Planner or VLA weight updates. Harnessing and VLA Ablation sec:planner_models measures how much each part of the harness contributes and what the VLA adds on top. Two language-model Planners, GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5, navigate the same 100 R2R-CE episodes under the same episode limits and with the same 8B NavGPT VLA. Only the tools exposed to the Planner change between rows, and the task prompt describes only those tools. The tools and their visual returns were developed through RSI ( ). What the Planner can do in each configuration. The eight tools fall into four groups ( ). Every configuration includes the four basic tools: observe forward and observe panorama to look at the current surroundings, navigate relative to turn and move by a given angle and distance, and terminate episode to end the episode. With the basic tools alone, the Planner moves the agent itself, so every environment action is a Planner decision. Three groups can be added. The VLA group, navigate by instruction, hands the full instruction, or the part that remains, to NavGPT VLA, which drives the agent until it signals a stop or reaches the delegation limit; the Planner then receives up to eight keyframes of the executed route, the endpoint views, and the execution status. A VLA stop ends only the delegation, and the episode ends only when the Planner calls terminate episode. The Map group, observe map, returns a top-down map of the area observed so far, on which visited places are numbered in visiting order. The Backtrack group, navigate to node and annotate node, lets the Planner return the agent to any numbered place and label places with what it has recognized there, so the map becomes something it can act on rather than only read. title: Self-Supervised Keyframe Discovery for Horizon-Invariant Behavior Cloning
summary: Behavior cloning (BC) in non-Markovian environments is a challenging problem because policies have to reason over contextual information over long horizons. Existing policy architectures rely on recurrent or attention-based mechanisms to capture long-term dependencies. However, recurrent models suffer from hidden-state collapse and gradient instability under backpropagation through time, while attention-based models are fundamentally limited by context length. To address these issues, we propose Keyframe Mnemonics, a novel self-supervised method that $\textit{discovers}$ a set of information-critical observations ($\textit{mnemonics}$) by learning an objective from randomly sampled past observations and using it as a reward for keyframe selection. We then train a BC policy that conditions on the discovered keyframes to model the action distribution. Under certain task-structure assumptions, our formulation provides context retention guarantees over an infinite horizon, while maintaining a small set of decision-relevant keyframes in the policy's working memory. We evaluate our method on synthetic memory domains, where mnemonic-conditioned BC policies achieve $100$% success rates (SR) and generalize to horizons orders of magnitude beyond training without performance degradation. Additionally, we evaluate on memory-intensive robot manipulation benchmark, achieving a $13.9$% average absolute SR improvement over the strongest baseline across $23$ tasks and retaining $80$% SR at $20\times$ longer horizons on a real robot. Code and videos are available at https://keyframe-mnemonics.github.io.

We evaluate our method on synthetic memory domains, where mnemonic-conditioned BC policies achieve success rates (SR) and generalize to horizons orders of magnitude beyond training without performance degradation. Additionally, we evaluate on memory-intensive robot manipulation benchmark, achieving a 13.9 average absolute SR improvement over the strongest baseline across 23 tasks and retaining 80 SR at 20 longer horizons on a real robot. Introduction The Markov assumption for decision processes is that the agent’s current state contains sufficient information to determine the optimal action with respect to its goal or objective puterman2014markov . In practice, however, real-world environments are non-Markovian and partially observable, where decision-making often requires retaining (``remembering'') information over time to provide context for future actions kaelbling1998planning, lauri2022partially . Recent advancements in policy learning have increasingly relied on behavior cloning (BC) zhao2023learning, chi2023diffusionpolicy, kawaharazuka2025vla-survey , in which policies are highly dependent on short observation contexts with a working memory spanning only a few seconds into the past. This makes such BC policies brittle on tasks that require remembering information cues over long horizons cherepanov2025memory . Recurrent models have been the architecture of choice for behavior cloning in such memory intensive partially observable environments and are typically trained using Back-Propagation Through Time (BPTT) werbos2002backpropagation, chevalier2018babyai . However, BPTT is difficult to scale, as it requires sequential gradient accumulation over episode timesteps pascanu2013difficulty . Truncated-BPTT tries to mitigate this issue but trades off information from distant past observations tallec2017unbiasing . Moreover, recurrent models suffer from hidden-state collapse due to repeated representation updates over time hochreiter2001gradient, pascanu2013difficulty . Attention-based architectures such as transformers vaswani2017attention address many representation learning challenges, but their finite context length limits retention of the full history in partially observable domains. Furthermore, increasing context through frame stacking incurs quadratic compute complexity vaswani2017attention , degrades at extreme horizons cherepanov2025elmur , and is prone to overfitting spurious correlations with visual observations de2019causal . Many hybrid architectures have been proposed that improve information retention through dedicated memory mechanisms cherepanov2025elmur, fang2025sam2act, koo2025hamlet, jang2025contextvla, shi2025memoryvla, chung2026rethinking, tan2026memoact or by learning recurrent summaries sorokin2022explain, zhou2025mtil, lei2026vpwem . However, these methods remain susceptible to state collapse beyond the horizons encountered during training, often leading to severe performance degradation on tasks that require generalization to longer horizons. To address these challenges in behavior cloning, we propose Keyframe Mnemonics (KM), a policy learning method that decomposes the original non-Markovian decision-making problem into two subproblems: (i) discovering observations (keyframes) that contain information relevant to the action distribution, and (ii) training a BC policy on demonstrations augmented with the identified keyframes. Our keyframe discovery process is self-supervised and leverages the intrinsic simplicity bias of neural networks~ arpit2017closer, valle2018deep, mingard2025deep to train a reward function that assigns high rewards to information-rich keyframes in the policy's context buffer. The reward learning process is driven by the mutual information advantage of keyframes with the expert action distribution, which is amplified through a novel training method that uses randomly sampled past observations as training samples for the reward function. We then train a selector policy using reinforcement learning to optimize the learned reward function and identify a set of decision-relevant keyframes, which we call Mnemonics (``something that assists memory''). Finally, we train BC policies conditioned on these mnemonics to match the expert action distribution. The trained policy is deployed together with the selector, which identifies keyframes at runtime and provides context to disambiguate actions under partial observability. Under certain assumptions, this architectural decomposition enables horizon-invariance i.e., memory retention beyond the training horizon, allowing BC policies to generalize on longer time scales where existing hybrid memory methods fail. We extensively evaluate Keyframe Mnemonics on synthetic memory benchmarks (Add~ hochreiter1997long , Scattered Copy~ sorokin2022explain , T-Maze~ bakker2001reinforcement ), grid worlds (MiniGrid Memory~ chevalier2023minigrid , LTMB-Hallway~ yue2024learning ), memory-intensive robot manipulation benchmark MIKASA-Robo~ cherepanov2025memory , and additionally on a real robot, demonstrating stable performance without degradation far beyond the training horizon. Our contributions are: [leftmargin=2em, topsep=0pt, itemsep=2pt] We propose a novel self-supervised algorithm to discover decision-relevant keyframes in non-Markovian expert demonstrations without explicit keyframe annotations (Figure fig:method , Algorithm~ alg:masked-sampling ). We provide a theoretical intuition of our method under task-structure assumptions, derive information retention guarantees, and support our hypotheses with empirical evidence. We demonstrate horizon-invariant performance of mnemonic-conditioned BC policies, with MLP policies achieving SR in synthetic and grid memory domains, Transformer policies improving absolute SR by on the MIKASA-Robo benchmark, and a flow-matching policy retaining SR at longer test horizons on a real robot. title: Skill-SLM: Agent Skill-driven Small Language Models for Reliable Robot Operation
summary: Small language models (SLMs) have been increasingly adopted for onboard robot operation because they enable intelligent decision-making. However, existing approaches are mainly distillation-oriented and rely on enumerating representative task-solution pairs. This makes dataset construction difficult and limits generalization to diverse robot tasks whose possible forms grow rapidly. This paper proposes Skill-SLM, a framework that reformulates SLM-driven robot operation as a task-decomposition and skill-composition problem. Given a natural language task instruction, Skill-SLM decomposes the task into subtasks, selects appropriate skills from the skill library, and orchestrates the selected skills into executable robot operations. First, to support the skill-driven workflow, we propose a novel robot operational skill aware context-free grammar (CFG) to extract the skills required to accomplish tasks and build the skill library accordingly. Then, we configure LLM teachers to induce and synthesize training datasets for the SLMs, enabling SLMs to decompose tasks and orchestrate skills reliably. Additionally, we employ a progressive skill orchestration strategy to improve the reliability of skill implementation and overall robot operation. Experiments on UAV operation tasks indicate that Skill-SLM substantially outperforms distillation-oriented baselines, especially on unseen tasks that require generalization of capabilities. Additional experiments on ground vehicle tasks further demonstrate that Skill-SLM can be applied to different robot platforms.

Introduction sec:intro Large language models (LLMs) have enabled robots to interpret human natural language instructions and generate executable actions for navigation~ L3MVN , planning~ CodeasPolicy , and manipulation~ manipulation . However, deploying LLMs on resource-constrained robot platforms (e.g., UAVs) is often impractical due to their substantial computational and memory requirements. As a result, increasing efforts have been focused on enabling onboard deployable language models (i.e., SLMs) to perform reasoning and decision-making reliably through task-specific training and knowledge distillation from LLMs~ Ro-SLM, PRISM, baumann2025enhancing, Small-nav, Small-VLA . Despite recent advances, a key challenge remains in enabling SLMs to generalize reliably to diverse robot tasks and novel instructions. Recent studies have enhanced SLMs' generalization ability by extensively enumerating and synthesizing representative task-solution examples~ Ro-SLM, PRISM . However, these data-driven approaches rely on the SLMs to memorize training examples, which limits their generalization when tasks require unseen combinations of learned capabilities or tasks were insufficiently represented during training. Covering these unseen cases by continually enumerating new task-solution examples is expensive, and SLMs' limited memorization capacity becomes unreliable when learned knowledge becomes large~ scaling-law . Moreover, it is difficult to anticipate all possible task variations in advance. Given the compositional nature of robotic operations, recent studies have investigated agent skills~ anthropic-agent-skills to enable LLMs to generalize to unseen tasks by decomposing them into subtasks and tackling them by composition of skills~ Skills4Robotics, skill-nav . However, SLMs' intrinsically smaller model scale hinders their ability to achieve reliable compositional reasoning like LLMs~ LLM-scaling . Specifically, SLMs can be distracted by irrelevant or ambiguous information in the context~ SLM-sensitivity and struggle to effectively interpret task-relevant context for a given task instruction, resulting in incorrect task decomposition and incorrect skill usage. In addition, SLMs can overlook skill dependencies and fail to coordinate skills into a coherent execution~ slm-skills . Earlier skills selected by SLMs can define targets, variables, or robot states that later skills must preserve, and incompatible preconditions can make a plausible operational code fail. These limitations highlight the urgent need for methods capable of bridging the broad generalization of compositional reasoning with reliable SLM-driven robot operation. To address these limitations, we propose Skill-SLM, a framework in which SLM agents solve robotic tasks by task decomposition and skill composition, as illustrated in Fig.~ fig:overall . Skill-SLM consists of two agents: a decomposition SLM agent decomposes a task instruction into subtasks and selects appropriate skills from the skill library; an orchestration SLM agent then orchestrates the selected skills into executable robot operations. Unlike prior methods that map task instructions to complete robot operations end-to-end, the proposed Skill-SLM captures the compositional nature of robotic tasks; it not only improves the seen task performance through compositional reasoning, but also facilitates generalization to diverse robotic tasks. Specifically, we first construct a skill library to support the skill-driven workflow. We configure an operational skill aware LLM CFG constructor to induce a CFG that captures the skills that can effectively complete the tasks. Based on the captured skills, we construct a skill library with expert knowledge, in which each skill is documented in terms of its functionality, usage, and dependencies. The SLM can refer to these skill documents when orchestrating skills into executable robot operational code. On top of that, we distill LLMs' reasoning to enable the SLM to effectively perform compositional reasoning, we leverage LLMs to synthesize two distillation datasets that capture different stages of the reasoning process. The decomposition dataset consists of task instructions, subtask descriptions, and selected skills, which trains the decomposition SLM agent to learn how to decompose tasks into subtasks and select the appropriate skills for each subtask. The orchestration dataset contains subtask descriptions, skill specifications, and their corresponding robot operation code, and is used to train the orchestration SLM agent to accomplish each subtask by orchestrating the selected skills into executable robot operation code. Additionally, to improve the reliability of the orchestration agent, we introduce a progressive orchestration strategy that generates executable robot operation code progressively while preserving the task context, intermediate variables, robot states, and cross-skill dependencies. We conduct extensive experiments on UAV and ground vehicle operations to evaluate the effectiveness and generalizability of Skill-SLM. Qwen3-8B~ qwen3 achieves \(100 \) task success rate on Seen-Pattern tasks, \(100 \) on New-Combination tasks, and \(94 \) on New-Capability tasks. Skill-SLM also generalizes to ground vehicle operations, achieving \(100 \), \(95 \), and \(100 \) task success rates on the three task sets, respectively. Compared with the baselines~ Ro-SLM, PRISM , our method consistently achieves higher task success rates, particularly on unseen tasks that require knowledge recombination. These results demonstrate that Skill-SLM is promising for reliable onboard SLM-driven robot operation across different robot platforms. Related Work sec:related Agent Skills Several prior studies have explored skill-like representations. SkiROS2~ skiros2 represents robot skills as parameterized procedures with explicit execution conditions. LRLL~ self-learned-skill proposed to learn skills via exploring and summarizing. These methods show that reusable skills can improve generalization, but they mainly focus on model-learned skills and are restricted to a constrained environment. The recent agent-skills paradigm~ anthropic-agent-skills provides a modular, file-based knowledge package that can be discovered and loaded by an agent when relevant~ agent-skills . Therefore, the agent can dynamically acquire and utilize skills as needed in solving different task scenarios, especially for tasks that are unseen in prior training or require knowledge recombination. Inspired by this principle, this studies investigated how a given task can be reformulated as an agent skill-driven problem. Skill Discovery and Characterization Prior work has investigated identifying skills. Ref.~ huaman2017taxonomy derives a taxonomy of manipulation benchmark tasks from existing evaluation protocols, while~ Pantano2022Capability systematically analyzes robot skill frameworks to identify recurring task--skill--primitive structures and common robot capabilities. More recently, the BEHAVIOR Robot Suite~ BEHAVIOR analyzes the 1,000 household activities in BEHAVIOR-1K to identify a set of core whole-body capabilities required for everyday manipulation. These approaches provide useful abstractions for characterizing task corpora, but largely rely on manually specified taxonomies, classification criteria, or capability categories. NavNuances~ NavNuance instead introduces a CFG-based decomposition of navigation instructions, enabling fine-grained analysis of model performance over task units. Its CFG is constructed by starting from a manually designed grammar and iteratively refining it with LLM assistance. In contrast, we leverage the semantic knowledge of LLMs to infer robot operations from the task corpus and automatically construct the CFG, eliminating the need for handcrafted production rules. SLM-enabled Robotics LLMs have been widely used to connect natural language instructions with robot planning, control, and tool use~ ChatGPTRobotics, CodeasPolicy, gemini-robotics, GSCE . However, relying on large cloud-hosted models can be impractical for robots operating with unreliable networks (e.g., disaster response) or privacy-sensitive scenarios. This has motivated recent work on SLM-enabled robotics, where smaller models that can be deployed on the robot's computing unit are configured for robotic tasks~ PRISM, baumann2025enhancing, Ro-SLM . For example, PRISM distills an LLM-enabled planner into an SLM for high-level robot planning~ PRISM and conducts parameter-efficient training with Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA)~ lora to reduce GPU memory usage. Ro-SLM~ Ro-SLM leverages LLMs to synthesize a dataset and train SLMs for mapping instructions to robot operational code. For a low-level robotic controller, Baumann et al.~ baumann2025enhancing train SLMs to generate parameters for model predictive control in an autonomous driving system. These approaches demonstrate the feasibility of transferring LLM capabilities to smaller models, but they still largely depend on enumerating representative task-solution mappings for SLMs to memorize. However, such enumeration becomes increasingly difficult as robot tasks become more diverse. Additionally, the small scale of SLMs makes memorization unreliable when the learned facts become large~ scaling-law . In contrast, Skill-SLM solves tasks by recombining reusable capabilities rather than memorizing all the task solutions. Method sec:method Overview Fig.~ fig:workflow presents the workflow of our Skill-SLM framework. Given a task \(T\), the goal of Skill-SLM deployed on the robot is to analyze the task and generate the corresponding robot operation code \(C\) for the robot to complete the task. In our framework, the decomposition agent first performs task decomposition and skill selection, and produces a subtask plan: \[ p = [(u_1, s_ j_1 ), (u_2, s_ j_2 ), , (u_t, s_ j_t )] \] where \(u_t\) is the subtask description, \( =\ s_1, ,s_K\ \) denotes a library of agent skills, and \(s_ j_t \) is the selected skill for the subtask \(u_t\). Then, the orchestration agent performs skill composition by orchestrating \(p\) progressively. At each step \(i\), the agent outputs a code segment \(c_i\), and the final code is obtained by concatenating the segments: \[ C = c_1 c_2 c_t \] Skill Library Construction sec:skill Operational Skill Discovery To s

title: Cross-Embodiment Robot Foundation World Models with Latent Actions
summary: The diversity of robot embodiments and action spaces makes it challenging to build robot world models that generalize across different embodiments. We introduce the Latent Action-Conditioned Robot World Model (LAC-WM), which operates within a learned unified latent action space shared across diverse embodiments. This unified action space improves the world model's performance when adapted to previously unseen robot embodiments. We compare LAC-WM with an Explicit Action-Conditioned World Model (EAC-WM), which conditions on explicit motion labels. Our results show that explicit action conditioning leads to disjoint action representations across embodiments, limiting downstream performance when adapting to new robots. We evaluate both models on dexterous manipulation tasks and a modified LIBERO benchmark. LAC-WM improves downstream performance over EAC-WM by up to 46.7% on dexterous manipulation and 11.7% on LIBERO. Crucially, the unified latent action space allows LAC-WM's downstream performance to scale positively with the number of embodiments used during pretraining. In contrast, the disjoint action space in EAC-WM leads to decreased performance as the number of pretraining embodiments increases. These results highlight the importance of a unified action space for efficient cross-embodiment learning, addressing a key challenge in robotics. Project website: https://lacwm.github.io/

Project website: Introduction sec:intro Robot action-conditioned video generation models, or robot world models, offer a complementary approach to robot policies based on imitation learning, allowing robots to predict future states and evaluate planned actions before execution, improving planning and decision-making. However, a fundamental and persistent challenge in robotics is the vast and evolving diversity of robot embodiments. Robots differ widely in their physical structure, sensors and actuators, and control strategies, and new embodiments are constantly emerging. This creates a critical need for robot world models that can efficiently learn from cross-embodiment data~ zheng2025universalactionsenhancedembodied,liu2025rdt1bdiffusionfoundationmodel,zheng2025xvlasoftpromptedtransformerscalable,doshi2024scalingcrossembodiedlearningpolicy,bu2025univlalearningacttaskcentric and adapt quickly to previously unseen robot forms. We propose learning a unified latent action space that aligns action representations across different embodiments, including both human and different robot agents. This latent space abstracts away embodiment-specific details while preserving task-relevant information, enabling the model to integrate heterogeneous data during pretraining. We show that such a unified latent space will empower the world model to learn more efficiently across embodiments during pretraining and adapt quickly to unseen embodiments through finetuning, laying the groundwork for a truly generalizable foundational world model for robotics. Latent action spaces have primarily been explored for extracting action representations from unlabeled video data~ lapa, chen2024igorimagegoalrepresentationsatomic . However, most robotic datasets come with action annotations, and advances in human pose estimation provide scalable motion information, including detailed hand poses and camera movements. This enables learning action spaces directly from motion data. Despite this, there is a lack of comparative analysis for action embedding alignment across different embodiments between representations derived directly from motion data and those learned through latent action models. We hypothesize that training action encoders solely on motion data leads to disjoint latent spaces for different embodiments ( ), which limits cross-embodiment knowledge transfer and degrades generalization performance on unseen embodiments. We focus on learning a foundational robot world model that learns efficiently from cross-embodiment data during pretraining and adapts quickly to unseen embodiments through finetuning. Specifically, we investigate two key research questions: (1) Do latent action models better unify cross-embodiment action representations compared to explicit action labels? and (2) Does a unified action space enhance cross-embodiment robot world model learning compared to a disjoint latent space? We propose the Latent Action Conditioned Robot World Model ( ), which predicts future observations conditioned on a unified latent action space. consists of four components: an inverse dynamics model (IDM), an forward dynamics model (FDM), a motion decoder and an action projector, as in~ . The IDM encodes pairs of consecutive image observations into latent actions, which condition the FDM to predict the next frame. The motion decoder, following~ nikulin2025laom , decodes latent actions back into explicit motion labels. The IDM and FDM are trained jointly on datasets combining human manipulation videos and robot data. Since future observations, required by the IDM, are unavailable at inference time, we train an action projector that maps explicit actions into the latent action space~ gao2025adaworldlearningadaptableworld , enabling the world model to directly consume action inputs. We evaluate in a cross-embodiment transfer setting, where the model is pretrained on multiple embodiments and fine-tuned on a previously unseen robot using an action projector. We compare against an explicit action-conditioned world model ( ), which directly encodes motion information into action latents. Our results show that produces higher-quality future predictions than and improves task success rate by up to 46.7 on dexterous manipulation. We further validate on a modified LIBERO benchmark with unseen object and location variants, where it improves the average success rate from 82.4 to 92.0 over . Moreover, exhibits positive scaling in downstream planning performance as the number of pretraining embodiments increases, whereas shows the opposite trend, likely due to its disjoint latent space, which hinders effective cross-embodiment learning. Related Work World Models in Robotics. World models (WMs) have emerged as a way to achieve controllable video generation~ bruce2024genie,zhang2025matrix,li2025hunyuan,po2025long,yang2023learning,valevski2024diffusion,yu2025gamefactory . Robotic world models serve as scalable and explainable compliments to imitation learning based policies. Prior work has explored training navigation world models~ hu2023gaia, bar2025navigation, gao2024vista, hassan2025gem with well-defined action spaces (e.g., velocity). Robot manipulation world models involve diverse action spaces due to differences in robot morphologies, and as a result, they typically rely on action-free video prediction during pretraining~ gupta2022maskvitmaskedvisualpretraining, wu2024ivideogptinteractivevideogptsscalable, assran2025v , or use text or video conditioning~ agarwal2025cosmos , adding action conditioning only during fine-tuning~ gupta2022maskvitmaskedvisualpretraining, wu2024ivideogptinteractivevideogptsscalable, agarwal2025cosmos, assran2025v .~ zhu2025irasimfinegrainedworldmodel incorporate action conditioning for a single robot embodiment but do not evaluate cross-embodiment transfer. In contrast, ~ directly tackles the challenge of heterogeneous action spaces with a unified latent action space, enabling efficient cross-embodiment learning and better generalization. Latent Action Modeling. Latent Action Models (LAM) have emerged as a promising approach to learn action representations from large-scale unlabeled data. Prior work has explored LAMs for training latent action policies for game environments~ schmidt2024learning , and fine-tuning expert-level policies from these, with limited labels. Other works have explored LAMs for robot manipulation, by extracting latent actions from large-scale unlabeled human videos as labels to fine-tune vision-language models, and subsequently vision-language-action (VLA) models~ lapa,chen2025motolatentmotiontoken, bu2025univlalearningacttaskcentric, jang2025dreamgenunlockinggeneralizationrobot,cui2024dynamoindomaindynamicspretraining,kim2025uniskillimitatinghumanvideos . liang2025clam, nikulin2025laom introduced an auxiliary motion decoding loss which aligns latent actions with explicit control actions, to encourage the latent space to capture actionable content. zhang2025latent explores various best practices for training LAMs. also uses a motion decoding loss and learns a continuous latent action space. Instead of focusing on policy learning as in prior work, we learn a unified latent action space from cross embodiment labeled datasets, for building robot world foundation models. Latent Action World Models. bruce2024genie,ren2025videoworld introduce a latent action model (LAM) paired with a world model, trained on datasets that include robot data. However, their approach does not involve cross-embodiment pretraining across diverse embodiments, nor does the world model support conditioning on raw robot actions at inference time. chen2024igorimagegoalrepresentationsatomic train LAMs with data augmentation to regularize latent actions that feed into a foundation policy and world models for robotic manipulation. However, they focus on action-free video pretraining and do not demonstrate adaptation to unseen robot embodiments. gao2025adaworldlearningadaptableworld demonstrate that a pretrained latent action-conditioned world model can be adapted for robot manipulation by projecting raw action signals into the latent action space. But they also focus on action-free video pretraining and lack comparisons with robot world models trained using explicit action labels. In contrast, we leverages labeled cross-embodiment data for robot world model training and investigate the comparison between a learned latent action space and directly encoding the motion labels. We show a unified latent action space benefits cross-embodiment learning with better downstream robot planning performance, particularly when adapting to unseen embodiments. title: Informationally Decoupled Trajectory Design for Sim-to-Real System Identification
summary: Sampling-based system identification estimates physically meaningful parameters by tuning a simulator to reproduce the target system dynamics, providing an interpretable approach to improving sim-to-real transfer. Yet when the collected trajectories do not distinguish the effects of different parameters, multiple parameter combinations can reproduce those trajectories, leading to unreliable parameter estimates. To address this challenge, we introduce an Informationally Decoupled Trajectory Design framework (IDTD), which formulates the objective for the exploration policy built on the Schur complement score derived from the Fisher information matrix. To faithfully reflect parameter separability in the exploration objective, IDTD normalizes the score against the per-parameter information, selects the most favorable trajectory segment for each parameter, and aggregates the resulting scores logarithmically. The optimized trajectory is therefore composed of complementary intervals, each exposing a distinct subset of parameters whose contribution to the motion over that interval can be attributed unambiguously. Across diverse simulation environments, ranging from a linear-dynamics system to the Go2 quadruped, G1 humanoid, and Crazyflie quadrotor, IDTD reduces the parameter identification error by 39.6% on average relative to the strongest prior active-exploration baseline and attains improved downstream policy transfer. Furthermore, we validate the proposed trajectory design on a real K1 humanoid, demonstrating that the resulting identified parameters accurately capture the real-system dynamics.
full_text: Informationally Decoupled Trajectory Design for Sim-to-Real System Identification Sangwoo Shin , Ashvin Anilkumar, Ryan Gao, Josiah P. Hanna University of Wisconsin--Madison\\ sshin237@cs.wisc.edu\\ Corresponding author. Sampling-based system identification estimates physically meaningful parameters by tuning a simulator to reproduce the target system dynamics, providing an interpretable approach to improving sim-to-real transfer. Yet when the collected trajectories do not distinguish the effects of different parameters, multiple parameter combinations can reproduce those trajectories, leading to unreliable parameter estimates. To faithfully reflect parameter separability in the exploration objective, normalizes the score against the per-parameter information, selects the most favorable trajectory segment for each parameter, and aggregates the resulting scores logarithmically. The optimized trajectory is therefore composed of complementary intervals, each exposing a distinct subset of parameters whose contribution to the motion over that interval can be attributed unambiguously. Across diverse simulation environments, ranging from a linear-dynamics system to the Go2 quadruped, G1 humanoid, and Crazyflie quadrotor, reduces the parameter identification error by on average relative to the strongest prior active-exploration baseline and attains improved downstream policy transfer. Furthermore, we validate the proposed trajectory design on a real K1 humanoid, demonstrating that the resulting identified parameters accurately capture the real-system dynamics. Introduction Reinforcement learning (RL) in massively parallel simulation has become a widely adopted approach for learning-based robot control, yet policies trained in simulation degrade on hardware whenever the simulated dynamics deviate from the target physical system~ hwangbo2019learning, sim2real_survey . A common remedy is domain randomization, which trains a policy over a distribution of physical parameters, such as inertial properties, actuator gains, and friction, so that the real system falls within its support~ tobin2017domain, peng2018sim . This approach, however, requires covering a wide range of parameters, which tends to produce conservative policies that sacrifice performance for robustness. System identification (SysID) offers an alternative approach. Rather than training against a broad range of possible dynamics, SysID explicitly estimates the physical parameters that make the simulator reproduce the target system dynamics. Within SysID, sampling-based methods have recently gained traction~ spi_active, asid , as massively parallel GPU simulation makes black-box search over physical parameters practical. These methods evaluate candidate parameter vectors through forward dynamics simulation and search for the parameters under which the simulated trajectories best match the recorded real-world trajectories. By avoiding differentiation through the simulator, sampling-based SysID can directly leverage modern physics simulators with contact and actuator dynamics~ mujoco, isaac, newton, genesis while retaining physically interpretable parameters. While sampling-based approaches make the parameter search practical, their success depends critically on solving the complementary problem of determining which trajectories should be collected from the target system for reliable identification. Prior work addresses this question by seeking informative trajectories, where informativeness is quantified through the Fisher Information Matrix (FIM), whose inverse lower-bounds the covariance of the parameter estimate~ cramer-rho . Based on this bound, active exploration methods search for a policy that collects trajectories minimizing the trace of the inverse FIM, aggregating the estimation uncertainty across all parameters into a single objective~ asid, spi_active . However, this criterion does not treat the amount of information and the separability of the parameters as distinct quantities, so increased excitation can improve the aggregate criterion even when some parameter effects become less distinguishable. Consequently, errors in different parameters can compensate for one another, allowing simulations using the identified parameters to closely match the real-world trajectories even when the individual parameters differ substantially from their true values. For instance, consider identifying the mass and the damping of a one-dimensional system, where a force is applied to a point mass. A trace-based excitation makes the mass move faster and more abruptly, since larger, more energetic motion carries more total information about the parameters. Under such motion, however, the sensitivities to and stay nearly collinear, so increasing the mass while reducing the damping produces nearly the same trajectory under the same control input. The criterion therefore keeps improving even though the two parameters remain difficult to tell apart. In this simple example, the excitation can be manually designed to alternate between acceleration-dominant ( ) and velocity-dominant ( ) phases to distinguish the mass from the damping. Extending such parameter-specific excitation to the dozens of coupled parameters in modern robot models, however, is highly challenging, as each parameter may require a different excitation regime. To address this challenge, we present Informationally Decoupled Trajectory Design ( ), which searches for motions under which every parameter leaves a unique effect on the trajectory that no other parameter can reproduce. Specifically, builds on a per-parameter score derived from the Schur complement of the Fisher information, which measures how much of a parameter's effect on the motion remains after the effects of all other parameters are accounted for. A parameter whose effect can be reproduced by the others scores near zero, while a parameter with a distinct effect scores high; a high score thus means the parameter is cleanly distinguishable, or decoupled, from the rest. Furthermore, to prevent the objective from being improved through excitation alone, for instance by moving a few responsive joints more aggressively without better separating their parameter effects, normalizes each score by the information carried by the corresponding parameter. It then evaluates the normalized scores across multiple trajectory segments to encourage complementary excitation of different parameters throughout the trajectory. As a result, designs trajectories that expose every parameter somewhere along the motion rather than accumulating information for only a small subset. We evaluate in simulation on a linear-dynamics system, Unitree Go2, Unitree G1, and Crazyflie, demonstrating improved parameter identification, target-system prediction, and downstream policy transfer. We further validate on a real Booster K1 humanoid, where the identified parameters more accurately capture the target-system dynamics. The main contributions of our work are as follows. (i) We address the challenging yet practical problem of designing exploration trajectories that distinguish the effects of physical parameters, enabling reliable sampling-based system identification. (ii) We propose , a trajectory design framework that explicitly balances information quantity with parameter distinguishability through a normalized Schur-complement score and parameter-wise trajectory coverage. (iii) We demonstrate that improves parameter identification accuracy and downstream policy transfer across simulated Unitree Go2, Unitree G1, and Crazyflie platforms, and better captures real-world dynamics on a Booster K1 humanoid. Related Works Sim-to-Real Transfer and System Identification Reducing the sim-to-real gap has been approached from two complementary directions. Domain randomization exposes the policy to a wide distribution of dynamics so that the real system falls within the training support~ tobin2017domain, peng2018sim ; the resulting robustness, however, comes at the cost of conservative behavior, and the randomization ranges themselves require tuning. System identification instead estimates the physical parameters of the specific robot and its environment from real-world data. Classical approaches exploit the linearity of rigid-body dynamics in the inertial parameters and estimate them by least squares over hand-designed excitation~ atkeson1986estimation, gautier1992exciting , but they require an explicit structured dynamics model and do not scale to the contact-rich, hard-to-model effects of real robots. As massively parallel simulation has become fast and reliable, system identification is increasingly performed by tuning simulator parameters until simulated trajectories match real trajectories. One line of work makes the forward dynamics differentiable with respect to the parameters, so the identification objective can be minimized by backpropagating gradients directly through the simulation~ chen2022realtime, contactexcitation . Its reliance on smoothed contact models, however, limits its scalability to contact-rich tasks. Recent work therefore favors sampling-based identification, which pairs the simulator with a black-box search algorithm and sidesteps differentiation while keeping the estimated parameters physically interpretable~ spi_active, asid . Our work follows the sampling-based paradigm but addresses the complementary question of how exploration should be designed so that every parameter leaves a distinct effect on the resulting trajectory, enabling reliable system identification. Active Exploration and Optimal Experimental Design The choice of excitation has long been recognized as central to identification quality. In the classical context, exciting trajectories are optimized offline against criteria defined on the regressor matrix, which linearly relates the unknown dynamic parameters to the measured forces for a given trajectory. A common objective is to minimize the condition number of the regressor, producing excitations that yield parameter estimates more robust to measurement noise~ swevers1997optimal, gautier1992exciting . The objective is inherently coupling-aware, since an ill-conditioned regressor indicates that different parameters influence the measurements along nearly identical directions. For policy-driven system identification, where the excitation is produced by a closed-loop policy, and ASID~ spi_active, asid optimize the A-optimal Fisher-information criterion to encourage informative trajectories. Contact-implicit trajectory optimization likewise maximizes over excited contact modes~ contactexcitation . Optimal experimental design offers related criteria, including D-optimality ( ) for reducing the overall uncertainty of the parameter estimate and E-optimality ( , the smallest eigenvalue of ) for improving the least informative direction~ pukelsheim2006optimal, dozzi2026 . In the transition from regressor-based trajectory design to sampling-based identification, the Fisher information has been carried over as the measure of a trajectory, whereas parameter separation is addressed only implicitly through aggregate objectives. The Schur complement provides an explicit characterization of parameter separation by quantifying the information that remains for a parameter subset after accounting for correlations with the remaining parameters~ ljung1999system . QOED~ qoed leverages this quantity to improve the distinguishability of a subset of task-relevant parameters, leading to improved sim-to-real policy transfer. However, system identification requires all physical parameters to be identifiable, rather than only a selected subset. To the best of our knowledge, is the first exploration object

title: When Listening Becomes Easier: Scrubbing Visual Cues for Shortcut-Free VLAs
summary: Shortcut learning is a prevalent issue in robot learning. The limited diversity of robot demonstration datasets can mislead policies into exploiting spurious correlations between tasks and irrelevant features, such as viewpoint or background. Collecting sufficiently diverse robot demonstrations is costly and inefficient, motivating algorithmic alternatives. We focus on vision-language-action (VLA) models and discover that different vision-language model backbones exhibit substantially different levels of susceptibility to visual shortcut learning. We find that model behavior correlates with our proposed representation-level metric, action margin, which requires no policy rollouts. Visual shortcuts consistently enter action representations in early layers, with models differing in the extent to which later layers correct them by incorporating language information. To boost models' attention to language, we introduce task scrubbing, a new domain-adversarial training method that decreases models' likelihood of using visual shortcuts and improves VLAs' generalization. Experiments in both simulation and the real world across multiple VLAs and visual cues show that task scrubbing improves out-of-distribution robustness and often eliminates visual shortcut learning.

Introduction Vision-language-action (VLA) models are general-purpose robot policies built on pretrained vision-language models~(VLMs)~ alayrac2022flamingo,liu2023visual for their visual and linguistic abilities~ brohan2023rt,kim2024openvla . Although a large variety of different VLA models~ black2024pi_0,shukor2025smolvla,zheng2026x, wang2026qwen have been proposed, they share a common design: a VLM encodes and processes visual and language information and produces representations which are then used to predict actions. Actions are predicted either by the same backbone~ kim2024openvla,belkhale2024minivla or by a separate transformer, commonly called an action expert, that attends to the VLM representations. This design has produced policies that transfer pretrained vision-language knowledge to diverse manipulation tasks and generalize beyond individual training environments~ brohan2023rt,black2024pi_0,intelligence2025pi . Its appeal rests on an implicit premise: the policy should inherit sufficiently strong visual-language understanding from the VLM to condition its actions on the language instruction. However, in practice, this premise is less reliable than benchmark performance suggests~ jiang2026we,fei2025libero,xu2026unmasking . VLAs remain brittle to visual perturbations and initial-state changes~ fei2025libero , may fail to generalize across linguistic paraphrases~ kim2026liberopara , and can lose useful pretrained structure while adapting their representations to precise spatial and action demands~ driess2025knowledge,grover2025enhancing,dalal2026generalizable . More generally, robot policies tend to rely on irrelevant features captured in their training distribution~ xing2025shortcut . For example, proxies such as viewpoint, background, object color, distractors, or proprioceptive state may provide a strong signal for task identity in the limited diversity of the training data~ swann2026sparse, grant2026not . This behavior is an instance of shortcut learning~ geirhos2020shortcut,xing2025shortcut . Models affected by shortcut learning achieve high in-distribution (ID) success but follow inconsequential cues when determining the task under out-of-distribution~(OOD) conditions and thus fail. We focus on visual shortcuts~( ): task identity-correlated visual features that the policy uses as substitutes for the language instruction. These shortcuts are especially common as small visual variations between tasks can easily enter training demonstrations through shifts in camera position, background changes, or task setup. When this unwanted association is broken, a shortcut policy executes the visual cue-consistent behavior instead of the instructed behavior. Existing work largely describes this failure as a data-diversity problem~ xing2025shortcut , without studying why different VLA architectures trained on the same data can have different shortcut propensities. It also remains unclear how shortcuts enter action computation or how the visual shortcut pathway can be suppressed without discarding useful visual information. To understand how model architectures influences shortcut susceptibility, we evaluate multiple existing VLAs and our own variants to better understand the effect of VLM choice. We find that shortcut susceptibility varies substantially across VLM backbones on the same dataset. Further, we introduce the ~metric, which tracks whether a model is likely to shortcut by the alignment of the action-token hidden states with task- and cue-consistent reference states. Using this metric, we can directly track the development of shortcut actions during inference and find a mechanistic explanation. Attention knockout~ geva2023dissecting shows that task-correlated visual features shift action representations toward the shortcut in early layers with models differing in whether later computation restores alignment with the instruction. Based on these findings, we introduce task scrubbing to encourage models to attend to language information. Task scrubbing is an adversarial auxiliary loss that causes visual representations that predict task identity to shift during training, making them less reliable for action prediction. The intervention increases the relative influence of language when the model learns to predict actions, without removing information from the visual input. Our contributions are: we show that shortcut susceptibility is strongly architecture dependent: VLA variants trained on the same data behave substantially differently, while VLM backbone size and general performance do not predict robustness; we introduce a systematic framework for analyzing shortcut behavior: tracks behavioral shortcut reliance without rollouts, while attention knockout identifies how visual and language information shape action representations; and we introduce task scrubbing, a gradient-reversal method that makes task prediction from the visual pathway harder during training and causes policies to rely more strongly on language, thereby reducing shortcut learning. Background and Related Work Vision-Language-Action Models VLAs map visual observations, language instructions, and, in many systems, proprioceptive state to robot actions~ brohan2023rt,kim2024openvla . They vary in how they connect pretrained visual-language representations to control. Some models predict tokenized actions autoregressively with the VLM backbone itself~ kim2024openvla,belkhale2024minivla , whereas others pass image and text representations to a separate action expert that generates continuous action chunks~ black2024pi_0,shukor2025smolvla . Multi-pathway systems such as make this separation more explicit by assigning goal semantics and motor generation to different components~ intelligence2025pi . Across these designs, the expected benefit is that the VLM supplies broad semantic and visual abstractions while the action component adapts them to motor execution. Despite their successes, VLAs face general robustness and representation-learning challenges. LIBERO-Plus~ fei2025libero documents brittleness under distractors, initial-state changes, and other visual variations, while LIBERO-Para shows that robustness to linguistic rephrasing cannot be assumed from VLM pretraining~ kim2026liberopara . VLM features may omit fine spatial or action-relevant details, motivating adaptation during policy training~ driess2025knowledge . However, broad fine-tuning can degrade pretrained visual-language structure and hurt generalization~ grover2025enhancing, dalal2026generalizable . Freezing the pretrained VLM to prevent information loss does not generally help and can reduce task performance without improving language generalization~ kim2026liberopara . VLAs therefore face a tension between adapting representations to predict actions accurately and preserving the general structure to enable generalization. Various approaches have been proposed to improve representations, such as using stronger VLMs~ wu2026vlanext , utilizing more informative visual embeddings~ miao2026jepa , or adding representation-preserving objectives~ driess2025knowledge, grover2025enhancing . Larger systems such as combine broader data, model, and training changes to improve generalization~ intelligence2026pi . These results suggest that architecture and training affect representation quality and robustness. Shortcut Learning in Robot Policy Training Shortcut learning occurs when a policy exploits a predictive correlation that is easier to learn than the intended task rule and consequently fails under distribution shift~ geirhos2020shortcut . In generalist robot policies, insufficient dataset diversity and fragmentation allow task identity to become entangled with particular scenes, embodiments, camera configurations, or trajectories~ xing2025shortcut . More data reduces this problem only when it introduces the relevant variation. Mechanistic studies find weak prompt control when visual appearance already determines the behavior and identify internal features associated with memorized trajectories~ grant2026not,swann2026sparse . These findings challenge the assumption that a successful VLA necessarily learns a compositional mapping from instruction and scene to action. The model may instead interpolate among visually indexed motor programs. Existing mitigations attempt to break shortcut correlations through broader data collection~ xing2025shortcut . Such interventions can be costly, benchmark-specific, and difficult to transfer. Removing shortcut-prone observation channels can also improve generalization~ zhao2025you , but permanently discarding an input removes information that other tasks may require. AC-VLA addresses visual shortcut reliance by selectively removing wrist-camera observations when the gripper is closed~ peng2026ac . DeLock takes an alternative approach of recovering the pretrained knowledge after fine-tuning using a contrastive prompt and steering~ huang2026breaking . We expand on prior analysis and investigate how the model's vision-language backbone impacts a policy's propensity to follow visual shortcuts. Rather than permanently removing information or requiring additional data, we develop a training modification which causes VLAs to avoid relying on visual shortcuts. Adversarial Representation Learning Domain-adversarial representation learning~ ganin2016domain is a general approach to make representations from different data sources indistinguishable to prevent models from improperly relying on them when making decisions. It relies on an auxiliary classifier to predict a selected attribute from a representation and reverses its gradient into the encoder~ ganin2016domain . The classifier learns to recover the attribute, while the encoder is trained to make that prediction difficult. This mechanism is commonly used to promote invariance to domains or nuisance variables, particularly in computer vision~ yang2024limits,feng2026rap , but has not yet been applied in related robotics settings. While making two sources of data completely indistinguishable can be very difficult, we find that continually shifting task-predictive visual representations during training can be sufficient to make the policy rely on the instruction rather than the visual shortcut. title: PCAsplat: Gaussian Splatting with Local PCA Regularization
summary: Gaussian splatting has emerged as a flexible representation for 3D reconstruction from posed images. However, existing methods are optimized primarily using rasterization-based losses, which supervise a splat only when it contributes to sampled camera rays. Gaussians that are occluded or contribute little to the sampled view therefore receive weak or no geometric gradients and may drift away from the underlying surface, producing undesired floaters. We introduce PCAsplat, a geometry-aware regularization framework for Gaussian splatting based on differentiable local principal component analysis (PCA). Our PCA regularizer acts directly on neighborhoods of Gaussian centers and can therefore update Gaussians that do not contribute to the current training view. We regularize the PCA eigenvalues to encourage Gaussians to move to the underlying surface with isotropic tangent-plane coverage. We also align each Gaussian normal with the PCA-estimated neighborhood normal to enforce consistent orientation. Experiments on DTU, Tanks and Temples, and NeRF Synthetic show that the splats produced by PCAsplat better approximate samples of the reference surface while substantially reducing undesired floaters. These surface-aligned splats enable downstream geometry-processing tasks, including point cloud segmentation, and direct Poisson reconstruction. Additionally, PCAsplat remains competitive under conventional novel view synthesis and mesh extraction tasks. Code will be released.

Introduction Gaussian splatting~ kerbl20233d is becoming the standard framework for novel view synthesis (NVS) and 3D reconstruction from images, offering a favorable trade-off between rendering quality, optimization speed, and interactive visualization. It represents a scene as a collection of anisotropic Gaussians with appearance attributes optimized via differentiable rendering. While Gaussian splatting is highly effective for NVS, Gaussians can be located far from the underlying surfaces, forming floaters both outside and inside objects (see , top-left). These floaters remain a challenge for using the learned representation directly in geometry-processing tasks such as segmentation and Poisson surface reconstruction. Methods such as 2DGS~ huang20242d , GOF~ yu2024gaussian , PGSR~ chen2024pgsr , and RaDe-GS~ zhang2026rade use losses based on rendered depth and normals to improve geometric reconstruction. However, these rendering-based losses supervise Gaussians through their contributions to sampled views. Gaussians that are occluded or contribute little to the view therefore receive weak or no geometric gradients from these losses and may drift away from the underlying surface, producing exterior and interior floaters. The learned representation may also contain oversized, diffuse, or poorly localized Gaussians. Although floaters may have little impact on training views, exterior ones can appear in novel views while interior ones may remain occluded, with both limiting the representation's use in downstream applications. Other approaches couple Gaussians to an auxiliary surface representation. GS-Pull~ zhang2024gspull pulls Gaussians onto the zero-level set of a learned neural signed distance function (SDF), while MILo~ guedon2025milo differentiably extracts a mesh from Gaussian parameters during training and enforces consistency between the mesh and the Gaussians. However, these approaches rely on an auxiliary representation that must also be optimized, and undesired floaters remain an issue. Overall, learning surface-aligned Gaussians suitable for downstream geometry processing remains a challenge. To address this problem, we introduce , a geometry-aware regularization framework for Gaussian splatting based on differentiable local principal component analysis (PCA). Our key idea is to regularize Gaussian neighborhoods directly in scene space through PCA statistics. This provides geometric supervision even to Gaussians that do not contribute to the current training view. For each Gaussian, we estimate a local 3D neighborhood and compute its covariance eigenspectrum to characterize local thickness and tangent-plane anisotropy. We use these statistics to encourage Gaussian centers to move toward the surface by reducing local thickness, while promoting isotropic tangent-plane coverage and aligning Gaussian normals with PCA-derived normals up to sign. Experiments on DTU, Tanks and Temples, and NeRF Synthetic show that achieves strong surface reconstruction results compared to current methods. It produces surface-aligned splats with fewer exterior and interior floaters ( , bottom-left and center), allowing for more accurate downstream geometry processing. yields substantially more accurate instance segmentation and more coherent object masks than current methods using the same segmentation pipeline ( , right). also remains competitive under conventional novel view synthesis and TSDF-based mesh extraction. In summary, our main contributions are: A differentiable local PCA framework for regularizing Gaussian neighborhoods directly in scene space, including Gaussians that do not contribute to the current training view. Geometric losses for learning surface-aligned Gaussians by moving them toward the surface, promoting isotropic coverage, and aligning their normals with PCA-normals. An evaluation of splats as surface samples, showing improved geometric accuracy and their use in downstream applications, including segmentation and Poisson reconstruction. Related Work Surface reconstruction from images is a long-standing problem in vision. Classical methods such as COLMAP~ schoenberger2016sfm combine structure from motion and multi-view stereo to recover camera poses and point clouds. Recently, feed-forward models such as VGGT~ wang2025vggt and VGGT- ~ wang2026vggtomega predict cameras, depth maps, and point clouds directly from unposed images. However, these methods lack a view-dependent appearance model for novel-view synthesis. In contrast, neural implicit methods jointly learn geometry and view-dependent appearance: VolSDF~ yariv2021volume , NeuS~ wang2021neus , and Neuralangelo~ li2023neuralangelo optimize neural SDFs for each scene through differentiable rendering. However, repeated neural-field evaluations along each ray make volume rendering computationally expensive. Gaussian splatting~ kerbl20233d enabled fast rasterization of explicit primitives but lacked geometry constraints. 2DGS~ huang20242d , Gaussian Surfels~ dai2024gaussiansurfels , and Quadratic Gaussian Splatting~ zhang2025quadraticgaussiansplattinghigh made splats surface-like through modified primitives or rendering formulations together with rendering losses to regularize geometric properties of the scene. SuGaR~ guedon2024sugar , GOF~ yu2024gaussian , and RaDe-GS~ zhang2026rade improve mesh extraction via surface alignment, opacity fields, or better depth rasterization. And, PGSR~ chen2024pgsr introduced multi-view consistency losses to further improve geometry. For mesh extraction, methods such as 2DGS, RaDe-GS, and PGSR fuse rendered depth maps using TSDF~ curless1996volumetric , which are based on ray-gaussian contributions. Consequently, accurate meshes do not necessarily imply surface-aligned Gaussian centers. Rendering-based geometric regularization augments photometric supervision with losses on rendered depth and normals, aiming to reduce undesired floaters. Mip-NeRF~360~ barron2022mip introduces a distortion loss that encourages rendering contributions to concentrate within a narrow interval along each ray, discouraging diffuse density and floaters. 2DGS and GOF adapt this loss to encourage surface alignment by reducing depth differences between contributing Gaussians along viewing rays. These differences are weighted by rendering contributions, which depend on opacity and accumulated transmittance. As such, Gaussians that are occluded or contribute little to a view may receive weak or no geometric gradients from these losses, allowing exterior and interior floaters to persist. complements this supervision with local PCA losses that act directly on 3D Gaussian neighborhoods, so Gaussians that do not contribute to the current training view can still receive geometric gradients. Hybrid Gaussian--surface representations couple Gaussians with auxiliary surface representations. GS-Pull~ zhang2024gspull pulls Gaussian centers onto the zero-level set of a neural SDF, at the additional computational cost of jointly optimizing this field. Its Gaussian-disk supervision addresses sparse, nonuniform support but remains sensitive to extreme sparsity. GSDF~ yu2024gsdf couples Gaussians and SDFs through depth and normal consistency, using Gaussian-rendered depth to guide SDF sampling and SDF values to control Gaussian growth and pruning. Gaussian-UDF~ li2025gaussianudf jointly learns 2D Gaussians and an unsigned distance field for open surfaces, using Gaussian centers and local planes to supervise distances. MILo~ guedon2025milo and GaussianWrapping (GW)~ gomez2026blobsspokeshighfidelitysurface differentiably extracts a mesh from Gaussian-derived pivots and learned signed distances, enforcing Gaussian--mesh rendering consistency. In contrast, we adapt local PCA, a classical method for estimating tangent planes and normals from point clouds~ hoppe1992surface,pauly2002efficient , to directly regularize Gaussian neighborhoods. We add losses for neighborhood thickness, tangent-plane coverage, and normal alignment to existing splatting objectives without learning auxiliary SDFs or extracting meshes during training.
