These results show that combining historical guidance with target-side behavioral validation can reduce the interaction cost of deploying frozen learned skills in new environments. Introduction sec:Introduction Learned visuomotor skills, including pretrained Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies, provide reusable manipulation capabilities and are increasingly composed in hierarchical systems for longer-horizon tasks~ kim2024openvla,huang2026roboharness,zhang2026harness,huang2022inner . However, a symbolically valid skill sequence is not necessarily physically executable, because the initiation configuration of an upstream skill affects both its own execution and the physical state handed to subsequent skills. An upstream skill may therefore succeed locally yet leave the system in a state from which the next skill cannot proceed; for example, successfully opening a drawer does not guarantee successful subsequent retrieval or placement. Thus, composing frozen learned skills requires determining not only which skill to invoke, but also from which initiation configuration it should be executed. Determining such initiation configurations in a new environment is challenging. Existing Task and Motion Planning (TAMP) methods primarily describe action applicability through geometric constraints and symbolic preconditions~ garrett2021integrated,garrett2020pddlstream , while learned precondition models estimate skill applicability from execution data~ liang2022learning,sharma2020relational . Recent memory-based methods further reuse historical execution experience to assist the invocation and composition of frozen policies~ huang2026roboharness,zhang2026harness . However, for a frozen black-box skill in a new environment, the reliability of different initiation configurations is generally unknown. Estimating target-specific capability through extensive rollouts requires substantial interaction, while directly reusing historical candidates may fail as environment geometry, visual appearance, and interaction conditions change. Historical experience is therefore useful as guidance, but insufficient as a decision criterion. This leads to the central question of this work: how can historical experience help discover reliable initiation configurations with fewer target interactions, while remaining robust to imperfect transfer? To address this problem, we propose EVIS, an Experience-Guided and Behavior-Validated Initiation Search framework. EVIS treats historical experience as a source of candidate proposals rather than final decisions. Historical execution records prioritize promising initiation configurations, while behavioral evidence from target-environment rollouts---i.e., observed outcomes under the intended execution objective---validates whether these candidates remain effective. This separates transfer from decision-making: history determines where to look first, whereas target-side outcomes determine whether a candidate should be trusted. When sufficient behavioral evidence supports a candidate, the search can terminate early; otherwise, it continues to seek alternatives. We evaluate EVIS in RoboCasa365~ nasiriany2026robocasa365 using a frozen pretrained VLA policy~ rldx2026 , on both single-skill and two-stage manipulation tasks. Two-stage composition provides the minimal setting that isolates inter-skill handoff effects: a single skill contains no handoff, whereas adding one downstream skill is sufficient to test whether an upstream initiation configuration leaves a physical state that supports subsequent execution. Across unseen environments, historical guidance improves early candidate discovery under small interaction budgets. Behavioral validation filters unreliable transferred candidates, while continued search recovers part of the coverage lost when transfer is rejected. Our contributions can be summarized as: We treat the initiation configuration as an explicit execution interface for task-level planning over frozen learned skills, and seek reliable configurations in new environments with as few costly target-environment rollouts as possible. We propose EVIS, an Experience-Guided and Behavior-Validated Initiation Search framework that uses historical execution experience to prioritize promising candidates, while target-environment rollouts determine whether a candidate should be accepted or the search should continue. We evaluate EVIS on RoboCasa365 environments using a frozen pretrained VLA policy. EVIS reduces target-environment interaction and improves reliable candidate discovery under small interaction budgets. Related Work sec:related_work Skill Applicability and Composition Skill applicability and composition have long been studied in hierarchical control and planning. The options framework formalizes skill initiation and termination~ sutton1999between , while skill chaining learns skills that reach the initiation sets of subsequent skills~ konidaris2009skill . In task and motion planning, PDDLStream integrates symbolic planning with black-box samplers for continuous feasibility constraints~ garrett2020pddlstream . Learned precondition models further estimate manipulation applicability from execution data using object relations~ sharma2020relational or point-cloud representations for contact-rich controllers~ liang2022learning . Unlike these approaches, which primarily model skill applicability or feasibility, EVIS searches for effective initiation configurations of frozen learned skills under limited target interaction, evaluating them by whether they support successful execution of the composed skill sequence. Policy Orchestration and Execution Memory Language-guided robotic systems connect high-level task reasoning with low-level execution in different ways. SayCan grounds skill selection in learned affordances~ ahn2022can , Inner Monologue incorporates online execution feedback into high-level planning~ huang2022inner , and Code as Policies composes perception and control interfaces through generated programs~ liang2023code . More recent execution-memory systems reuse past experience to organize and invoke frozen VLA primitives. HarnessVLA reuses task-specific execution traces and persistent execution memory to guide primitive composition across deployment variations~ zhang2026harness , while RoboHarness uses execution memory and online evidence for capability-aware policy routing and compatible skill handoffs~ huang2026roboharness . EVIS addresses a complementary problem: it transfers execution experience across environments specifically to guide the search over initiation configurations, while using a small number of target-environment rollouts to validate whether transferred candidates remain reliable. Experience-Guided Search and Candidate Discovery Historical information can accelerate expensive black-box search. Intelligent Trial and Error uses a precomputed behavior repertoire for rapid robot adaptation~ cully2015robots , Most Likely Expected Improvement combines prior likelihood with expected improvement for data-efficient direct policy search~ pautrat2018bayesian , and ranking-weighted Gaussian process ensembles transfer previous optimization runs by weighting historical models according to their agreement with target observations~ feurer2018scalable . Relatedly, threshold-based pure exploration in multi-armed bandits studies how to identify satisfactory candidates with limited samples: the thresholding bandit problem identifies arms whose expected rewards exceed a prescribed threshold under a fixed budget~ locatelli2016optimal , while good-arm identification (GAI) seeks such arms using as few samples as possible~ kano2019good , with recent work extending GAI to anytime and fixed-budget settings~ jourdan2026anytime . EVIS builds on these ideas for initiation search of frozen learned skills, using execution experience from previous environments to prioritize candidates and limited target-environment rollouts to validate whether transferred candidates remain reliable. title: RoboAware: Learning to Coordinate Embodied Skills from Counterfactual Outcomes
summary: Embodied coding agents can combine modular robot skills with frozen end-to-end policies, yet effective composition requires anticipating which policy family will succeed in the current physical state. We present RoboAware, which builds on coding agents' skill orchestration by learning only a state-conditioned responsibility coordinator from counterfactual outcomes. Inspired by the success of REPL, we propose the $P^5$ schema and formulate a hierarchical MDP based on it. $P^5$ organizes skills uniformly into five semantic stages, defining where responsibility can be compared. To address the lack of counterfactual branch outcomes in existing work, we introduce State-Locked Counterfactual Branching (SCB), which restores the same training state to generate and execute a code block from each admissible family, exposing outcomes that selected-branch experience leaves unobserved. Building on this, we propose Execution-Aware Learning (EAL), which combines Monte Carlo tree search with Q-learning to distill these outcomes into family-conditioned values. At deployment, the coordinator selects the policy family according to observable context, and the frozen coding agent generates the next local code block. Comprehensive single-episode evaluations on 100 tasks show that RoboAware reaches a 77.0% overall success rate, with SOTA averages of 90.0% on RoboSuite, 73.8% on diverse LIBERO-Pro task clusters, and 90.0% on challenging RoboTwin bimanual tasks, outperforming existing code-as-policy and VLA-harness baselines.
full_text: Introduction Performing general-purpose embodied manipulation in diverse and unstructured environments remains challenging in the absence of low-level executor adaptation. Recent progress toward this goal has followed two major paradigms, namely end-to-end policies and coding agents, each with distinct strengths and limitations. Within the end-to-end paradigm, task-specific visuomotor controllers excel at contact-rich control but typically lack native support for open-vocabulary rebinding~ ACT,DiffusionPolicy,DP3 . Vision-language-action (VLA) and world-action models (WAMs) support language-conditioned execution~ RT-1,RT-2,OpenVLA,pi0 , yet become unreliable under compositional and state-distribution shifts. Coding agents, by contrast, enable Code-as-Policy~ CaP,Cap-X,VoxPoser by flexibly composing program modules for long-horizon tasks. Their physical competence, however, is bounded by the exposed primitives, limiting fine-grained, closed-loop correction during contact-rich interactions. These complementary advantages inspire hybrid frameworks in which coding agents generate modular API compositions or invoke frozen end-to-end policies, most commonly VLAs, as contact-rich primitives~ HarnessVLA,HVLA,RoboHarness . Nevertheless, high-level coding agents lack inherent awareness of the divergent consequences of invoking different skill executors. They struggle to choose among an explicit modular composition, any available self-contained policy, and their possible switching patterns. For instance, modular execution can remain stable under task-distribution shift, whereas end-to-end execution excels in case of unexpected interruption. This raises a critical research question: How can we endow coding agents with outcome-aware execution responsibility over embodied skills? We address this question with , a framework that learns a responsibility boundary between modular composition and end-to-end execution from counterfactual outcomes. Here, a policy family is the sole high-level coordination action; the API library comprises typed APIs together with their bound low-level backends; responsibility denotes which family should control the next semantically meaningful skill transition. The first challenge is to define where responsibility can be compared. The space of low-level code generation is too expansive and unstructured to provide a tractable basis for responsibility assignment. Inspired by the success of REPL-style programming~ REPL-Plan , we propose the Skill Schema to address this limitation. The schema organizes embodied skills into semantically meaningful stages from perception to execution in 3D space. We formulate a finite-horizon hierarchical MDP that selects a policy family at each stage. At the lower level, we curate an API library combining typed modular interfaces for composability and controllability with end-to-end policies for contact-rich local execution. Conditioned on the selected family and current context, the frozen coding agent generates a complete local code block through the fixed API library. Learning is confined to the responsibility coordinator, while skill implementation leverages the coding agent's existing code-generation capability. The second challenge is to expose the missing outcome of the skills that were not selected. Many approaches execute open-loop skill sequences or code programs without attending to outcomes~ CaP,ProgPrompt,VoxPoser . Methods that obtain outcomes typically rely on VLM-based evaluations limited to the predicted outcome of the executed trajectory, and therefore inherit selection bias~ RoboHarness,VLAProbe . We introduce State-Locked Counterfactual Branching ( ) , which leverages simulator (1) save-restore mechanisms and (2) oracle outcome judgments to execute every admissible family from an identical physical state, producing a same-state set of potential outcomes at each decision point. To convert these set-wise outcomes into deployable family selection, we formulate Execution-Aware Learning ( ) , in which Monte Carlo tree search (MCTS) treats restorable decision states as nodes and admissible policy families as edges, while Q-learning distills the explored outcomes into a family-conditioned value function . The family-wise values encode a relative responsibility preference over modular composition and the end-to-end family, reflecting expected remaining skill- and task-level return under an observation. During deployment, the coordinator assigns responsibility by maximizing induced by , and a coding agent generates executable code blocks accordingly to transition from one state to the next, without state restoration or privileged simulator state. We curate its lower-level API library around two complementary families, namely composable modular components and end-to-end policies for contact-rich local skills. We introduce to acquire paired locked-state outcomes, and to learn family-conditioned through MCTS-guided exploration and Q-learning. We recover the coordinator from and evaluate it on 100 tasks across three benchmarks, obtaining a SOTA 77.0 overall success rate. Ablations confirm the effectiveness of our designs. title: DAMP: Humanoid Locomotion via Denoised Belief Learning and Adversarial Motion Priors
summary: Humanoid robots possess the structural capability to traverse complex terrains. However, achieving stable t raversal without relying on perceived information remains challenging, particularly in complex environments. This paper introduces DAMP, a reinforcement learning framework aimed at achieving robust and naturalistic humanoid locomotion over challenging terrains, with the assumption that no perceived information is available. The framework leverages recurrent neural networks to capture temporal dependencies and implicitly infer privileged and other task-relevant latent information. By aligning the learned representations with the task objective, the method enables robust and goal-consistent policy learning. This end-to-end framework achieves transfer learning from simulation to real-world environments, demonstrating the proposed method's robustness and generalization capabilities. The video of the real-world demonstration can be found at the following link: https://youtu.be/AkI7TZB2DDM.
full_text: Humanoid robots possess the structural capability to traverse complex terrains. However, achieving stable t raversal without relying on perceived information remains challenging, particularly in complex environments. This paper introduces DAMP, a reinforcement learning framework aimed at achieving robust and naturalistic humanoid locomotion over challenging terrains, with the assumption that no perceived information is available. The framework leverages recurrent neural networks to capture temporal dependencies and implicitly infer privileged and other task-relevant latent information. By aligning the learned representations with the task objective, the method enables robust and goal-consistent policy learning. This end-to-end framework achieves transfer learning from simulation to real-world environments, demonstrating the proposed method's robustness and generalization capabilities. The video of the real-world demonstration can be found at the following link: https://youtu.be/AkI7TZB2DDM. INTRODUCTION Humanoid robots face significant challenges when traversing complex terrains such as stairs, uneven surfaces, and obstacles. Compared with quadrupeds, humanoids exhibit a higher center of mass, greater degrees of freedom, and more complex kinematic structures, which collectively compromise stability and robustness in challenging environments. Traditional model-based control strategies, including zero-moment point control (ZMP) kajita2003biped , model predictive control (MPC) wieber2006trajectory , and whole-body control (WBC) sentis2006whole , have demonstrated effective gait generation for humanoid locomotion. However, these approaches rely heavily on accurate modeling of environmental dynamics, limiting their applicability in scenarios involving complex terrain interactions such as obstacle traversal ramuzat2022benchmarking . Reinforcement learning (RL) provides a model-agnostic alternative that improves adaptability to unknown or dynamically changing environments. Representative frameworks, such as the Hybrid Internal Model (HIM) long2024hybrid and DreamWaQ Made2023DreamWaQLR , have shown strong performance in quadrupedal locomotion and can be transferred to humanoids. Estimator-based RL methods long2024hybrid,Made2023DreamWaQLR,kumar2021rma have successfully reduced the sim-to-real gap and enabled traversal over diverse terrains. These pipelines were later extended to humanoids huang2025think,wang2024toward,cui2024adapting , providing basic terrain-crossing capabilities. Nevertheless, purely task-driven RL often struggles to generate natural and energy-efficient motions, particularly under sparse contact events or complex terrain transitions, and still fails on high-difficulty terrains such as 10 cm continuous steps or 20 cm railings. To address these limitations, subsequent work incorporated exteroceptive sensing, such as depth cameras and LiDAR. Methods like Perceptive Internal Model long2025learning and Humanoid Parkour zhuang2024humanoid enable traversal of sparse high obstacles. However, these approaches introduce additional computational overhead and are susceptible to sensor drift, limiting long-term autonomous deployment. In parallel, imitation learning (IL) has been explored to improve motion naturalness. Methods such as adversarial motion prior (AMP) can produce smooth and human-like behaviors, but they depend on high-quality demonstration data and often exhibit limited generalization. Huang et al. huang2025think combined HIM with AMP, achieving improved stylistic locomotion performance. Humanoid imitation learning has further evolved through motion imitation with style priors, generative modeling, teleoperation, and multimodal feedback. Early work such as DeepMimic peng2018deepmimic and its extensions won2020scalable relied on dense motion tracking rewards to reproduce high-fidelity skills. AMP peng2021amp introduced style discriminators to jointly optimize motion realism and task objectives. More recently, generative approaches such as BeyondMimic liao2025beyondmimic leveraged diffusion models to translate human demonstrations into diverse robotic behaviors. Wen et al. wen2025constrained further integrated elevation maps into AMP to enable perception-based locomotion in simulation. The Denoising World Model Gu-RSS-24 , proposed by Gu et al., combines a recurrent neural network (RNN) with a denoising mechanism for observation data, enhancing the robustness of the model by mitigating noise in the input information. However, strategies relying on gait rewards still face certain difficulties in continuous obstacle crossing. Inspired by these findings, we propose Denoised Belief Learning with Adversarial Motion Priors (DAMP), a framework for stable and task-compliant humanoid locomotion with enhanced motion naturalness. DAMP adopts a LSTM-based encoder–decoder architecture to implicitly infer latent and privileged information. During training, adversarial imitation learning and dynamic reward interpolation are jointly employed to enhance locomotion performance on challenging terrains. The entire pipeline is trained in a single-stage, end-to-end manner, resulting in a hardware-deployable policy. We deploy DAMP on the Noetix N2 noetixrobotics2025products humanoid robot and validate its effectiveness through extensive real-world experiments over complex terrains, demonstrating smooth, robust, and natural locomotion. METHOD This paper proposes a single-stage end-to-end learning framework that directly generates desired joint position commands from onboard proprioceptive observations using a recurrent neural network (RNN). title: WARP-VLA: Wrist-Camera Adaptation for View-Robust Policy Execution in Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Despite recent advances in Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) for robotic manipulation, their performance remains sensitive to changes in camera configuration. The problem becomes more evident in cross-setup deployment, as reproducing the exact camera pose used for training is nearly impossible. Unlike fixed external views, wrist views are more challenging because the camera moves with the robot, causing even small mounting variations to alter fine-grained geometric cues. To address this, we propose WARP-VLA, a camera-view robust VLA for diverse wrist camera configurations. WARP-VLA adopts a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture where individual experts learn view-specific feature transformations, and a router combines them based on implicit view information. This allows the policy to be deployed without requiring camera extrinsic parameters as additional input. Through experiments on the LIBERO benchmark, WARP-VLA improves the average success rate of pi-0.5 from 39.2% to 78.3% under wrist-view perturbations. The real-robot experiments further show that the feature-level adaptation learned in simulation successfully transfers to diverse deployment settings. To facilitate reproducibility and future research, we release our wrist viewpoint robustness benchmark and a plug-and-play implementation.
full_text: Overview of WARP-VLA. (a) Changes in wrist-camera configuration alter interaction-relevant visual cues and degrade VLA performance. (b) Existing methods rely on novel view synthesis or explicit camera geometry to handle viewpoint changes. (c) Our method, WARP-VLA, aligns perturbed wrist camera features with the canonical feature space through an anchor-guided mixture of experts, enabling calibration-free and plug-and-play adaptation at deployment without further policy fine-tuning. INTRODUCTION Recent advancements in Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) have shown promising performance across various manipulation tasks~ rt22023arxiv,kim2024openvla,pmlr-v305-black25a,bjorck2025gr00t,kim2025fine,shukor2025smolvla,pmlr-v305-wen25b,team2025gemini,li2024cogact . However, VLAs often fail to maintain their performance when deployed on real robots due to discrepancies between training and deployment environments. Variations in camera configuration are particularly critical since visual observations directly determine the actions generated by VLAs. In practice, reproducing the exact camera configuration during deployment is difficult because many robot datasets do not provide camera calibration information, including camera extrinsics and focal lengths. Even when such information is available, physical factors such as mounting tolerances and robot vibrations can introduce additional viewpoint changes during execution. This problem is especially pronounced for wrist cameras, which provide fine-grained visual information required for precise manipulation~ jangir2022look,pmlr-v164-valassakis22a . Unlike external cameras that observe the workspace from fixed viewpoints, wrist cameras capture close-range views of the interaction region. Consequently, even small variations in wrist-camera configurations can alter interaction-relevant visual information, such as the spatial relationship between the gripper and objects, as depicted in~ (a). Furthermore, reproducing the original camera configuration is more difficult for wrist cameras because their mounting arrangements vary across robot and camera hardware. Together, these challenges highlight the need for robustness to wrist-camera variations to ensure reliable deployment of VLA policies. Prior work has explored improving VLA robustness to camera variations, primarily focusing on external cameras. Extending these approaches to wrist cameras is a natural starting point. As shown in~ (b), these methods typically address viewpoint changes by incorporating camera geometry or synthesizing observations from target viewpoints. For example, camera-conditioned methods encode camera poses through Pl\"ucker ray embeddings~ jiang2026knowyourcamera , while view synthesis approaches generate observations from the viewpoints used during policy training~ heo2026anycamvla . However, such approaches require accurate camera calibration or additional camera-specific models, which limits their applicability when the original wrist-camera configuration is unavailable. For wrist cameras, inaccurate calibration can also compromise the geometry-based conditioning or view synthesis used to interpret close-range interactions. To this end, we introduce Wrist-camera Adaptation for view-Robust Policy (WARP-VLA), a view-invariant VLA framework that implicitly learns and adapts diverse wrist camera view features through a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture, as illustrated in~ (c). WARP-VLA uses multiple experts to represent each camera-dependent transformation in wrist camera features observed during training. In a new camera setting, the framework combines nearby view experts through feature-conditioned routing weights, enabling smooth adaptation across view variations. Since WARP-VLA performs adaptation at the feature level, it provides a plug-and-play module applicable to other VLA policies trained in different simulation environments. This allows VLA policies to handle diverse wrist views in real-world deployment without additional policy fine-tuning. To evaluate robustness to wrist-camera perturbations, we adapt the LIBERO~ liu2023libero and LIBERO-Plus~ fei25libero benchmarks to introduce a comprehensive wrist-view evaluation protocol covering diverse camera configurations. Through extensive experiments in simulation and on real robots, we demonstrate that WARP-VLA achieves strong robustness across diverse wrist-camera configurations while preserving performance under the original camera setup. Specifically, WARP-VLA generalizes across representative VLA backbones such as without requiring policy-specific modifications. Notably, applying WARP-VLA to improves the average success rate under wrist-camera perturbations from 39.2 to 78.3 . Furthermore, as shown in the real-world deployment results in~ (d), the baseline struggles to locate the object for grasping when the camera position changes, whereas WARP-VLA successfully grasps the object. Our contributions are threefold: We introduce a systematic benchmark for evaluating VLA robustness to wrist-camera variations, including a view-augmented dataset constructed from the LIBERO benchmark with diverse wrist-camera configurations. We propose WARP-VLA, a feature adaptation framework based on an MoE architecture that learns view-specific transformations and combines them through feature-conditioned routing without camera calibration. We demonstrate robust performance across diverse wrist-camera configurations and compatibility with different VLA backbones through extensive experiments in simulation and on real robots. RELATED WORK View-Invariant VLAs Recent VLAs train a single policy on large-scale datasets to improve generalization across tasks and robot embodiments~ rt22023arxiv,kim2024openvla,bjorck2025gr00t,rt12022arxiv,octo_2023,black2024pi . Nevertheless, such policies assume similar settings during training and deployment, leaving them sensitive to different camera configurations. The fundamental challenge is that camera viewpoint changes alter not only visual appearance but also the geometric correspondence between observations and actions. A straightforward approach to improving viewpoint robustness is to expose policies to diverse camera views during training. VISTA~ tian2024vista and RoVi-Aug~ chen2024roviaug expand viewpoint coverage through synthesized demonstrations, reducing the need to collect additional demonstrations from different camera positions. These methods reduce multi-view data collection but leave policies to infer geometry from augmented observations. To provide explicit geometric cues, KYC~ jiang2026knowyourcamera conditions policies on camera parameters, and StereoVLA~ deng2025stereovla incorporates stereo cues. OC-VLA~ zhang2026grounding and CamVLA~ li2026fixed further simplify visual-action correspondence by predicting camera-frame actions and converting them into robot-frame commands. However, limited training-view coverage remains a challenge. To avoid policy retraining, AnyCamVLA~ heo2026anycamvla instead uses novel view synthesis (NVS) to transform test-time observations into the policy's training viewpoints. This allows a frozen policy to handle camera changes without additional demonstrations or policy fine-tuning, but the NVS model still requires fine-tuning on multi-view images for the simulation domain. Geometry-Aware VLAs Incorporating geometric priors has been demonstrated to be an effective approach to improving VLA robustness to viewpoint changes. Explicit-geometry methods, including SpatialVLA~ qu2025spatialvla , GeoVLA~ sun2025geovla , PointVLA~ li2026pointvla , and Any3D-VLA~ fan2026any3d , introduce depth or point-cloud representations into the policy. However, making these cues useful also requires effective integration with action prediction ~ yang2026understanding . GeoAware-VLA~ abouzeid2025geoaware , G VLA~ peng2026g , and GAM~ han2026geometric incorporate geometric priors into visual encoding, cross-view fusion, or action decoding. To retain geometric knowledge without additional inference modules, Spatial Forcing~ li2026spatial instead aligns VLA features with geometric representations during training. These approaches make spatial information more accessible to the policy, while adapting perturbed wrist features to the canonical representations of a frozen VLA remains a distinct objective. title: VGGTWorld-VLA: Intent-Conditioned 3D World Evolution for Autonomous Driving
summary: VGGT provides a strong foundation for geometry-centric world models by recovering unified 3D scene geometry from visual observations. Although recent extensions enable temporal 3D prediction, their future evolution remains weakly conditioned on driving intentions and actions, limiting their ability to model alternative action-dependent futures. We propose VGGTWorld-VLA, an intention-conditioned extension of VGGT-World for controllable 3D world evolution in autonomous driving. First, we introduce an action--semantic conditioning mechanism that injects complementary driving semantics and ego-motion representations into the future-token stream, enabling different future geometry predictions for the same observed scene under alternative ego actions. Second, we develop a geometry--language--action bridge that adapts historical geometry, VLA semantic features, and maneuver and trajectory representations for joint conditioning of future geometry prediction. We evaluate future geometry prediction on NAVSIM, while conditioning ablations further examine the contributions of semantic and action information. Compared with the baseline, our method demonstrates competitive geometry prediction performance. Ablation studies further support the effectiveness of semantic and action conditioning. These results demonstrate the potential of semantic and action conditioning for controllable VGGT-based world prediction in autonomous driving.
full_text: VGGT provides a strong foundation for geometry-centric world models by recovering unified 3D scene geometry from visual observations. Although recent extensions enable temporal 3D prediction, their future evolution remains weakly conditioned on driving intentions and actions, limiting their ability to model alternative action-dependent futures. We propose VGGTWorld-VLA, an intention-conditioned extension of VGGT-World for controllable 3D world evolution in autonomous driving. First, we introduce an action--semantic conditioning mechanism that injects complementary driving semantics and ego-motion representations into the future-token stream, enabling different future geometry predictions for the same observed scene under alternative ego actions. Second, we develop a geometry--language--action bridge that adapts historical geometry, VLA semantic features, and maneuver and trajectory representations for joint conditioning of future geometry prediction. We evaluate future geometry prediction on NAVSIM, while conditioning ablations further examine the contributions of semantic and action information. Compared with the baseline, our method demonstrates competitive geometry prediction performance. Ablation studies further support the effectiveness of semantic and action conditioning. These results demonstrate the potential of semantic and action conditioning for controllable VGGT-based world prediction in autonomous driving. Introduction Recovering 3D scene geometry from visual observations is fundamental to autonomous driving, where decisions depend on depth, spatial structure, and scene motion~ zuo2026dvgt . Visual Geometry Grounded Transformer (VGGT)~ wang2025vggt unifies camera estimation, depth prediction, point-map reconstruction, and point tracking in a feed-forward model. Its strong generalization and unified geometry tokens provide a promising foundation for representing driving scenes. More importantly, these representations can potentially support not only reconstruction of the observed scene, but also prediction of its future 3D evolution~ sun2026vggtworld . Following VGGT, several studies have adapted geometry foundation models to autonomous driving. DriveVGGT~ jia2025drivevggt and DVGT~ zuo2026dvgt improve metric reconstruction for multi-camera driving scenes, while DynamicVGGT~ he2026dynamicvggt extends geometry estimation to dynamic 4D reconstruction. VGGDrive ~ wang2026vggdrive injects VGGT features into a driving VLM, and DVGT-2~ zuo2026dvgt2 jointly models dense geometry and trajectory planning. These developments highlight the potential of VGGT-based representations for driving scene understanding, providing a foundation for extending geometry reconstruction toward future world prediction. VGGT-World~ sun2026vggtworld extends VGGT from static reconstruction to temporal world modeling by predicting the evolution of frozen geometry tokens with an autoregressive flow transformer, enabling efficient and geometrically consistent future 3D prediction. Nevertheless, its future evolution is primarily determined by historical observations and is not explicitly conditioned on driving intentions or actions~ sun2026vggtworld . It therefore cannot adequately distinguish the different physical futures induced by alternative behaviors, such as lane keeping, lane changing, or yielding. Existing geometry-aware driving models, including VGGDrive and DVGT-2, mainly use current geometry for planning rather than evaluating actions through their future 3D consequences~ wang2026vggdrive,zuo2026dvgt2 . High-level semantic representations can provide the missing driving intent, but directly integrating them with VGGT-World is non-trivial because semantic, action, and geometry tokens occupy different representation spaces. The central problem addressed in this work is therefore how to condition geometry-native world evolution on driving semantics and actions, enabling future 3D predictions to explicitly reflect the physical consequences of driving decisions. As illustrated in Fig.~ fig:motivation , the same observation can lead to different future viewpoints and 3D observations under different ego actions. Without explicit action conditioning, the predicted future may therefore be inconsistent with the intended driving behavior. To address this problem, we propose VGGTWorld-VLA, a VGGT-native world-action modeling framework for autonomous driving. We use VLA-derived semantic representations together with ego-action conditions to guide geometry-native world evolution. First, an action--semantic 3D world evolution module injects driving semantics and action representations into the future branch of VGGT-World, enabling the predicted 3D geometry to reflect action-dependent geometric changes. Second, a geometry--language--action bridge adapts semantic, action, and geometry representations for joint conditioning of future geometry prediction. In this way, the proposed framework connects driving context and intended ego motion with future 3D prediction while preserving VGGT-World as the primary world-modeling backbone. We evaluate VGGTWorld-VLA on NAVSIM~ dauner2024navsim for future geometry and depth prediction. Compared with VGGT-World, our method reduces depth RMSE by 13.7 and improves by 4.11 percentage points, while AbsRel remains comparable with a modest increase. Ablation studies further examine the contributions of action representations and semantic conditioning, while action-input interventions demonstrate the model's use of scene-aligned action information. Our contributions are summarized as follows: We extend VGGT-World with semantic and action conditions, enabling controllable future 3D world evolution. We introduce a geometry--language--action bridge that adapts driving semantics, multi-representation ego actions, and geometry features for joint conditioning of future geometry prediction. Experiments on NAVSIM demonstrate improved latent prediction quality and future-depth RMSE and threshold accuracy, including 13.7 lower RMSE relative to VGGT-World, supported by ablation studies and controlled action-input interventions. Related Work VGGT for Autonomous Driving. Visual Geometry Grounded Transformer (VGGT)~ wang2025vggt unifies camera estimation, depth prediction, point-map reconstruction, and point tracking within a feed-forward architecture, providing a general geometric representation of visual scenes. Its strong generalization has motivated several extensions for autonomous driving. DriveVGGT~ jia2025drivevggt introduces calibration constraints and cross-camera consistency for metric multi-camera reconstruction, while DVGT~ zuo2026dvgt recovers globally aligned driving geometry from unposed multi-view images. DynamicVGGT~ he2026dynamicvggt further models point-level motion for dynamic 4D reconstruction. Beyond perception, VGGDrive~ wang2026vggdrive injects VGGT features into a driving vision-language model, and DVGT-2~ zuo2026dvgt2 jointly predicts dense geometry and ego trajectories. These studies demonstrate the value of VGGT representations for driving perception and planning, but mainly reconstruct observed scenes or directly use current geometry for action generation, without explicitly reasoning about the action-dependent evolution of the future 3D world. World-Action Models. World models predict future states from historical observations, while world-action models further condition this evolution on agent actions, enabling alternative futures to be evaluated before execution~ wang2024drivewm,gao2024vista,li2025wote . VGGT-World~ sun2026vggtworld establishes a direct connection between geometry foundation models and world modeling by predicting the temporal evolution of frozen VGGT tokens rather than future RGB frames. This geometry-native formulation offers an efficient representation of future depth and 3D structure, but its prediction remains primarily observation driven. Meanwhile, recent driving models such as DriveVLA-W0~ li2025drivevlaw0 , CoWorld-VLA~ huang2026coworldvla , and WCog-VLA~ yan2026wcogvla incorporate future images, world tokens, or agent evolution into action learning. These studies highlight the connection between future world modeling and action learning~ li2025law,zheng2025world4drive . Our work focuses on conditioning VGGT-native future geometry prediction on ego actions and driving semantics, with an emphasis on controllable 3D world evolution. Vision-Language-Action Models. Vision-language-action models introduce semantic knowledge and high-level reasoning into autonomous-driving policies~ pan2024vlp,xu2025drivegpt4v2 . Early studies such as DriveLM~ sima2024drivelm , LMDrive~ shao2024lmdrive , and DriveVLM~ tian2024drivevlm connect visual understanding and language reasoning with driving decisions. More recent methods, including SimLingo~ renz2025simlingo , OpenDriveVLA~ zhou2025opendrivevla , AutoVLA~ zhou2026autovla , and DiffVLA~ jiang2025diffvla , strengthen language--action alignment, adaptive reasoning, and continuous trajectory generation. Although these models exhibit strong semantic reasoning and planning capabilities, most operate on image or latent visual representations and lack an explicit mechanism for predicting how different intentions and actions alter future 3D geometry. In contrast, our VGGTWorld-VLA uses VLA-derived semantic representations together with given ego-action conditions to control VGGT-based world evolution, connecting semantic reasoning and action-conditioned future 3D prediction within a unified geometry-native framework. Method sec:method Figure~ fig:framework shows VGGTWorld-VLA, which predicts future VGGT geometry tokens conditioned on historical geometry, ego actions, and driving semantics. A geometry--language--action bridge connects geometry features from two historical frames, action representations from a given trajectory and its maneuver descriptor, and semantic features from multi-camera observations and a textual prompt. The predicted tokens are decoded into future depth and 3D geometry using the pretrained VGGT decoder~ wang2025vggt . Real future images provide supervision and evaluation targets only. World prediction is the primary task, with auxiliary trajectory supervision during joint fine-tuning. The three branches retain their distinct information sources: geometry describes the observed scene, action specifies ego motion, and semantic features provide complementary scene context. title: Acting from Belief, Looking When Needed: A Bayesian Spatial World Model for Navigation under Intermittent Perception
summary: Robot navigation commonly uses wide-coverage, high-frequency sensing to reduce partial observability; this reliance becomes restrictive when another task temporarily redirects a shared sensor from navigation, interrupting navigation-relevant observations. We study navigation under intermittent perception: acting from an internal spatial belief and looking again only when execution needs a new observation, potentially freeing the shared sensor for other tasks between navigation observations. ALONE, a Bayesian spatial world model, propagates a structured spatial belief using executed actions and corrects it with selectively acquired observations; learned priors over common geometric structures infer unobserved structure from available observation history. It decodes the belief into a spatial estimate for the motion-planning module and predicts a reliability map expressing confidence in the estimate's accuracy. ALONE requests an observation only if insufficient reliability hinders navigation and new evidence should make relevant-region spatial information more reliable; otherwise, it continues acting from the propagated belief. We instantiate ALONE for drone navigation with intermittent single-camera depth images. Across two simulated scene families, it achieves 98% and 97% closed-loop success at a 10 Hz decision rate. Among successful trials, median fractions of decision steps requiring a new depth observation are only 0.9% and 1.3%, respectively, demonstrating high navigation success with substantially reduced observation demand. Real-world indoor flight experiments further validate navigation under intermittent depth observations, with all 10 trials successful.
full_text: Robot navigation commonly uses wide-coverage, high-frequency sensing to reduce partial observability; this reliance becomes restrictive when another task temporarily redirects a shared sensor from navigation, interrupting navigation-relevant observations. We study navigation under intermittent perception: acting from an internal spatial belief and looking again only when execution needs a new observation, potentially freeing the shared sensor for other tasks between navigation observations. It decodes the belief into a spatial estimate for the motion-planning module and predicts a reliability map expressing confidence in the estimate's accuracy. ALONE requests an observation only if insufficient reliability hinders navigation and new evidence should make relevant-region spatial information more reliable; otherwise, it continues acting from the propagated belief. We instantiate ALONE for drone navigation with intermittent single-camera depth images. Across two simulated scene families, it achieves 98 and 97 closed-loop success at a 10 Hz decision rate. Among successful trials, median fractions of decision steps requiring a new depth observation are only 0.9 and 1.3 , respectively, demonstrating high navigation success with substantially reduced observation demand. Real-world indoor flight experiments further validate navigation under intermittent depth observations, with all 10 trials successful. Introduction introduction Most robot navigation systems treat perception as an always-on service. To reduce partial observability, they enlarge sensing coverage, observe at high frequency, fuse multiple sensors, and continually update a local map or state estimate~ elfes1989occupancy,hornung2013octomap,mirchev2021variational,mirchev2023prism . This perception-first strategy is effective, but assumes that sensing can remain continuously directed toward navigation. The assumption becomes restrictive when another task redirects a shared sensor, interrupting navigation-relevant observations. Humans provide a familiar counterexample. A person can continue walking while visual attention briefly shifts to another task, relying on recent observations, self-motion, and priors to maintain an internal understanding of the surroundings. Such natural gaze behavior is task-dependent and is directed toward the information needed for ongoing action~ land2006eye,hayhoe2005eye . How long this understanding remains useful depends on environmental predictability. A corridor supports predictable continuation and thus longer observation-free motion, whereas irregular forest geometry leaves upcoming obstacles weakly constrained. These priors support inference between observations; perception returns when reliability is insufficient for the next action. This observation motivates navigation under intermittent perception: can a robot act from an internal spatial belief and look again only when execution requires new evidence? To this end, the robot must infer current spatial structure from partial action--observation history, preserve alternatives not resolved by available evidence, and determine where its estimate is accurate enough for the motion-planning module's current query. The observation policy should request new evidence only when insufficient reliability hinders navigation and an observation is expected to improve the relevant region. Existing methods provide individual pieces of this capability. Mapping and spatial memory preserve acquired evidence~ elfes1989occupancy,hornung2013octomap,mirchev2021variational,mirchev2023prism,kayalibay2022tracking,parisotto2017neuralmap,chaplot2020neural,liu2024volumetric,wang2023esceme,chen2025mapnav ; learned world models propagate latent states and predict hidden or future structure~ lecun2022path,hafner2019planet,hafner2025dreamerv3,bar2025nwm,assran2025vjepa2,zhou2025persistent,zheng2024occworld ; and belief-space planning or active perception adapts motion and sensing to uncertainty~ platt2010belief,atanasov2014information,vandenberg2011lqgmp,bajcsy1988active . They do not by themselves provide one learned spatial belief that is propagated between observations, decoded into a spatial estimate and reliability map, and corrected by requested evidence. Prediction, action, and observation therefore remain separate rather than forming a closed loop. We call the resulting framework ALONE, reflecting its two operating modes: Acting from belief while perception is suspended and Looking Only when Needed for Execution. At its core, a decision-queryable Bayesian spatial world model maintains a structured spatial belief. Its action-conditioned prior performs learned spatial completion: learned geometric priors infer unobserved structure from the partial action--observation history. An observation-conditioned posterior corrects this completion when evidence returns. The belief yields a spatial estimate for the motion-planning module and a reliability map indicating confidence in its accuracy at each queried location. We term this probability query-space reliability. ALONE requests an observation only when insufficient reliability restricts navigation and the relevant region is expected to be visible; otherwise, it acts from the maintained belief. We instantiate ALONE for drone navigation using intermittent depth images from a single camera and a vector-quantized occupancy representation. ALONE preserves high navigation success while reducing observation demand by up to two orders of magnitude. Open-loop and ablation experiments further validate spatial-belief prediction and correction, learned spatial completion, query-space reliability, and the observation policy. Contributions. Our contributions are threefold: (1) a Bayesian spatial world model that maintains a structured spatial belief through action-conditioned propagation and observation-conditioned correction, using learned geometric priors to infer unobserved structure and providing a spatial estimate together with an explicitly supervised reliability map for planning; (2) a navigation policy that uses spatial reliability to select motion actions and determine when new observations are needed, allowing the robot to continue acting from its belief between observations; and (3) an implementation for drone navigation using a single depth camera, evaluated through open-loop spatial inference, closed-loop navigation comparisons, and real-world flight experiments. The results demonstrate high navigation success with substantially reduced observation demand. Related Work related_work Spatial Mapping and Memory Occupancy mapping integrates measurements into persistent free-space and occupancy estimates~ elfes1989occupancy,hornung2013octomap , while probabilistic spatial models jointly estimate maps and agent states~ mirchev2021variational,mirchev2023prism,kayalibay2022tracking . Neural, topological, volumetric, episodic, and semantic memories encode task-relevant spatial structure~ parisotto2017neuralmap,chaplot2020neural,liu2024volumetric,wang2023esceme,chen2025mapnav . These approaches primarily organize acquired evidence rather than propagate unresolved spatial hypotheses through observation-free motion or assess whether the resulting local structure supports a motion-planning query. ALONE instead propagates a learned categorical spatial belief with executed actions and corrects it with later observations. Predictive World Models Latent world models learn action-conditioned dynamics for planning and behavior learning~ hafner2019planet,hafner2025dreamerv3 . Recent work extends prediction to navigation, visual representations, persistent 3D scenes, and occupancy forecasting~ bar2025nwm,assran2025vjepa2,zhou2025persistent,zheng2024occworld . Yet prediction alone does not establish whether a spatial estimate reliably supports current action selection. ALONE uses learned geometric priors to infer unobserved structure and predicts a reliability map for the estimate, so the same belief supports both action selection and observation decisions. Uncertainty-Aware Planning and Active Perception Belief-space planning incorporates state uncertainty into trajectory optimization~ platt2010belief,vandenberg2011lqgmp , while active perception selects sensing actions or viewpoints using information gain or task-relevant uncertainty~ atanasov2014information,bajcsy1988active . These methods commonly assume that a suitable belief or uncertainty estimate is available. ALONE instead learns, propagates, queries, and corrects the spatial belief underlying its observation decision. It requests an observation when insufficient reliability restricts navigation and the responsible region is expected to be visible; the returned evidence corrects the maintained belief, closing the loop among prediction, action, observation, and correction. Without a navigation observation, it propagates the belief with the executed action; the motion-planning module generates candidates from the decoded estimate, and the navigation policy selects one to execute. When insufficient reliability restricts navigation and new evidence is expected to resolve the relevant region, ALONE resumes perception and corrects the belief before the next decision. Observation intervals thus adapt to environmental predictability and decision-relevant uncertainty. We next formulate this setting, describe belief prediction and correction, and define the navigation policy. Navigation under Intermittent Perception sec:problem_formulation We consider navigation in a partially observable environment where another task may redirect a shared sensor. title: Environmental Feedback Modeling Matters: Rethinking Feedback Treatment in Agentic Hindsight Self-Distillation
summary: Reinforcement learning is commonly used to train language agents in interactive environments, but cannot be directly applied when rewards are unavailable. Recent methods use environmental feedback as privileged context for hindsight self-distillation, but our analysis suggests that simply conditioning the teacher on feedback is insufficient, motivating us to rethink how environmental feedback is used in agentic self-distillation. Given that environmental feedback contains rich supervision for modeling how the environment responds to agent actions, we introduce \textit{agentic SElf-distilLation with environmental Feedback modeling} (SELF), a framework that jointly optimizes environmental feedback modeling and hindsight self-distillation. SELF learns to predict environmental responses while distilling guidance from a feedback-conditioned self-teacher into the policy. Our analysis reveals a mutually reinforcing mechanism: environmental feedback modeling strengthens hindsight supervision and policy learning, while self-distillation enhances the model's ability to model environmental feedback. With Qwen3-8B, SELF outperforms SDPO and GRPO by 6.4 and 4.1 percentage points in $τ$-bench success rate, and by 10.71 and 3.57 percentage points in AppWorld task goal completion, respectively. These results show that SELF uses environmental feedback more effectively within agentic self-distillation, improving agent capabilities.

SELF learns to predict environmental responses while distilling guidance from a feedback-conditioned self-teacher into the policy. Our analysis reveals a mutually reinforcing mechanism: environmental feedback modeling strengthens hindsight supervision and policy learning, while self-distillation enhances the model's ability to model environmental feedback. With Qwen3-8B, SELF outperforms SDPO and GRPO by 6.4 and 4.1 percentage points in -bench success rate, and by 10.71 and 3.57 percentage points in AppWorld task goal completion, respectively. These results show that SELF uses environmental feedback more effectively within agentic self-distillation, improving agent capabilities. Introduction In recent years, training language agents to solve complex tasks in interactive environments involving tool use and code execution has become increasingly important~ yao2023react,trivedi2024appworld,choudhury2025better . A common training approach is Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR)~ lambert2025tulu3 , where algorithms such as Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO)~ shao2024deepseekmath use trajectory-level rewards to optimize the policy. In some settings, however, reliable rewards are unavailable~ tian2026autorubric,liu2026dynacf , and environmental feedback becomes the primary source of external information for agent training. This feedback arises naturally from interactions and includes tool outputs, code execution results, and environmental state changes caused by the agent's actions. Since such feedback typically describes action consequences rather than providing direct supervision for policy learning, using it effectively in agent training remains a challenge. Recent methods tackle this challenge through hindsight self-distillation. SDPO~ hubotter2026sdpo conditions a self-teacher on environmental feedback, while OEL~ ye2026oel further extracts transferable knowledge from interaction experience. Our analysis shows that, despite containing sufficient information for policy improvement, such feedback yields only modest gains when used in these ways, suggesting that the key limitation lies in how it is exploited during training. Although environmental feedback does not directly supervise action generation, it provides direct targets for learning how the environment responds to agent actions. We therefore ask: Can learning to predict environmental feedback enable more effective use of it in agentic self-distillation? Our analysis reveals a mutually reinforcing relationship: environmental feedback modeling improves hindsight self-distillation, while self-distillation in turn strengthens environmental feedback prediction. Building on this finding, we introduce agentic SElf-distilLation with environmental Feedback (SELF), a framework that jointly optimizes environmental feedback modeling and hindsight self-distillation. For each interaction transition, SELF uses the realized feedback in two complementary ways: as a prediction target for learning how the environment responds to the agent's action, and as privileged context for a self-teacher whose action distribution is distilled into the student policy. By jointly learning from these two signals within a shared model, SELF enables more effective use of environmental feedback for policy improvement. We evaluate SELF on -bench Retail~ yao2025taubench for multi-turn customer-service interactions with domain-specific tools, and AppWorld~ trivedi2024appworld for code-based task completion across applications. Across Qwen3-4B-Instruct and Qwen3-8B (non-thinking)~ yang2025qwen3 , SELF outperforms feedback-learning baselines and reward-trained GRPO~ shao2024deepseekmath in task success and goal completion. With Qwen3-8B, SELF surpasses SDPO~ hubotter2026sdpo and GRPO by 6.4 and 4.1 percentage points in -bench success rate, and by 10.71 and 3.57 percentage points in AppWorld task goal completion, respectively, which demonstrates SELF's effectiveness in turning environmental feedback into useful supervision for policy improvement. Further analyses show that SELF also retains strong generalization capabilities beyond the training environments. Our key contributions can be summarized as follows: [leftmargin=10pt, topsep=-2pt, itemsep=1pt, partopsep=1pt, parsep=1pt] We identify a mutually reinforcing mechanism: environmental feedback modeling improves hindsight self-distillation, while self-distillation strengthens environmental feedback prediction. We propose SELF, an agent training framework that learns from environmental feedback by jointly optimizing environmental feedback modeling and hindsight self-distillation. We empirically show that SELF improves performance on -bench Retail and AppWorld, outperforming both existing self-distillation approaches and reward-trained GRPO, which demonstrates its effectiveness in enabling agentic self-distillation to make better use of environmental feedback. Related Work sec:related_work Agentic Self-Distillation. Agentic self-distillation provides dense policy supervision without requiring a separate stronger teacher. OPSD~ zhao2026opsd constructs student and teacher policies from the same model, conditioning the teacher on privileged reference information. SDPO~ hubotter2026sdpo instead conditions the self-teacher on textual feedback and distills its feedback-informed predictions into the policy. SDFT~ shenfeld2026sdft uses demonstration-conditioned self-distillation to acquire new knowledge and skills while mitigating forgetting. RLSD~ yang2026rlsd further combines self-distillation with RLVR, using privileged teachers for token-level credit while retaining verifier rewards to determine the policy-update direction. Learning from Environmental Feedback. Environmental feedback contains rich information about the realized consequences of agent actions, and recent methods exploit this information in different forms. OCSD~ yang2026ocsd contrasts replay contexts with and without future observations to calibrate policy updates, while HERO~ liu2026hero converts subsequent observations into turn-level hindsight diagnoses. OEL~ ye2026oel extracts transferable experiential knowledge from interaction trajectories before distilling it into the policy. Kleine Buening et al.~ buening2026aligning use raw user follow-up messages as hindsight information for self-distillation. AHEAD~ jin2026ahead conditions the teacher on environment feedback and supplements critical error steps with generated corrective hints, whereas OpenClaw-RL~ wang2026openclawrl converts next-state signals into process rewards or hindsight guidance for online agent learning. These approaches use realized feedback to construct or refine supervision for action generation. Environmental Feedback Modeling for Policy Learning. A complementary line of work directly learns the predictive structure contained in interaction feedback. ECHO~ shrivastava2026echo and PaW~ lu2026paw incorporate environment prediction into policy optimization, while AAWM~ cai2026aawm studies decision-oriented modeling targets rather than directly reconstructing future observations. Early Experience~ zhang2026earlyexperience uses next states produced by agent actions as supervision for implicit world modeling and self-reflection. Most closely related, RLTF~ song2026rltf studies both feedback-conditioned self-distillation and feedback modeling, where textual critiques are predicted as an auxiliary objective. In contrast, SELF models environmental responses directly from interactive trajectories and uses the same realized feedback both as a prediction target and as privileged context for hindsight self-distillation. Our analysis further shows that these objectives mutually reinforce each other. Methodology sec:method We present SELF, a framework that improves agentic self-distillation by explicitly modeling environmental feedback. We first formalize agent–environment interaction and the problem of learning from environmental feedback. We then describe on-policy hindsight self-distillation, which uses realized feedback as privileged information to construct policy supervision. Finally, we introduce the environmental feedback modeling objective and show how it is jointly optimized with hindsight self-distillation within the framework. Problem Formulation sec:problem --Environment Interaction. We consider an agent that interacts with an environment through actions and observable feedback, including tool outputs, code execution results, and state changes. Let denote a task instruction, the initial observation, and the feedback returned after action . Each transition associates an action with its observed consequence, without requiring access to latent environment states. A trajectory is , where is the number of interaction turns, and denotes the trajectories collected at round . Training uses only the resulting actions and environmental feedback, without task rewards, outcome labels, or external teachers. For feedback modeling, the observed feedback is represented by the point-mass target . Hindsight Self-Distillation sec:hindsight_self_distillation Hindsight self-distillation provides a general approach for converting environmental feedback into supervision for policy learning. We consider its on-policy form, where trajectories are collected by the current policy and distillation is performed on the action prefixes encountered along these trajectories~ agarwal2024onpolicy . For each transition , the student predicts the action using only the information available before the environmental feedback is observed, while a self-teacher additionally conditions on the realized feedback as privileged hindsight information. The student and teacher use distinct prompting interfaces, and , respectively. For an action containing tokens, we define the student and teacher next-token distributions as where both distributions are evaluated on the same on-policy action prefix , but only the teacher has access to the realized environmental feedback. The teacher parameters are maintained as an exponential moving average (EMA)~ tarvainen2017mean of the student parameters, , where is the EMA decay coefficient. The feedback-conditioned teacher is distilled into the student through the reverse-KL objective~ gu2024minillm where and stops gradients through the teacher. The collected action therefore determines the contexts at which the two distributions are compared, rather than serving as a ground-truth action target. This formulation allows information available only after an action is executed to supervise a policy that must act without access to that information at inference time~ choudhury2025better . In our analysis, however, hindsight self-distillation in this form yields only modest policy improvements, suggesting that conditioning the teacher on feedback alone does not fully exploit the information contained in environmental feedback.
