title: From Solo to Ensemble: A Hierarchical Framework for Composable Multi-Agent Human-Object Interaction
summary: Physics-based human-object interaction has achieved robust single-agent manipulation skills, yet extending them to multi-agent cooperative tasks remains challenging. Existing approaches typically adapt interaction policies through task-specific fine-tuning, which entangles low-level contact-rich execution with high-level coordination and limits reuse across object geometries, interaction types, and team sizes. We propose a hierarchical framework that converts a single-agent HOI policy into a reusable Object-oriented Motion Skill. Specifically, we reinterpret teacher rollouts as object-oriented action supervision by extracting short-horizon object-proxy motions from executed trajectories, and distill task-specific teachers into a low-level skill operating in an Object-oriented Action Space. For downstream tasks, the distilled skill is frozen as a reusable executor, while a high-level policy coordinates multiple agents by generating region-wise object-oriented actions conditioned on the shared object, task goal, agent states, and local manipulation regions. This formulation shifts multi-agent HOI learning from direct contact-rich full-body control to compact object-level proxy-motion coordination. Experiments on diverse HOI tasks show that the distilled Object-oriented Motion Skill supports robust proxy-motion execution and enables composable policy learning across different interaction types, object geometries, and team sizes.
full_text: Physics-based human-object interaction has achieved robust single-agent manipulation skills, yet extending them to multi-agent cooperative tasks remains challenging. Existing approaches typically adapt interaction policies through task-specific fine-tuning, which entangles low-level contact-rich execution with high-level coordination and limits reuse across object geometries, interaction types, and team sizes. We propose a hierarchical framework that converts a single-agent HOI policy into a reusable Object-oriented Motion Skill. Specifically, we reinterpret teacher rollouts as object-oriented action supervision by extracting short-horizon object-proxy motions from executed trajectories, and distill task-specific teachers into a low-level skill operating in an Object-oriented Action Space. For downstream tasks, the distilled skill is frozen as a reusable executor, while a high-level policy coordinates multiple agents by generating region-wise object-oriented actions conditioned on the shared object, task goal, agent states, and local manipulation regions. This formulation shifts multi-agent HOI learning from direct contact-rich full-body control to compact object-level proxy-motion coordination. Experiments on diverse HOI tasks show that the distilled Object-oriented Motion Skill supports robust proxy-motion execution and enables composable policy learning across different interaction types, object geometries, and team sizes. Introduction Physics-based character control has made substantial progress in learning robust full-body skills from motion imitation, adversarial motion priors, latent skill learning, and unified humanoid controllers~ peng2018deepmimic,peng2021amp,peng2022ase,tessler2023calm,tessler2024maskedmimic . Recent human-object interaction (HOI) methods further extend these advances to contact-rich object manipulation and human-scene interaction~ wang2023physhoi,wang2024skillmimic,tevet2024closd,pan2025tokenhsi,xu2025intermimic . However, multi-human HOI introduces a distinct coordination challenge: multiple humanoids must coordinate contact locations, motion directions, and force application around the same manipulated object. Existing methods have explored transferring interaction skills to multi-human tasks. For example, CooHOI~ gao2024coohoi adapts learned interaction policies to cooperative manipulation through object-level coupling. Such transfer is typically realized through policy initialization or task-specific fine-tuning. Although the adapted policy can solve a specific cooperative task, it still entangles low-level motor skill and high-level coordination within a single task policy. As a result, the learned behavior is difficult to reuse, compose, or transfer to new object geometries and cooperative configurations. Our key insight is that a single-human HOI policy should not be directly fine-tuned into a task-specific multi-human policy. Instead, it should be preserved and converted into a reusable Object-oriented Motion Skill that can realize local proxy motions across downstream HOI tasks. With this skill, downstream learning only needs to reason in the Object-oriented Action Space. This leads to a hierarchical and decoupled control framework, where the low-level Object-oriented Motion Skill handles contact-rich execution and the high-level policy performs compositional object-level coordination through proxy-motion planning. To make the skill reusable, the control interface should neither be tied to a specific task goal nor over-constrain the humanoid motion. We therefore define the Object-oriented Action Space as short-horizon motions of an object proxy, allowing the low-level policy to learn how to realize desired proxy motion through contact selection, balance control, and full-body coordination. Specifically, we reinterpret rollouts from single-human HOI teacher policies as object-oriented action supervision by extracting future object-proxy motions from their executed trajectories. This converts task-specific teachers into an Object-oriented Motion Skill that can be frozen and reused as a low-level executor. In downstream tasks, a high-level policy observes the shared object, task goal, agent states, and local manipulation regions, and generates region-wise object-oriented actions. In this way, downstream RL no longer optimizes contact-rich full-body control directly, but instead learns cooperative decision making within the compact Object-oriented Action Space. Our contributions are threefold: [leftmargin=*] We establish a transferable formulation for physics-based multi-human HOI, shifting the focus from task-specific cooperative policy learning to transferable object-oriented motion coordination. We develop a distillation-based hierarchical learning framework that converts single-human HOI knowledge into a reusable Object-oriented Motion Skill, enabling high-level policies to coordinate multiple humans through short-horizon object-proxy motions. We validate the framework on cooperative HOI tasks, showing that an Object-oriented Motion Skill distilled from a single-human skill supports robust proxy-motion execution and enables high-level policy learning across different interaction types, object geometries, and team sizes. Related Work sec:relatedwork Human-Object Interaction Motion Synthesis and Physics-Based Control. Character animation and motion synthesis have extensively studied human motion in 3D scenes and human-object interaction, including kinematic human-scene and dynamic-object interaction methods~ li2019putting,zhang2020generating,Xuan_2023_ICCV,Zhao:ECCV:2022,lee2023lama,wang2022humanise,wang2024move,starke2019neural,Zhao:ICCV:2023,starke2020local,jiang2022chairs,zhang2022couch,zhang2024core4d . Recent diffusion-based approaches further improve motion diversity and controllability by conditioning on scene constraints, text, action labels, or object trajectories~ ho2020denoising,huang2023diffusion,tang2024unified,yi2025generating,zhao2024dart,li2023object,li2023controllable,pi2023hierarchical,peng2023hoi,zhangopenhoi,jiang2024scaling,jiang2024autonomous . However, such kinematic generation methods often lack physical validity, especially for long-horizon contact-rich interactions that require sustained contacts, force exchange, and object dynamics. Physics-based character control addresses this issue by learning closed-loop policies for physically plausible full-body behaviors from motion imitation, adversarial motion priors, latent skills, and large-scale motion datasets~ peng2018deepmimic,peng2021amp,peng2022ase,tessler2023calm,luo2024universal,juravsky2024superpadl,tessler2024maskedmimic . These techniques have been extended to physics-based HOI and human-scene interaction, enabling contact-rich behaviors such as object catching and manipulation, scene-level interactions, dynamic HOI imitation, reusable sports skills, task-tokenized scene interaction, and whole-body HOI control across diverse objects~ merel2020catch,chao2021learning,xie2023hierarchical,hassan2023synthesizing,wang2023physhoi,wang2024skillmimic,zhang2023learning,liu2017learning,liu2022motor,xie2022learning,pan2025tokenhsi,xu2025intermimic . While these methods substantially improve physical realism and task coverage, their control abstractions are usually tied to reference motions, task labels, or single-human interaction settings. Multi-Character Interaction and Cooperative Object Manipulation. Compared with single-human HOI, cooperative interaction introduces a stronger coordination challenge: a shared object-level task must be decomposed into per-human contacts, motions, and force application. Existing multi-person datasets and kinematic animation methods have enabled visually plausible human-human interactions and choreographic motions~ kundu2020cross,shen2019interaction,fieraru2020three,xu2024inter,liu2025core4d,zhang2024hoi,kogashi2026mmhoi,le2023music,siyao2024duolando,won2014generating,liang2024intergen,tanaka2023role,shafir2023human,ghosh2024remos,tan2025think,zhang2025reactffusion,zhao2025freedance,fan2024freemotion,ghosh2025duetgen,javed2024intermask . However, these methods mainly target motion synthesis and do not guarantee physically valid contacts, forces, or shared object dynamics. Recent physics-based multi-character methods improve physical plausibility by combining generated motions with controllers or converting multi-human motions into executable policies~ huang2025diffuse,tevet2024closd,karunratanakul2023guided,zhang2024tedi,luo2023perpetual,liu2024physreaction,ji2025towards,li2025interagent , but they mostly focus on human-human interaction, sports, reaction, or collision avoidance rather than contact-rich cooperative object manipulation~ haworth2020deep,rempe2023trace,luo2024smplolympics . Cooperative object manipulation has also been explored in legged robotics, including multi-robot payload transport, pushing, and collaborative carrying~ nachum2020multiagent,devincenti2023centralized,10341700,Turrisi_2024,feng2025learning,pandit2025multiquadrupedcooperativeobjecttransport . These systems demonstrate object-level coordination, but they typically rely on quadrupedal morphology, engineered manipulation interfaces, or task-specific control designs, and do not address full-body humanoid HOI with motion priors. Most closely related to our setting, CooHOI~ gao2024coohoi learns cooperative human-object interaction through shared object dynamics, but its adaptation still couples low-level motor execution with task-specific multi-human coordination. In contrast, our method preserves single-human HOI skills as a reusable low-level skill operating over object-oriented proxy motions, enabling high-level policies to compose local object motions across object geometries, interaction types, and team sizes. Method sec:method Our method builds a composable HOI control hierarchy around object-oriented proxy motions. Sec.~ sec:object_motion_skill first introduces the Object-oriented Motion Skill, a reusable low-level policy that realizes short-horizon motions of object proxies through physically feasible humanoid control. Its Object-oriented Action Space provides a compact interface between high-level task reasoning and contact-rich execution. Sec.~ sec:object_centric_hierarchy then trains task-specific high-level policies on top of the frozen skill, allowing single- and multi-human HOI tasks to be solved by generating region-wise proxy motions rather than full-body motions or torque-level actions. Fig.~ fig:pipeline provides an overview of the full pipeline. Low-Level Policy: Generalizable Object-oriented Motion Skill sec:object_motion_skill Definition of Object-oriented Action Space. We decouple high-level HOI reasoning from low-level physical execution by introducing an Object-oriented Motion Skill, a reusable low-level policy controlled through an Object-oriented Action Space. Instead of directly tracking full-body reference motions or optimizing toward a task-specific goal, the skill realizes short-horizon motions of a manipulated object proxy. For clarity, we formulate the action space for a single humanoid and omit the agent index. Let denote the humanoid state and denote the object proxy observed by the low-level skill. We represent either a complete object or a task-relevant local region as a compact cuboid proxy with unified kinematic and bounding-box features. title: 2DGS-Planner: Rasterization-based Path Planning in 2D Gaussian Splatting Map
summary: Gaussian splatting provides an explicit and efficiently rasterizable scene representation for robot navigation. However, individual Gaussian primitives may not reliably represent obstacles as they are jointly optimized through alpha-composited rendering from a finite set of reconstruction views. We propose 2DGS-Planner, a path planner for ground robots that reads planning-relevant geometry from a 2D Gaussian splatting (2DGS) map through rasterization, rather than treating individual Gaussian primitives as obstacles. During offline roadmap construction, multi-view attribution converts rendered normal dispersion into structural scores for non-ground disks supported by the reconstruction views. These scores guide adaptive node sampling on the ground. Path-aligned orthographic queries validate candidate edges, while cylindrical queries estimate local clearance fields that are cached on the edges. During online planning, graph search initializes a route, and path refinement reuses the cached fields while accounting for the robot's dimensions and ground constraints. Experiments demonstrate improved roadmap connectivity, more accurate clearance estimation, and higher planning success compared with the tested baselines. These results support rasterization as an effective geometric query interface for planning directly on Gaussian maps. Code and data are available at https://2dgs-planner.github.io/
full_text: Gaussian splatting provides an explicit and efficiently rasterizable scene representation for robot navigation. However, individual Gaussian primitives may not reliably represent obstacles as they are jointly optimized through alpha-composited rendering from a finite set of reconstruction views. We propose 2DGS-Planner, a path planner for ground robots that reads planning-relevant geometry from a 2D Gaussian splatting (2DGS) map through rasterization, rather than treating individual Gaussian primitives as obstacles. During offline roadmap construction, multi-view attribution converts rendered normal dispersion into structural scores for non-ground disks supported by the reconstruction views. These scores guide adaptive node sampling on the ground. Path-aligned orthographic queries validate candidate edges, while cylindrical queries estimate local clearance fields that are cached on the edges. During online planning, graph search initializes a route, and path refinement reuses the cached fields while accounting for the robot’s dimensions and ground constraints. Experiments demonstrate improved roadmap connectivity, more accurate clearance estimation, and higher planning success compared with the tested baselines. These results support rasterization as an effective geometric query interface for planning directly on Gaussian maps. Code and data are available at https://2dgs-planner.github.io/ . Introduction sec:introduction Autonomous navigation requires spatial reasoning about the environment to find safe and efficient paths. This reasoning is closely tied to how the environment is represented, since planners interact with a map through the spatial queries it can support efficiently. Occupancy grids enable graph-based search through discrete occupancy lookups~ elfes1989occupancy , while signed distance fields provide differentiable distance queries for gradient-based trajectory optimization~ ratliff2009chomp, oleynikova2017voxblox . Point-based geometric maps can be queried directly for collision checking in sampling-based planning~ karaman2011sampling . Recently, learned scene representations have been explored as environment maps for navigation~ adamkiewicz2022vision, kwon2023renderable, dai2026neural, splatnav, splatblox, gsplanner . -based approaches obtain collision evidence directly from the learned density~ adamkiewicz2022vision . Other methods rely on rendered outputs for localization, image-goal navigation, and traversability-aware planning~ kwon2023renderable, dai2026neural . Both approaches rely on evaluating an implicit field, which can be computationally expensive for real-time planning. ~ 3dgs provides an explicit alternative, encoding scenes with Gaussian primitives and rendering images from arbitrary viewpoints through differentiable rasterization. Existing -based planners generally treat the primitives directly as obstacles or convert the map into an intermediate geometric representation~ splatnav, splatblox, gsplanner . However, visually plausible renderings do not guarantee that the underlying primitives align with the composited surface (Fig.~ fig:primitive_reliability ). Individual primitives may therefore fail to reliably represent scene geometry. Two properties of GS training motivate rasterization-based geometric queries. First, the primitives are jointly optimized through their contributions to alpha-composited renderings, so the training objective constrains the composited geometry rather than any individual primitive. This motivates querying the composited geometry instead of treating primitives as independent obstacles. Second, this supervision comes from only a finite set of posed training views. Geometry outside their observation support is therefore less constrained by the training data. A planner should consider not only the rendered surface geometry but also how well that surface was observed during training. We therefore propose ~(Fig.~ fig:teaser ), a ground-robot path planner that treats rasterization as the geometric query interface to a map. We build on ~ 2dgs , whose training aligns each disk with the local surface through a normal consistency term, so that surface normals become a rendered channel alongside depth and alpha. The framework constructs a roadmap directly from rasterized geometric queries without converting the scene into an intermediate geometric representation. During offline roadmap construction, multi-view attribution derives structural scores from rendered normal dispersion. Scores from non-ground disks supported by the reconstruction views guide adaptive node sampling on the ground, placing more nodes near corners and cluttered areas and fewer in open regions. Path-aligned orthographic queries validate candidate connections, while cylindrical queries estimate local clearance fields that are cached on retained edges. During online planning, graph search finds an initial path, which is then refined using the cached fields while accounting for the robot’s dimensions and ground constraints. The main contributions are as follows: We propose , a ground-robot path planner that queries 2DGS maps through rasterization without an intermediate geometric representation. We introduce multi-view attribution that converts rendered normal dispersion into structural scores for adaptive roadmap sampling. We formulate path-aligned orthographic and cylindrical queries for edge validation and local clearance estimation, with the clearance fields cached for path refinement. We evaluate the proposed framework from geometric reasoning to complete planning, including structural attribution, clearance estimation, end-to-end path planning, and real-world robot experiments. Related Work sec:related_work Rasterization-based Geometry in Gaussian Splatting rw:rendering ~ 3dgs represents a scene with volumetric Gaussian primitives, while ~ 2dgs replaces them with planar Gaussian disks to impose a surface-oriented geometric representation. During rasterization, the renderer computes ray--disk intersections and alpha-composites the intersected disks along each ray, yielding geometric quantities such as depth and surface normals in 3D. Recent methods have increasingly exploited such rasterized quantities as geometric signals. PGSR~ pgsr renders plane distances and normals for surface reconstruction, while RaDe-GS~ radegs derives depth and surface normals directly from rasterized 3D Gaussians. 3DGUT~ wu2025threedgut further extends Gaussian rasterization beyond standard pinhole projection to support secondary rays. These methods use rasterization primarily for rendering or reconstruction, while we use it as a geometric query interface for path planning on a fixed map. Planning on Gaussian Splatting rw:planning GS-based motion planning and control differ in how they obtain collision information. Splat-Nav~ splatnav constructs safe corridors from Gaussian ellipsoids, while SAFER-Splat~ safersplat formulates control barrier functions over the primitives. SPLANNING~ splanning derives collision-probability bounds from a normalized Gaussian field, and FOCI~ foci optimizes trajectories using overlap between Gaussian representations of the robot and the scene, including trajectories for a legged ground robot. Other approaches use auxiliary geometric representations. Splatblox~ splatblox supports wheeled and legged outdoor navigation through a traversability-aware , while LiftNav~ liftnav uses a joint TSDF--GS map for semantic navigation and trajectory optimization. SplatlessDF~ splatlessdf couples with a separately parameterized continuous distance field that supplies distance and gradient queries for planning. Rendering has also been used directly for collision avoidance. ReMoSPLAT~ remosplat renders depth from virtual cameras attached to a mobile manipulator and uses the resulting distances for reactive control. Whereas ReMoSPLAT targets reactive collision avoidance, we use rasterization for ground-robot path planning on a fixed map, with queries organized around candidate ground motions to evaluate and retain clearance for subsequent refinement. title: PathTime-VLA: Path-Time Decoupling for Factorized Post-Training of Vision-Language-Action Policies
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies typically predict actions at fixed time intervals, coupling the route a robot follows with its execution pace. This coupling complicates adaptation from teleoperation: useful geometric guidance comes with timing shaped by interface delays and operator behavior. Our key insight is to bring the path-time parameterization of classical motion planning into the learned action representation of a VLA. We introduce PathTime-VLA, which represents motion as a progress-indexed interaction path $X(s)$ and a positive interval-time profile. The latter defines a monotone time law $t(s)$, yielding controller commands $X(s(t))$. For a given path, alternative executions are expressed through the time profile, allowing chunk-wise speed choices without changing the geometric prediction target. This representation supports a staged post-training procedure: demonstrations and DAgger interventions establish a target-domain prior, Speed-DQN learns execution multipliers from robot interaction, and Path-AWR uses rollout outcomes to refine the diffusion path generator. A path-conditioned action expert realizes the resulting motions while maintaining distinct learning interfaces for path generation and execution timing. Across three tasks, the complete method achieves $58/60$ successes versus $57/60$ for PathTime-VLA under BC + DAgger at fixed $1\times$, with approximately $39$-$52\%$ shorter mean completion times over successful trials.

title: WAND: Learning Robust Navigation under Complex Wind Disturbances and Dense Obstacles for Quadrotors
summary: Robust navigation in cluttered environments remains a fundamental challenge for quadrotors, particularly when strong wind disturbances arise, which perturb vehicle dynamics, limit control authority, and substantially increase collision risk. Existing learning-based navigation policies typically rely on obstacle perception and proprioceptive observations, requiring the policy to infer time-varying disturbance effects implicitly and thereby limiting robustness under partial observability. This paper proposes WAND (Wind-Aware Navigation with Disturbance Estimation), a reinforcement learning framework for navigation under time-varying wind disturbances in dense obstacle fields. Specifically, WAND estimates wind-induced disturbance acceleration from historical proprioceptive states using a Temporal Convolutional Network (TCN). This estimation is integrated into the policy via a zero-initialized residual module, \emph{WindAdapter}, while simultaneously providing feedforward compensation for low-level control. The dual use of the estimate couples disturbance-conditioned navigation with feedforward disturbance rejection. Across 12 wind-disturbed simulation settings, WAND improved the observed success rate by 8.3 percentage points on average relative to feedforward compensation alone. Controlled opposite-crosswind experiments further showed wind-direction-dependent trajectory adaptation. In indoor fan-induced flight tests, WAND succeeded in 18 of 20 trials, demonstrating the feasibility of real-time onboard navigation.

Bin Zhao is also with Northwestern Polytechnical University, Xi'an 710072, China (e-mail: bin@nwpu.edu.cn). Xuelong Li is with the Institute of Artificial Intelligence (TeleAI), China Telecom, Beijing 100033, China (e-mail: xuelong li@ieee.org). Specifically, WAND estimates wind-induced disturbance acceleration from historical proprioceptive states using a Temporal Convolutional Network (TCN). This estimation is integrated into the policy via a zero-initialized residual module, WindAdapter, while simultaneously providing feedforward compensation for low-level control. The dual use of the estimate couples disturbance-conditioned navigation with feedforward disturbance rejection. Across 12 wind-disturbed simulation settings, WAND improved the observed success rate by 8.3 percentage points on average relative to feedforward compensation alone. Controlled opposite-crosswind experiments further showed wind-direction-dependent trajectory adaptation. In indoor fan-induced flight tests, WAND succeeded in 18 of 20 trials, demonstrating the feasibility of real-time onboard navigation. Aerial Systems: Perception and Autonomy, Reinforcement Learning, Autonomous Vehicle Navigation INTRODUCTION n recent years, micro quadrotors have seen rapid adoption in exploration 2021epic , emergency rescue rescue2022 , and urban delivery delivery2017 . Driven by breakthroughs in low-power computing and micro-sensing lowcost_diff2025, lowcost_rgb2025 , these vehicles can now operate under extreme Size, Weight, and Power (SWaP) constraints, granting them access to dense and confined environments. In such settings, the wind disturbance experienced by the vehicle can vary over time as the airflow interacts with surrounding structures, for example, through flow acceleration near gaps or recirculation around obstacles UCE2006, edge_flow2008 . Due to their limited actuation authority, micro quadrotors are highly susceptible to unsteady airflow, increasing the risk of collision in cluttered environments. Traditional navigation stacks separate geometric planning from low-level control. Geometry-oriented planners fast_planner2019,ego_planner2021,super2025 focus on trajectory feasibility, whereas robust planners tube_mpc2017,motion_plan2021 and predictive controllers cmpcc2021 account for disturbances or tracking uncertainty but depend on assumed models and sufficient control authority. Strong, rapidly varying wind can therefore leave residual tracking errors that erode trajectory clearance in confined environments. In contrast, learning-based methods integrate perception and control through learned navigation policies. NavRL navrl2025 learns safe navigation in dynamic clutter, while end-to-end approaches map LiDAR cloud2025,e2e_learning2025 or visual features learning_agile2023 to low-level commands and support sim-to-real transfer ctbr2022 . However, these policies primarily condition on obstacle perception and proprioception rather than explicit wind estimates. They therefore infer time-varying aerodynamic effects implicitly, although the same observation can require different actions under different winds. This partial observability complicates robust wind-aware navigation. To address this issue, we propose WAND, a wind-aware RL framework for safe navigation in windy, cluttered environments. A Temporal Convolutional Network (TCN) estimates wind-induced disturbance acceleration from proprioceptive histories, and the proposed WindAdapter encodes this estimate into wind-conditioned features. The policy combines these features with obstacle perception and the current proprioceptive state, while the same estimate is reused for feedforward compensation. As illustrated in Fig.~ flight example , WAND is deployed onboard for real-time navigation in a cluttered indoor environment under fan-induced airflow. Our contributions can be summarized as follows: We propose WAND, a wind-aware RL framework for quadrotor navigation in cluttered environments under wind disturbances. WAND explicitly estimates wind-induced disturbance acceleration from proprioceptive histories and integrates it into the policy through a zero-initialized residual WindAdapter, while also reusing it for feedforward compensation during execution. We validate WAND through simulation and real-world flight experiments under diverse wind conditions, demonstrating improved robustness and disturbance-adaptive behaviors compared with baseline methods. RELATED WORK Hierarchical Navigation in Cluttered Environments Autonomous navigation in cluttered environments has been widely studied within hierarchical planning frameworks. Representative methods such as Fast-Planner fast_planner2019 and EGO-Planner ego_planner2021 achieve real-time collision-free trajectory generation by exploiting geometric constraints derived from occupancy maps. More recent works gcopter2022, super2025 further improve computational efficiency and trajectory quality in dense obstacle fields, demonstrating strong performance in structured navigation tasks. However, these planners are primarily designed for geometric feasibility and typically rely on the low-level controller to track the reference trajectory with sufficient accuracy. To improve tracking robustness against external disturbances, prior works have explored disturbance-compensation strategies cmpcc2021 . Nevertheless, in most hierarchical pipelines, disturbance rejection is primarily handled by the tracking controller. As a result, the planned trajectory may not explicitly account for time-varying aerodynamic effects, and severe wind gusts can drive the quadrotor beyond the intended safety margins, increasing the risk of collision. Learning-Based Navigation Learning-based navigation directly learns obstacle-avoidance and goal-reaching behaviors from data. Early learning-based approaches demonstrated sim-to-real navigation in clutter with CAD2RL cad2rl2016 and privileged learning for high-speed flight in unstructured environments wild2021 . Building on this, Song et al. learning_agile2023 combine imitation and reinforcement learning through a privileged learning-by-cheating framework that tightly couples perception and control. Xu et al. cloud2025 and Fan et al. e2e_learning2025 design task-relevant LiDAR representations for safe and reactive navigation, while NavRL navrl2025 addresses dynamic environments with moving obstacles through tailored state representations and adaptive architectures. Yu et al. mav2025 leverage memory-augmented latent representations with varying-speed strategies to enhance navigation performance. History-conditioned latent adaptation has been applied to quadrotor control by inferring a latent representation of vehicle and environment parameters from recent state--action histories and conditioning the controller on that representation zhang_quad2023 . In WAND, temporal conditioning is grounded in a supervised estimate of wind-induced disturbance acceleration, thereby making the conditioning signal physically interpretable. Complementary onboard estimators recover wind or external forces from proprioceptive or visual--inertial measurements DOB2024,VIMO2019,HDVIO2023 , while adaptive learning and control methods improve dynamics prediction or trajectory tracking under wind disturbances neural_fly2022,piwan2025 . WAND integrates these directions by using the explicit disturbance estimate both to adapt obstacle-aware navigation actions and to provide low-level feedforward compensation. title: CAPABLE: Capability-Aware Policy Adaptation via Behavioral Latent Encoding
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies assume the embodiment on which they were trained and can fail when a joint fault changes how commanded actions are physically executed. Existing fault-recovery methods often require task-specific retraining, fault labels, explicit diagnosis, or privileged embodiment information. We introduce CAPABLE, a unified capability-aware adaptation framework for frozen VLAs that integrates self-supervised capability inference with residual reinforcement learning. CAPABLE infers capability, how much of the commanded motion each joint actually realizes and how that motion contributes to end-effector behavior, online from command-response history and kinematics using a temporal encoder shared across joints, Jacobian grounding, cross-joint attention, and self-supervised physical prediction. The resulting representation conditions a residual policy that adds bounded corrections to the VLA arm action without fault labels or faulty-joint identifiers. Across 28 LIBERO tasks, CAPABLE raises success on an actuator excluded from fault training from 24.8% to 59.3%, outperforming a parameter-matched global-history baseline by 17.4 points while preserving healthy performance. Leave-one-actuator-out experiments across six joints show that this transfer is not specific to one actuator, and additional evaluations characterize transfer to unseen fault families and demonstrate recovery on a physical Franka Panda. https://capable-vla.github.io/

Introduction A manipulator is midway through placing a plate into a drawer when one of its motors stalls. The vision-language-action policy driving it is unaffected. It continues to issue actions that are semantically correct for the task, and the arm continues to move, but it no longer moves the way the policy assumes. The plate never arrives. Incidents of this kind are a reliability and a safety concern, and are documented in space robotics~ canadarm2002,canadarm2026,curiosity2016 , surgical robotics~ davinci2013 , and industrial manipulators~ flexspline2018,ur5phm2021 . Prevailing practice is to halt the robot once a fault is detected. Stopping is safe but costly when repair is slow or the robot is hard to reach. We are interested in the harder alternative, which is to continue the task with a body that has changed. Vision-language-action (VLA) policies are an attractive starting point, since they supply a strong semantic and visuomotor prior for language-conditioned manipulation~ driess2023palme,brohan2022rt1,zitkovich2023rt2, ghosh2024octo,black2024pi0,kim2025openvla,kim2025oft . Their training data, however, assume the robot retains the healthy embodiment. A joint failure breaks that assumption at the level of physics, and no amount of visual or linguistic competence repairs it. The fault itself is not directly observable. Moreover, the fault space—spanning the affected joint, failure type, and severity—is too large to cover during training, requiring recovery to generalize to previously unseen actuator failures. Existing methods address only parts of this problem. Classical fault-tolerant control detects the fault and redistributes motion across the remaining joints~ zhang2008ftc,blanke2006ftc,xie2021locked , but does not consider the VLA's closed-loop behavior or task progress. Learning-based methods either train a task policy from scratch~ pham2024joint or require explicit fault information or supervision~ briscoe2026deft,jo2026jparc . Prior work evaluates held-out joints, but does not establish systematic transfer for a frozen multi-task VLA without fault labels, affected-joint supervision, or healthy reference trajectories. Our central observation is that a fault need not be identified by its type or cause. Instead, it can be represented by the remaining capability of each actuator, measured by how much of a commanded motion the joint realizes and how that motion affects the end effector in the current configuration. This capability can be inferred without privileged information from each joint’s command–response history. Because capability is represented consistently across all joints, an estimator learned from failures of one joint can transfer to another. We propose CAPABLE (Capability-Aware Policy Adaptation via Behavioral Latent Encoding), a residual reinforcement-learning controller that keeps the VLA frozen and adds a correction to its arm action~ johannink2019residual , using an off-policy actor-critic for sample-efficient residual policy learning~ ball2023rlpd . CAPABLE encodes each joint's command--response history using one temporal encoder shared across all seven joints. The shared map recognizes common command--response signatures across actuators rather than learning a separate encoder per joint (Fig.~ fig:teaser ). Each joint's live Jacobian column grounds this estimate in the current configuration, and cross-joint attention combines all joints into a representation of what motions the arm can still produce. A self-supervised objective that predicts realized joint and end-effector motion ties this representation to physical behavior, and the representation conditions a Soft Actor-Critic policy~ haarnoja2018sac through FiLM. No fault label, faulty-joint identifier, or fault-specific demonstration enters any network during training or deployment; at deployment the networks are fixed and capability is re-estimated at every control step. Our contributions are: A capability formulation of actuator faults for frozen VLAs, which represents a fault by what each actuator can still realize, infers it from command--response history and kinematics without fault labels, and uses it to correct a frozen generalist through bounded residual RL. A per-actuator factorized architecture for held-out-actuator transfer that shares one temporal encoder across joints, grounds it in the live Jacobian, composes joints with attention, and trains it with self-supervised physical prediction; removing any of these components significantly reduces held-out-joint success. An evaluation that separates factorization from capacity, comparing against a parameter-matched unfactorized encoder across 28 tasks, six held-out joints, five unseen fault families that mark where transfer holds and where it fails, and a physical robot. Related Work Adapting Pretrained Robot Policies Large robot datasets~ walke2023bridge,khazatsky2024droid have enabled VLA policies that map visual observations, language instructions, and robot states to actions~ brohan2022rt1,zitkovich2023rt2,ghosh2024octo,black2024pi0,kim2025openvla,kim2025oft . Because retraining these large models is expensive, recent work adapts them after pretraining. VLA-RL fine-tunes the VLA using reinforcement learning~ lu2025vlarl , while RobustVLA trains it against observation noise and action perturbations~ zhang2025robustvla . Other methods use test-time or recovery-oriented reinforcement learning to adapt the policy to new tasks and environments~ liu2026ttvla,liufu2026repo,zhang2026agentic . Residual learning freezes the base policy and learns correction on the base action~ johannink2019residual,silver2018rpl . These methods generally assume that the robot's physical capabilities remain unchanged. CAPABLE also keeps the base VLA frozen, but conditions its corrections on an online estimate of the robot's remaining actuator capabilities. Fault-Tolerant Control and Learned Adaptation Classical fault-tolerant control follows two main strategies. Passive methods tolerate a predefined set of faults, while active methods diagnose the fault and reconfigure the controller~ zhang2008ftc,blanke2006ftc . For redundant manipulators, motion can be replanned around a locked joint~ xie2021locked . Other methods estimate the remaining effectiveness of an actuator before applying compensation~ huang2025estimator . Both approaches require an explicit model of the fault. Learning-based methods instead infer changes in the robot's dynamics from recent interaction history~ yu2017uposi,kumar2021rma,nagabandi2019meta . Fault-tolerant locomotion policies can recover from locked or unpowered joints, but their training often uses privileged fault information through teacher policies, privileged critics, or fault-specific experts~ liu2022limping,xu2025acl,gravina2026gait,turrisi2026moe . Learning-Based Fault Recovery Pham et al.~ pham2024joint formulate Franka joint failure as a POMDP and train a recurrent PPO policy for permanent and intermittent failures on a drawer task, establishing that history-based~ tezerjani2024slam,khoshnazar2026future can compensate for an unknown impaired actuator. Their policy is trained for the task directly rather than wrapped around a pretrained multi-task VLA. DEFT~ briscoe2026deft uses an embodiment- and task-conditioned diffusion model to generate fail-active trajectories with broad simulated failure coverage, conditioning on an explicit embodiment vector. J-PARC~ jo2026jparc is the closest VLA-specific study. It trains an action calibrator on locked-joint faults using healthy reference rollouts and fault-presence and affected-joint supervision, then evaluates transfer to restricted ranges, friction, and held-out joints. CAPABLE uses task reward and self-supervised physical prediction in place of all of these signals. Weight Sharing Across Actuators Sharing one module across the parts of a body is a well-established route to morphology-agnostic control. NerveNet propagates messages over the kinematic graph~ wang2018nervenet , shared modular policies apply a single policy to every limb~ huang2020smp , and transformer variants attend over limb tokens~ kurin2021amorpheus, gupta2022metamorph . That literature shares modules across morphologies to generalize over bodies. We share a module across actuators of one body to generalize over which actuator has failed, grounding the shared tokens in the live Jacobian so the estimate becomes a configuration-specific correction. The components themselves are standard, combining recurrent state for partial observability~ hausknecht2015drqn,cho2014gru , attention for composition across entities~ vaswani2017attention , and FiLM for conditioning~ perez2018film . The policy does not observe \(f\) and must therefore infer its physical effects from execution history. The actor produces and the applied correction is The executed action is The gripper passes through untouched; the sparse reward is the LIBERO task-success predicate. title: REACT: Rolling Denoising and Dual Decoupling for Reactive Robot Control with VLA Models
comment: Accepted to CoRL 2026 as Spotlight. Project page: https://react-vla.github.io
summary: Flow-based vision-language-action (VLA) models generate action chunks for temporally coherent robot motion, but chunked control creates a fundamental closed-loop trade-off: long chunks provide smooth execution, whereas frequent replanning improves reactivity at the cost of action discontinuities. We introduce REACT, a rolling-denoising framework that makes flow-based VLAs more reactive while preserving long-horizon context. Instead of regenerating entire action chunks from scratch, REACT maintains a persistent action buffer with staggered flow timesteps. At each control step, the full horizon is denoised using the latest observation, the cleanest action block is executed, partially refined future blocks are shifted forward, and fresh noise is appended to the tail. As a result, each executed action block is refined across multiple recent observations before deployment. To support real-time control, we further introduce dual decoupling, which separates sensing, VLM encoding, DiT denoising, and action execution, enabling high-frequency observation updates and action streaming under practical compute constraints. Across the RoboTwin 2.0 simulation benchmark and real-world tasks spanning bimanual manipulation and dynamic control on multiple robot platforms, REACT improves task success and reduces reaction latency while producing smoother trajectories than frequent-replanning and asynchronous baselines.

Vision-language-action (VLA) models have become a promising framework for general-purpose robot control by unifying perception, language grounding, and action generation. Many modern VLAs~ brohan2022rt,zitkovich2023rt,kim2024openvla,black2024pi_0,zhao2023learning,chi2025diffusion,intelligence2025pi_ generate continuous action chunks with diffusion or flow-matching objectives. Action chunking improves temporal consistency, reduces compounding errors, and preserves multimodal action coherence. However, it also introduces a closed-loop control limitation: once a chunk is being generated or executed, new observations cannot immediately influence the future actions that remain inside the chunk. Existing methods improve closed-loop reactivity mainly by reducing or hiding inference latency. Asynchronous inference overlaps prediction with execution, but the next chunk may still be generated from stale observations and can introduce discontinuities when the controller switches between chunks. RTC-style methods mitigate this issue by freezing committed actions and inpainting future actions~ black2026real,black2025training , while other methods accelerate VLA inference through token optimization, compression, system-level optimization, or faster flow inference~ xu2026vla,pei2025action,yang2026efficientvla,ma2025running,lu2026faster . We argue that latency alone does not fully characterize dynamic robot control. A closed-loop VLA must simultaneously incorporate fresh observations at high frequency and produce executable actions continuously. We capture these two requirements with input throughput and output throughput. This exposes a coherence-freshness trade-off: long chunks preserve smooth, mode-consistent motion but reduce observation freshness, whereas frequent replanning improves reactivity but weakens temporal coherence. To address this trade-off, we propose REACT, a rolling denoising framework for flow-based VLAs. REACT maintains a persistent action buffer with staggered flow times instead of regenerating each chunk from scratch. At each control step, it denoises the active buffer using the latest observation, executes the cleanest front block, shifts partially refined blocks forward, and appends fresh noise. Thus, each executed block is refined across multiple recent observations while the policy retains a long action horizon. For deployment, we introduce dual-decoupling, which separates sensing, VLM encoding, DiT denoising, and action execution without changing model weights, enabling high-frequency observation updates and continuous action streaming. We also introduce matched staircase training to align flow supervision with rolling inference. Across RoboTwin 2.0 simulation, real-world bimanual manipulation on ARX X5 and Franka R3, and targeted Pour Rice and Reaction Game evaluations, REACT improves the success--reactivity trade-off and trajectory smoothness compared with frequent-replanning and asynchronous baselines. Our contributions are: [leftmargin=*, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt, parsep=0pt] We identify the coherence--freshness trade-off in chunked flow-based VLA inference and introduce input/output throughput as system-level measures of closed-loop responsiveness. We propose REACT, a rolling denoising mechanism that preserves full-horizon action consistency while refining future actions across consecutive observations. We develop dual-decoupled inference and matched staircase training, enabling high-throughput real-time control with improved success, smoothness, and reactivity. Related Work VLA policies and dynamic reactivity. Action chunking is a dominant imitation-learning formulation for visuomotor control, producing action sequences rather than single commands~ lai2025action,zhao2023learning,chi2025diffusion . It relies on expressive models such as action-chunking transformers, diffusion policies, and flow-matching policies~ zhao2023learning,george2023one,chi2025diffusion,chi2024universal,black2024pi_0,lipman2022flow,he2026demystifying,he2025latent . Recent work scales them with pretrained vision-language backbones into vision-language-action (VLA) models for generalist robot control~ brohan2022rt,zitkovich2023rt,kim2024openvla,black2024pi_0,intelligence2025pi_,o2024open,cheng2024navila,zhen20243d,zheng2025tracevla,liu2025rdt,he2025falcon , enabling task and embodiment generalization through larger robot datasets and visual-language pretraining~ o2024open,khazatsky2024droid,walke2023bridgedata,fang2023rh20t,mandlekar2018roboturk,team2025gemini,reuss2025flower . Yet chunked VLA policies create a coherence--reactivity conflict: longer chunks improve temporal consistency, but observations refresh only at boundaries, so scene changes can leave robots executing stale-context actions. inference acceleration and asynchronous inference. Prior work improves VLA responsiveness by reducing inference latency or hiding it with asynchronous execution~ yu2025survey,guan2025efficient . Latency reduction uses compact VLA architectures~ budzianowski2025edgevla,wen2025tinyvla,shukor2025smolvla,chen2025nanovla,williams2025lite,reuss2025flower , token caching or pruning~ xu2026vla,pei2025action,liu2025vla , compression~ zhang2026mole,yang2026efficientvla,chen2025rlrc , and faster generation via speculative decoding, flow acceleration, system optimization, or quantization~ wang2025spec,jia2026action,pertsch2025fast,lu2026faster,ma2025running,dai2025actionflow,wang2025bitvla . Asynchronous execution predicts the next action chunk during current-chunk execution to remove inter-chunk pauses~ zhao2025vla,jiang2025asyncvla,xie2026dynamicvla,cai2026xiaomi,liu2026learning , but direct chunk switching can cause observation-state mismatch, discontinuity, performance drops, and trajectory jitter~ liao2025delay,xie2026dynamicvla . RTC inpaints future actions conditioned on committed prefixes, while training-time RTC, REMAC, and VLASH condition prediction on executed or predicted prefixes~ black2026real,black2025training,wang2026real,tang2025vlash . These methods reduce or mask latency, but input throughput remains tied to action-execution cadence and may hurt performance or trajectory continuity. denoising for generative and robotic policies. Rolling denoising extends diffusion sampling from whole-sample refinement to sequential generation, emitting clean variables while appending noisy future ones. Vision and motion methods implement this idea through causal factorization, streaming diffusion, or rolling buffers for frame- or token-level decoding~ ruhe2024rolling,kim2024fifo,kodaira2025streamdit,deng2024causal,zhang2024tedi . Robotic diffusion policies roll action buffers, relay noise, or model observation-execution delay to avoid full sequence regeneration~ hoeg2024streaming,chen2025responsive,liao2025delay . However, they target non-VLA policies and do not address VLA inference, where VLM encoding and DiT denoising are coupled bottlenecks. brings rolling denoising to VLA stacks: executed actions exit, noisy actions enter, and active chunks are refined with updated visual-language embeddings. Dual Decoupling separates input processing from action generation, recovering async-like throughput while preserving trajectory continuity. title: Humanoid World Action Model With Joint State--Action Generation
summary: Humanoid robots are a promising platform for general-purpose manipulation. Recent Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies learn actions directly from multimodal observations, while World Action Models (WAMs) further incorporate future visual prediction to improve action generation. However, in hierarchical humanoid systems, VLA and WAM policies output reference actions that are subsequently realized through whole-body control, robot dynamics, balance, and contact. This hierarchy creates an action--execution gap: the reference produced by the policy can differ from the motion realized by the robot. Without explicitly modeling the realized body state, future visual prediction must jointly explain scene evolution and discrepancies between reference actions and executed motion, making it difficult to associate an action with its physical outcome. We propose HWAM, a Humanoid World Action Model with joint state--action generation, which makes the robot's post-execution proprioceptive state an explicit prediction target. By jointly generating reference actions and their realized body states, HWAM directly incorporates supervision of executed motion into action learning. HWAM is trained through three complementary conditional paths. The Policy path jointly denoises state--action trajectories conditioned only on current observations, matching deployment conditions. Forward Dynamics Modeling (FDM) predicts future visual observations conditioned on actions and post-execution states, while Inverse Dynamics Modeling (IDM) reconstructs the joint trajectory from visual transitions. Together, these paths connect policy references, realized body motion, and visual outcomes. HWAM achieves the highest success rate among evaluated baselines on three real-robot tasks on the LimX OLI humanoid. On Candy Picking, HWAM achieves a 70.6% success rate, compared with 43.3% for Fast-WAM.

On Candy Picking, HWAM achieves a 70.6 success rate, compared with 43.3 for Fast-WAM. Code, dataset, and project page are available at . Introduction General-purpose humanoid robots are expected to understand human instructions and execute diverse tasks in complex physical environments. Recent Vision-language-action (VLA) models have become a promising approach to this problem by unifying visual perception, language understanding, and action generation in a single multimodal policy. Systems such as PaLM-E, RT-2, and OpenVLA show that semantic knowledge from large vision-language models can support robot control and transfer across tasks and scenes palm-e, rt2, openvla . World Action Models (WAMs) further introduce future visual or latent-state prediction into action generation, allowing predicted futures to provide additional supervision or information for control wam_survey, uwm, wam_zero . These advances have moved robot policies beyond pure action regression toward predictive and generative control. General-purpose humanoid manipulation requires both task-level motion decisions and execution-level whole-body dynamics control. We adopt a hierarchical control architecture: a high-level vision--language--action policy generates reference trajectories in kinematic space from visual observations, language instructions, and the current proprioceptive state, while a low-level whole-body tracking controller uses real-time proprioceptive feedback to adapt these references to execution dynamics and drives the robot through joint servoing. This division allows the high-level policy to learn task behavior from demonstrations that primarily provide poses and motion trajectories, while reusing the low-level controller's whole-body coordination and feedback control capabilities humanplus, omnih2o . Accordingly, the action \(a_t\) in this paper denotes a motion reference supplied to the low-level tracking controller, rather than a torque applied directly to an actuator, and it is not assumed to be realizable point by point. Figure~ fig:hierarchy summarizes this hierarchical control interface. This hierarchical interface also introduces a discrepancy between the high-level reference and the actual body response. The low-level tracking policy adapts reference motion to the current body state, contact conditions, and dynamic constraints, so the realized motion can deviate from the reference. For example, a reference trajectory may request simultaneous trunk motion and arm extension; adjustments to trunk motion made by the low-level controller to maintain balance can also change the hand trajectory at contact. Thus, even a kinematically feasible reference does not ensure the intended task outcome after low-level execution. The high-level policy needs to learn the body responses produced by low-level tracking and adaptation to robot dynamics, so that reference generation can account for actual execution outcomes. We refer to the discrepancy between a high-level reference action and its physical realization as the action--execution gap. This gap complicates action learning through future visual prediction. A policy reference can differ from the state realized after low-level execution. If this intermediate state is not modeled, the model must learn simultaneously how the policy action is physically realized and how the realized motion changes the scene. This makes the relation between the policy action and its future visual outcome difficult to learn. HWAM addresses this problem by explicitly placing the post-execution state in the action-generation target and then connecting the joint state--action trajectory to visual transitions in both directions. Dataset statistics reveal larger discrepancies between commanded joint references and measured proprioceptive states in mobile humanoid manipulation than in stationary bimanual manipulation, including under steady-state conditions (Section~ sec:execution_gap ). This observation motivates representing the post-execution proprioceptive state explicitly instead of asking a policy to relate a high-level action directly to its downstream visual consequence. Prior work has explored body-state representations and prediction for humanoid control~ humanoid_policy, hex . We propose HWAM, a humanoid-oriented World Action Model that incorporates post-execution states into its trajectory generation target. Joint generation is a natural extension of the WAM action stream: state and action share a temporal structure and can be modeled by the same trajectory generator. At each temporal position, we align action \(a_ t+h \) with proprioceptive state \(s_ t+h+1 \) and represent them as the joint state--action target The state and action channels are concatenated before token projection and jointly denoised by a shared state--action generator. This gives action generation access to the evolving state estimate throughout denoising. We study how the resulting joint target interacts with visual training objectives to improve closed-loop task performance. Building on conditional world-action modeling~ uwm, cosmos3 , HWAM incorporates post-execution states into three training paths. The Policy path jointly denoises state--action trajectories conditioned on current visual observations, language, and proprioception, without generating future video. This supervises policy references together with their measured execution outcomes. Forward Dynamics Modeling (FDM) supplements this objective by conditioning future visual prediction on actions and post-execution states, explicitly accounting for realized body motion when predicting scene changes. Inverse Dynamics Modeling (IDM) adds supervision in the reverse direction, using visual transitions to jointly predict actions and the body states they produce. The three paths connect policy references to both execution states and visual outcomes. At deployment, predicted states continue to participate in joint denoising, while only the actions are sent to the low-level controller. Our evaluation asks whether the action--execution gap is observable in robot data, whether a joint state--action target becomes effective when combined with bidirectional visual grounding, and whether the resulting policy improves real-robot manipulation. We evaluate stationary and mobile manipulation on the LimX OLI humanoid and a task-specific clothes-folding setting on ALOHA~ aloha . Our main contributions are: Post-execution state--action generation. We pair each high-level action with its temporally aligned post-execution proprioceptive state and denoise the two channels as one joint target. Execution-state grounding. Post-execution states serve as conditions for future-video prediction in FDM and as joint prediction targets with actions in IDM and Policy, connecting execution-state supervision to visual transitions. Controlled real-robot evidence. A factorial ablation identifies the interaction between the joint target and the three-path training formulation, and real-robot experiments evaluate the resulting model on humanoid and bimanual manipulation. Related Work Vision-Language-Action Models Vision-language-action (VLA) models unify visual perception, language understanding, and robot control. PaLM-E integrates embodied observations into a multimodal language model for reasoning and planning palm-e . RT-2 transfers vision-language knowledge to robot control via action tokenization, while OpenVLA explores open-source VLA learning from large-scale demonstrations rt2, openvla . Recent systems improve generalization through heterogeneous data and continuous action generation. For instance, achieves open-world generalization via multi-source co-training, enabling manipulation in novel environments pi05 , and its successor introduces a steerable generalist foundation model with emergent compositional generalization and cross-embodiment transfer pi07 . In NVIDIA's GR00T series, GR00T N1 is an open foundation model for generalist humanoid reasoning and skills, combining a pretrained vision-language module with a diffusion Transformer action generator for cross-embodiment manipulation groot_n1 . Its updates, GR00T N1.5 and N1.7, enhance instruction following and upgrade the VLM backbone to Cosmos-Reason2-2B (Qwen3-VL) with large-scale human and simulation pretraining, improving generalization and long-horizon reasoning groot_n15, groot_n17 . World Action Models and Joint Generative Policies World Action Models incorporate future prediction into policy learning. Existing approaches include cascaded models that first generate future observations and then infer actions, as well as joint models that generate future visual variables and actions within a shared generative framework wam_survey . Unified World Models (UWM) couple video and action diffusion and use modality-specific diffusion steps to represent policies, forward dynamics, inverse dynamics, and video generation uwm . Cosmos 3 distinguishes forward dynamics, inverse dynamics, and a policy mode that jointly predicts video and action~ cosmos3 . Motus integrates understanding, video, and action experts in a Mixture-of-Transformers architecture and supports multiple conditional generation modes within one model motus . Fast-WAM retains video co-training while predicting actions from current observations without explicit future-video synthesis at inference time fast_wam . Joint generative trajectory modeling provides a related precedent. Diffuser models state--action trajectories with a diffusion model and generates complete trajectories through iterative denoising diffuser . Cosmos Policy jointly predicts actions and a future state containing proprioception and images~ cosmos_policy . Body-State Representations for Humanoid Control Body-state representations help humanoid policies coordinate high-dimensional configurations, multiple effectors, and contact-dependent motion. HumanPlus and OmniH2O use hierarchical control to connect task-level motion references with whole-body execution humanplus, omnih2o . humanoid_policy use a shared state--action representation to learn humanoid policies from human and robot demonstrations. title: SkillWeave: Weaving Heterogeneous Demonstrations into Long-Horizon Manipulation Skills
comment: IROS 2026 Workshop on Haptics and Dexterous Manipulation
summary: Dexterous manipulation requires both large-scale task progression and precise contact-rich interaction, making it challenging to collect demonstrations that effectively support both regimes. We present SkillWeave, a heterogeneous demonstration framework for long-horizon dexterous manipulation that combines teleoperation for coarse reaching and transport with kinesthetic teaching for precise, contact-rich skills. To address the visual mismatch introduced by the demonstrator's presence during kinesthetic data collection, we propose an object-mask-conditioned diffusion policy that uses offline object segmentation for training supervision and a lightweight learned mask predictor at deployment, avoiding online segmentation and image inpainting. To mitigate distribution shift between independently trained sub-task policies, we introduce successor-aware terminal steering, which selects among actions sampled from the predecessor policy to guide the system toward states supported by the successor's demonstrated initial-state distribution. Across three real-world long-horizon tasks, SkillWeave achieves 27% average end-to-end success. Mask-conditioned kinesthetic policies improve dexterous sub-task success to an average of 65%, while successor-aware handoffs achieve an average composition efficiency of 87%. These results show that matching demonstration modality to interaction regime, explicitly addressing kinesthetic visual mismatch, and steering policy handoffs toward successor-supported states substantially improves long-horizon dexterous manipulation. Videos and code are available at skillweave-authors.github.io .

Department of Computer Science, Keio University, Japan. College of Engineering, University of California, Berkeley, USA. Bosch Center for Artificial Intelligence, Pittsburgh, PA, USA. We propose , a framework that learns from multi-modal demonstration, where teleoperation is used for long-horizon coverage and free-space reaching (blue box), and kinesthetic teaching is used for precise contact-rich interaction (red box). Through policy composition with our proposed inference-time steering mechanism, is able to combine policies trained with individual sub-tasks and achieve long-horizon task success. fig:figure1 Dexterous manipulation requires both large-scale task progression and precise contact-rich interaction, making it challenging to collect demonstrations that effectively support both regimes. Mask-conditioned kinesthetic policies improve dexterous sub-task success to an average of 65 , while successor-aware handoffs achieve an average composition efficiency of 87 . Videos and code are available at skillweave-authors.github.io . Introduction Dexterous manipulation combines high-dimensional control with repeated and often discontinuous changes in contact. Such behaviors have been studied through model-based control, reinforcement learning, and sim-to-real transfer kolbert2017contact,openai2020dexterous . Demonstrations offer a complementary route by placing the learner directly on task-relevant state--action trajectories. They have been used both to accelerate reinforcement learning and to train expressive visuomotor policies through behavior cloning rajeswaran2018dexterous,chi2023diffusion . Demonstration data can also be obtained or expanded through human videos and automated trajectory generation qin2022dexmv,chen2026videomanip,mandlekar2023mimicgen . Regardless of its source, however, the resulting policy can learn only from the states and interactions represented in the data; demonstration collection therefore directly shapes the capabilities and failure modes of the learned behavior~ lin2024datascaling , and the specific type of demonstration collection strategy used thus has a strong effect on the properties of the downstream policy yoo2025kinesoft . Teleoperation captures task progression and spatial coverage, but retargeting and indirect contact feedback can limit precision during dexterous interaction naughton2024respilot,zhang2025kinedex . On the other hand, kinesthetic teaching provides direct guidance through robot-feasible contact configurations, but introduces demonstrator occlusion into the recorded images chen2025dexforce,zhang2025kinedex . These complementary limitations motivate our central hypothesis: under long-horizon dexterous manipulation, which alternates between free-space motion and contact-rich interaction, each phase should be demonstrated through the modality best suited to its interaction regime. We combine teleoperation demonstrations for task-level coverage with kinesthetic demonstrations at contact-rich phases. Collecting each subtask separately also makes the data cheaper to gather, since a failed attempt costs one subtask rather than the whole episode. However, data matched to the modulus of subtasks alone do not guaranty a successful composition. Each boundary introduced by the decomposition must be reached through two different processes: the demonstrator reaches it during data collection, whereas at deployment it must be reached by the preceding policy. Small prediction errors accumulate throughout that subtask, causing the predecessor's terminal state to drift away from the states represented in the demonstrations. The successor policy therefore begins from an out-of-distribution state and may fail despite succeeding in isolation; this mismatch can compound over a sequence of subtasks. This terminal-to-initial distribution mismatch is a known limitation of naive skill composition ~ lee2019composing,lee2022adversarial . Illustrated by , we address this issue by inserting a short bridging motion between consecutive policies. The bridge guides the robot from the predecessor's realized terminal state toward the region of states represented by the successor's demonstrated initial state distribution. Kinesthetic data also creates an observation mismatch: the demonstrator occludes the object during training but is absent during autonomous execution. Prior approaches remove visible embodiments through inpainting bahl2022human,chen2024mirage,zhang2025kinedex , which requires reconstructing unobserved content near the interaction region. We instead use SAM~3 to generate object masks offline for the training demonstrations~ carion2025sam3 . These masks supervise a learned mask predictor whose output conditions the diffusion policy during deployment. This removes SAM~3 and image inpainting from the online control loop. Our experiments test three claims: matching demonstration modality to interaction regime improves long-horizon, contact-rich manipulation; bridging into the successor's demonstrated initial states is necessary when independently learned behaviors are composed; and object-mask conditioning makes kinesthetic policy learning more robust to changes in background and scene. In summary, this paper makes the following contributions: We introduce a multi-modal demonstration framework that uses teleoperation for long-horizon coverage and free-space reaching, and kinesthetic teaching for precise contact-rich interaction. We develop successor-aware terminal steering to guide predecessor policies toward the successor's start-state distribution, reducing distribution shift at policy boundaries for reliable long-horizon composition. We develop an object-mask-conditioned diffusion policy for kinesthetic demonstrations. SAM~3 provides offline training masks, while a learned predictor supplies masks during deployment, improving robustness across backgrounds and scenes without online SAM~3 or image inpainting in the control loop. Related Work sec:related_work Demonstration Collection for Manipulation Robot learning from demonstration commonly relies on teleoperation, kinesthetic teaching, or observation of human behavior~ argall2009survey . These modalities expose the learner to different state--action distributions, making data coverage and diversity as important as demonstration count ~ lin2024datascaling . Early dexterous teleoperation systems mapped observed human motion to robot actions through hand-pose estimation and kinematic retargeting~ qin2022one . More recent systems improve usability and data quality through immersive visual feedback, higher-rate tracking, and haptic interfaces ding2024bunny,iyer2025openteach,cheng2025television . However, they retain an embodiment-matching problem: differences between human and robot kinematics can make reachable human poses inaccurate or infeasible for the robot. ResPilot reduces this mismatch through learned residual corrections, but remains limited by the underlying retargeting interface~ naughton2024respilot . These errors become particularly important during contact, where small configuration errors can change the resulting force or invalidate a grasp. Kinesthetic teaching avoids retargeting by directly guiding the robot. DexForce extracts force-informed actions from kinesthetic demonstrations, but replays trajectories to obtain demonstrator-free images~ chen2025dexforce . Because replay is open loop, the object need not follow its original motion, so the recovered images may not correspond to the states in which the recorded actions were executed. KineDex instead preserves the original interaction and removes the demonstrator through segmentation and inpainting~ zhang2025kinedex , trading motion inconsistency for reconstruction error in occluded regions. Existing systems therefore improve single modalities but fail to combine modalities tailored to distinct task phases. We address this by pairing teleoperation for long-horizon coverage with kinesthetic teaching for contact-rich corrections. Finally, demonstrations are commonly converted into visuomotor policies via behavior cloning; for instance, Diffusion Policy models this as conditional denoising over action sequences, supporting multimodal prediction and receding-horizon execution~ chi2023diffusion . Skill Composition Long-horizon execution requires one skill's terminal states to fall within the next skill's initiation distribution. Prior work addresses this mismatch using learned transition policies lee2019composing , terminal state regularization lee2022adversarial , or feasibility-guided fine-tuning and switching chen2023sequential . These methods require additional reinforcement-learning interaction and modify or augment the constituent policies. Related methods instead keep a single policy near its training distribution sun2025latentbarrier or improve continuity between its action chunks he2026focalpolicy , rather than connect independently trained skills. We use an explicit bridging motion to connect two policies while leaving their parameters unchanged. Visual Invariance in Demonstration Learning Early approaches improved visual robustness through augmentation or by removing the acting embodiment from images. GenAug uses generative image editing to vary objects and scenes, but does not address occlusion of task-relevant content ~ chen2023genaug . WHIRL inpaints humans and robots to construct an embodiment-invariant objective, while Mirage cross-paints a source robot over the target robot during deployment~ bahl2022human,chen2024mirage . These methods depend on reconstructing occluded pixels, which can introduce artifacts near contact regions. Object-centric methods instead suppress irrelevant appearance through structured representations. VIOLA operates on object proposals, and GROOT uses object-centric 3D features~ zhu2023viola,zhu2023groot ; however, both assume that task-relevant objects remain observable. More recently, SHADOW replaces robot pixels with composite masks, but requires calibrated robot geometry and test-time masking; its masks can also obscure robot--object contacts~ lepert2025shadow . KineDex applies inpainting to kinesthetic demonstrations, inheriting the difficulty of reconstructing objects hidden by the demonstrator~ zhang2025kinedex . Our method avoids image reconstruction and uses segmentation only as training-time supervision. title: ManiUnit: A Manipulation Skill Dataset and Benchmark for Long-Horizon Tasks
summary: Long-horizon mobile manipulation requires a robot to navigate multi-room environments and execute a sequence of manipulation skills under a single natural language instruction. Learning and evaluating these skills present three challenges: similar observations under a fixed task instruction may make skill selection ambiguous; even when a preceding skill succeeds, the robot state inherited by the next skill may deviate from its demonstrated starting states and affect execution; and task-level metrics hinder skill-specific diagnosis, while early failures leave later skills untested. We therefore introduce ManiUnit, a manipulation skill dataset and benchmark built from 50 BEHAVIOR-1K activities. Its dataset contains 137,899 segments across 21 skill types and 417 subtasks, and its benchmark contains 1,260 test instances. Correspondingly, ManiUnit pairs each segment with an explicit subtask instruction; measures sensitivity to perturbations of the robot's starting base position or joint configuration; and restores intermediate simulator states and defines local success conditions so that each skill can be evaluated without executing preceding stages. Evaluations of representative vision-language-action (VLA) policies show that similar aggregate scores can hide substantial per-skill differences. The tested starting-state perturbations also degrade execution: on the full benchmark, joint perturbations reduce success rates by approximately 56% relative to those from demonstrated starting states. On two long-horizon activities, a skill policy trained on ManiUnit segments achieves 78.7% local manipulation success, compared with 49.3% for a task policy trained on complete demonstrations. The trained skills further support complete-task execution on these activities, as coordinating the task and skill policies through a planner raises full-task success from 4.0% to 18.0%.
