Introduction sec:intro Enabling robots to complete long-horizon mobile manipulation tasks in everyday environments is a central challenge for embodied AI. Unlike tabletop manipulation, which operates in a fixed workspace, this setting requires robots to navigate across multi-room environments and execute a sequence of interdependent manipulation skills guided by a single natural language instruction. Recent vision-language-action (VLA) models zitkovich2023rt2,kim2025openvla,black2025pi0,black2025pi05,nvidia2025gr00t,gemini2025robotics have achieved strong results on tabletop benchmarks: StarVLA- starvla2026 , for example, reaches 95.7 success on LIBERO liu2023libero and 88.8 under the randomized setting of RoboTwin 2.0 chen2026robotwin . Despite this progress, reliable execution of long-horizon tasks remains challenging: the winning entry in the 2025 BEHAVIOR Challenge achieved a full-task success rate of only 12.4 on the held-out test set larchenko2025task , leaving substantial room for improvement. Consider one such task, ``make microwave popcorn,'' which requires navigation interleaved with opening the microwave door, picking up the popcorn bag, placing it inside, closing the door, and turning on the microwave. Such sequences pose three challenges for skill learning and evaluation. (1)~Skill ambiguity: when a policy follows the same task instruction throughout execution, it needs to infer the current stage from its observations and act accordingly. This inference can break down when different stages share similar visual context: before loading food, the robot faces a closed microwave door and must open it, but after placing the food inside and closing the door, it again faces the same closed door yet must now turn on the microwave instead of opening the door. (2)~Starting-state mismatch: during sequential execution, even a successfully completed skill may leave the robot in a base position or joint configuration that differs from the starting states in the next skill's training demonstrations, and this mismatch can cause a policy that succeeds from demonstrated starting states to fail when following a preceding skill. (3)~Evaluation opacity: overall task success reflects both navigation and manipulation, making it difficult to identify which skills limit performance; moreover, an early failure can prevent later skills from being attempted. These challenges motivate treating individual manipulation operations as units of training and evaluation. We therefore introduce ManiUnit, a manipulation skill dataset and benchmark built by segmenting long-horizon BEHAVIOR-1K demonstrations li2023behavior into such operations. Figure~ fig:overview maps each challenge to the corresponding design choice. For skill ambiguity, ManiUnit attaches an explicit subtask instruction to each segment, naming the operation, the objects it acts on, and the spatial context, keeping the intended operation explicit during skill learning and evaluation. For starting-state mismatch, ManiUnit evaluates each skill under three conditions: the demonstrated state, a base-position perturbation, and a joint-configuration perturbation. These controlled tests measure how variations in the robot's starting state affect skill execution. For evaluation opacity, ManiUnit constructs test instances by restoring intermediate simulator states and defining local success conditions for each subtask, so every skill can be evaluated independently without first executing the stages that precede it. The dataset covers 50 activities with 21 skill types, 417 subtasks, and 137,899 segments with a mean duration of 17.9 seconds, each paired with head and wrist RGB streams, robot states, and actions. The benchmark contains 1,260 test instances, drawn from 20 operation starts per skill type under the three starting-state conditions. Evaluating representative VLA policies on ManiUnit shows that similar aggregate scores can hide substantial differences in per-skill performance. The evaluations also reveal pronounced sensitivity to the tested starting-state perturbations: on the full benchmark, joint perturbations reduce success rates by approximately 56 relative to those from demonstrated starting states. On Turning On Radio and Picking Up Trash, we compare task and skill policies initialized from the same pretrained weights. The skill policy trained on ManiUnit segments achieves 78.7 local manipulation success, compared with 49.3 for the task policy trained on complete demonstrations. To deploy these skills in complete tasks, a planner coordinates the task and skill policies and supplies the appropriate subtask instructions (Figure~ fig:overview , bottom). On the same activities, the combined system achieves 18.0 full-task success, compared with 4.0 for the task policy alone. Our contributions are threefold. (1) We introduce the ManiUnit dataset: 137,899 segments from 50 BEHAVIOR-1K activities with explicit subtask instructions, organized by skill type and subtask to support mixed-skill training and targeted data selection. (2) We construct the ManiUnit benchmark: 1,260 test instances from restored intermediate states with local success conditions and separate base and joint perturbations, enabling independent per-skill evaluation and measurement of starting-state sensitivity. (3) We evaluate representative VLA policies to characterize skill performance and starting-state sensitivity, and show on two long-horizon activities that ManiUnit-trained skills improve local manipulation success and support complete-task execution through policy composition. ManiUnit Dataset and Benchmark sec:maniunit Overview sec:dataset_overview sec:dataset_statistics To study manipulation skills independently within long-horizon tasks, we construct ManiUnit from the 2025 Challenge demonstrations of 50 BEHAVIOR-1K activities~ li2023behavior . ManiUnit comprises a dataset of manipulation segments paired with explicit subtask instructions and a benchmark for evaluating selected operations from restored starting states. Figure~ fig:pipeline summarizes how the source demonstrations are processed into these training and evaluation resources. The dataset distinguishes three levels of organization. A identifies an operation category, such as Pour. A is defined by an instruction specifying the operation, objects, and spatial context, such as ``pour the grated cheese from the tupperware onto the pizza dough.'' A records one demonstrated execution of that subtask. Grouping segments by skill type and subtask allows researchers to pool demonstrations across source activities or select data for particular operations. ManiUnit-Full contains 21 skill types, 417 subtasks, and 137,899 segments. We also curate ManiUnit-Lite, a subset of 10,588 segments across 7 skill types, to reduce the computational cost of repeated experiments. Table~ tab:skill_inventory in Appendix~ app:overview reports the per-skill inventory of ManiUnit-Full. For evaluation, we select operation starts from the source demonstrations and restore the corresponding robot and scene states. For each selected subtask, we manually define a local BDDL goal that specifies the object states and relations required to complete the manipulation operation. The restored state, subtask instruction, and local goal together form a test instance, allowing the operation to be evaluated without executing preceding task stages. To measure sensitivity to starting-state variations, we construct three conditions for each selected start: Original, Base Perturbation, and Joint Perturbation. The Full and Lite evaluation suites contain 1,260 and 186 test instances, respectively. Sections~ sec:dataset_construction and~ sec:benchmark_construction describe the dataset and benchmark construction procedures. Dataset Construction sec:data sec:construction sec:dataset_construction As shown in Figure~ fig:pipeline , the source demonstrations contain RGB observations, robot states, and actions, together with temporal annotations of navigation and manipulation. Each annotation records an action label, the participating objects, and the action's start and end frames. However, these intervals do not always correspond to the manipulation segments needed for training. For example, pushing an object into reach and picking it up may be annotated separately despite contributing to the same Pick Up operation, while a recorded pickup interval may also include navigation before grasping or inactivity afterward. To preserve complete manipulation operations while reducing surrounding navigation and inactivity, we extract and merge the relevant action intervals and refine their boundaries. We then curate an explicit subtask instruction for each resulting segment. Segment extraction and merging. We first extract manipulation intervals based on the annotated actions. For each source activity, we manually specify which annotations to retain and apply this selection across its episodes. For example, in the Picking Up Trash activity, we retain all annotated pickup and placement actions, each yielding an initial segment. The recorded start and end frames of each retained annotation provide the initial segment boundaries. Since supporting motions may be annotated separately from the operation they serve, we define merging rules to combine them into complete manipulation segments. In the board-game example in Figure~ fig:pipeline , pushing the game toward the bed edge prepares it for grasping. We therefore combine the push and subsequent pickup into one Pick Up segment. The merged segment spans the start of the first contributing action through the end of the last, retaining all intervening frames. Appendix~ app:extraction_rules details the extraction and merging rules. Temporal boundary refinement. We refine the boundaries of the extracted and merged segments to reduce navigation and inactivity around the target operation. title: Lamarck's Driving School: Discovering Autonomous Driving Training Strategies through Evolutionary Competition
summary: Autonomous driving capabilities depend strongly on the distribution of scenarios encountered during training. Existing methods commonly construct or dynamically adapt training scenario distributions using surrogate criteria such as realism, difficulty, or risk. However, these predefined surrogates may misrepresent training value, leading to inefficient use of training resources. To address this limitation, we propose a Lamarckian evolutionary framework that replaces surrogate-based guidance with competition among candidate distributions. We formulate training strategy discovery as a multi-stage bilevel optimization problem and use Lamarckian evolution algorithm to approximate its solution. At the outer level, Darwinian crossover, mutation, and selection explore the scenario distribution space; at the inner level, policy learning acquires new capabilities, and Lamarckian inheritance transfers them to subsequent stages, allowing scenario distributions and policy capabilities to co-evolve. The resulting evolutionary trajectories reveal recurring stage-wise regularities among high-value distributions, characterized by capability accumulation through stage-wise challenge rotation. We further distill these regularities into a lightweight, reusable Lamarckian Training Strategy. Experiments show that, compared with the baseline, the complete framework reduces performance loss by up to 25.07%, while the lightweight strategy still achieves a 19.13% reduction. These results demonstrate that evolutionary competition can both discover effective training strategies and reveal reusable stage-wise patterns in how the value of training distributions changes with policy capability. Code is available on GitHub.

title: RESETTLE: Robotic Recovery through Disagreement-Triggered Retrieval and Efficient Corrective Control
summary: Reliable robotic manipulation requires timely intervention to correct emerging deviations and restore progress after execution errors. However, recovery methods based on repeated vision-language reasoning or iterative online optimization can incur substantial latency, delaying intervention. To address these challenges, we introduce RESETTLE(Robotic rEcovery through diSagrEement-Triggered reTrievaL and Efficient Corrective Control), a model-agnostic framework that provides computationally efficient recovery at the action-execution interface of frozen robot policies. RESETTLE triggers recovery when two action proposals independently sampled under identical conditioning persistently disagree. It retrieves a same-task demonstration reference using an adapted V-JEPA encoder and combines a state-servo prior with a guarded visual residual to execute one corrective action without online trajectory optimization or additional vision-language reasoning, then returns control to the base policy. Across six base policies in simulation, RESETTLE achieves up to 8.70%, 6.28%, and 6.83% absolute success-rate gains on LIBERO-Plus, Meta-World, and RoboCasa Tabletop, respectively, with further improvements on four real-world tasks using two policies. In QwenPI-based comparisons, its monitoring-and-recovery computation latency is 74.04%--93.57% lower than VoLoAgent's monitoring-and-planning latency for grasp and place tool calls. It also raises Harness VLA's LIBERO-Pro Swap success from 42% to 50%, demonstrating compatibility with high-level agentic planning. Code available at: https://github.com/JIA-Lab-research/RESETTLE

Code available at: Introduction Timely recovery is essential for reliable robotic manipulation, helping robots correct potentially harmful motions before an error occurs and restore task progress after errors. For example, adjusting the gripper orientation while approaching a moka pot can help avoid an ineffective grasp, whereas repositioning the gripper after a bowl is dropped can enable regrasping and subsequent placement. These interventions support continued execution by addressing both emerging problems and the consequences of earlier mistakes. Despite substantial progress in vision--language--action (VLA) policies and world--action models (WAMs)~ intelligence2025pi_,ye2026starvla,yang2026beyond,kim2024openvla,yuan2026fast,ye2026world,cen2025worldvla,ma2026dit4dit , environmental changes and imperfect actions can still drive execution into unfamiliar states where the policy struggles to make progress, highlighting the need for timely corrective intervention. To equip robots with such corrective capabilities, existing approaches broadly follow three strategies. First, corrective policy training incorporates recovery behavior through additional supervision: DAgger collects expert labels on learner-visited states~ ross2011reduction , while IntervenGen generates recovery trajectories from human interventions~ hoque2024intervengen . Both expand the policy's corrective experience but require additional data and policy updates. Second, VLM-supervised recovery coordinates corrective behaviors through semantic assessment. Agentic Robot uses visual verification to trigger corrections and retries~ yang2025agentic , while VoLoAgent switches between policy execution and recovery tools~ chen2026volo . This supports flexible task-level recovery, but repeated verification and recovery computation introduce latency. Third, inference-time action correction preserves base-policy weights while adjusting action generation. LPB uses expert-feature distance to trigger dynamics-guided denoising on diffusion policies~ sun2026latent . When extended to generalized VLA/WAMs, however, we observe greater overlap between feature-distance distributions of successful and failed executions, reducing its effectiveness for error detection; VLA-Corrector detects visual prediction discrepancies and applies gradient-guided replanning~ pan2026vla , while the online gradient computation adds recovery overhead. To push forward this line of research direction, we ask: Can we efficiently identify when a frozen policy needs assistance and directly generate corrections before deviations escalate into task failure? To answer this question, we introduce RESETTLE, a framework for efficient action-level recovery with frozen robot policies. Many generative robot policies sample actions from noise conditioned on observations and task instructions~ chi2025diffusion,black2024pi_0 . This sampling process allows us to probe the stability of action choices under identical conditioning. For QwenPI, Figure~ fig:analysis_action shows that training-data inference and successful executions align in the dominant low-disagreement region, whereas failed executions exhibit heavier tails. Motivated by this observation, RESETTLE monitors two independently sampled proposals and triggers intervention when their disagreement persists. To guide recovery, we use successful demonstrations as empirical anchors without requiring them to cover the policy's entire feasible operating range. We initialize the recovery representation from V-JEPA 2-AC~ assran2025v and adapt it through dynamics prediction and corrective-action supervision, encouraging features useful for reference matching and control. The adapted encoder retrieves the nearest same-task demonstration reference in its representation space, together with the associated robot state. A state-servo prior provides motion toward this reference state, while a guarded visual residual uses current and reference observations to adjust the motion to the scene. Each intervention executes one corrective action before returning control to the base policy with a fresh observation. This design directly constructs recovery actions without online trajectory optimization or additional vision-language reasoning. Our experiments assess both the effectiveness and computational cost of local recovery. Across six base policies on LIBERO-Plus, Meta-World, and RoboCasa Tabletop~ fei2026libero,yu2020meta,nasiriany2024robocasa , RESETTLE improves aggregate task success while keeping the base policies frozen. Further improvements across four real-world tasks with two policies support its applicability beyond simulation. In QwenPI-based comparisons, measured monitoring-and-recovery computation latency is 74.04 --93.57 lower than VoLoAgent's combined monitoring-and-planning latency for grasp and place tool calls, supporting the efficiency of direct correction. Integration with Harness VLA on LIBERO-Pro Swap~ zhang2026harness,zhou2025libero further demonstrates that action-level recovery complements high-level agentic planning. Our contributions are twofold: i) We introduce RESETTLE, an efficient action-level recovery framework that combines persistent disagreement monitoring, demonstration retrieval, and direct corrective control for frozen VLA policies and WAMs, without base-policy fine-tuning, additional vision-language reasoning calls for recovery, or online trajectory optimization; ii) We validate its effectiveness in simulation and real-world manipulation, quantify reductions in monitoring-and-recovery computation latency, and demonstrate that local recovery complements high-level agentic planning through integration with Harness VLA. Related Work related_work Generative VLA and World-Action Models. Generative policies such as Diffusion Policy, , and SmolVLA produce actions through diffusion or flow matching~ chi2025diffusion,black2024pi_0,shukor2025smolvla . Video-action architectures such as DiT4DiT and FastWAM incorporate visual dynamics into policy learning, with FastWAM omitting explicit future-video generation at inference~ ma2026dit4dit,yuan2026fast . Together, these approaches advance policy representations and action generation. RESETTLE complements these capabilities through execution recovery at the action interface, leaving base-policy weights and action-generation mechanisms unchanged. Latent World Models and JEPA-Based Control. DINO-WM and V-JEPA 2-AC predict visual latents under candidate actions and use online optimization for goal-directed control~ zhou2024dino,assran2025v . INTACT learns an intent-to-action interface with latent dynamics supervision, enabling control without online search~ sun2026intact . RESETTLE uses dynamics supervision during training, initializing its encoder and predictor from V-JEPA-2-AC. Its deployment role is selective recovery: demonstration states anchor a servo prior, refined by a guarded visual residual, before control returns to a frozen policy. The dynamics predictor is inactive at deployment. Failure Recovery in Visuomotor Policies. DAgger incorporates expert labels on learner-visited states into policy training, while RACER uses language-annotated recovery trajectories~ ross2011reduction,dai2025racer . Further, agia2024unpacking combine temporal action consistency with VLM for progress monitoring. The existing works show that semantic supervision supports failure diagnosis~ duan2024aha , constraint-based replanning~ guo2024doremi , and recovery coordination ~ yang2025agentic,chen2026volo . LPB and VLA-Corrector preserve policy weights, but they rely on gradient-guided action refinement which adds computational burden~ sun2026latent,pan2026vla . Instead, our RESETTLE monitors persistent disagreement under identical conditioning and directly constructs reference-based corrections, avoiding online dynamics prediction, gradient guidance, and additional VLM reasoning while complementing high-level supervision. Preliminaries sec:preliminaries Diffusion and Flow Matching in VLAs and WAMs. We consider VLA and WAM policies that generate action chunks via diffusion or flow matching, conditioned on observations and task instructions. Each chunk specifies commands for multiple future control steps. Diffusion models learn to denoise action sequences, while flow-matching models learn a velocity field that transforms noise into actions~ chi2025diffusion,black2024pi_0 . At inference, sampled noise is iteratively transformed into an action chunk. Different noise samples can yield different chunks under identical conditioning, reflecting variability in the learned conditional action distribution. Comparing these samples provides an action-disagreement signal without updating the base policy's weights. Action-Conditioned Prediction with V-JEPA 2. V-JEPA 2 learns visual representations from large-scale unlabeled video data by predicting masked video regions in a learned feature space. Its action-conditioned extension, V-JEPA 2-AC, predicts future visual representations from visual context, robot states, and actions~ assran2025v . This formulation motivates learning representations that capture action consequences, providing a foundation for selecting corrective actions during recovery. We adapt the pretrained V-JEPA 2 encoder offline using action-conditioned prediction with residual supervision. At deployment, the adapted encoder supports reference retrieval and residual action prediction to guide corrective actions. As shown in Figure~ fig:method , our method addresses three decisions: . Given the current observation, robot state, and task identity, it monitors action disagreement, retrieves a successful reference when intervention is triggered, and generates a corrective action efficiently. Note that our method requires no access to the base policy's internal representations. Disagreement-Based Intervention. At each nominal decision, we generate two action chunks from independent noise samples under identical observations and task conditioning. We measure their temporally weighted disagreement using an embodiment-specific action metric. title: MiniWAM: Learning Compact Future Targets for Efficient World-Action Modeling
summary: World modeling has emerged as an effective co-training objective for robot policies, giving rise to World Action Models (WAMs) that jointly predict actions and future states. However, most WAMs predict future states in the native representation space of pretrained visual backbones, resulting in high-dimensional targets with substantial training cost. We introduce MiniWAM, which instead predicts compact future representations learned from privileged current-future transitions. To construct these targets, we propose Predictive Representations via Inverse Spatiotemporal Modeling (PRISM), which combines inverse-dynamics supervision with feature reconstruction to emphasize control-relevant transition information while preserving useful future-state information. With the learned PRISM encoder frozen, MiniWAM is trained to jointly predict the resulting targets and robot actions from current observations. With 65$\times$ fewer native future feature tokens, MiniWAM consistently outperforms native future-feature prediction with both DINOv3 and WAN2.1 VAE features, while achieving up to an 8$\times$ speedup in world-action training. At 0.25B parameters, MiniWAM is already competitive with substantially larger WAMs on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboTwin 2.0 simulation benchmarks. Representation analyses further show that PRISM contributes behavioral structure beyond feature reconstruction alone. These results demonstrate that effective world-action modeling does not require predicting native visual futures, and that compact predictive representations provide a strong and substantially more efficient target for policy learning. The project page is available at: https://j1dan.github.io/MiniWAM.

The project page is available at: https://j1dan.github.io/MiniWAM . Introduction Learning to predict future observations alongside robot actions provides a powerful training signal for robot control. Recent World Action Models (WAMs) exploit this idea by jointly learning robot actions and future visual states, encouraging policy representations to capture environment dynamics relevant to control kim2026cosmos, ye2026world, yuan2026fast, yuan2026dreamwam, cen2025worldvla . This paradigm has led to strong results across simulated and real-world manipulation. However, it also introduces a substantial computational burden. Most WAMs model the future through high-dimensional visual representations, typically dense video-VAE latents inherited from video-generation models wan2025wan . Predicting these representations requires processing large spatiotemporal token sequences, making world modeling considerably more expensive. Yet preserving every detail in the native feature space may not be necessary for action learning. Prior work has increasingly sought to improve the efficiency of WAMs by reducing the cost of future generation yuan2026fast , sparsifying world--action interaction zhao2026faster , or shrinking the model and token budget devoted to visual prediction li2026efficient . A complementary line of work replaces dense visual prediction with compact latent future supervision, using representations of future observations to shape policy-internal latent states zheng2025flare,su2026world,luo2026being . Together, these approaches suggest that the benefits of future modeling need not rely on explicit high-dimensional visual rollouts. However, existing efficiency-oriented WAMs still retain rich visual representations as their world-modeling targets, while latent approaches primarily incorporate future information through internal policy states or auxiliary conditioning spaces. This leaves a distinct question: can we directly learn a compact yet control-relevant future representation that replaces dense visual prediction as the world-modeling target of a WAM for efficient training? To learn such a representation, we propose Predictive Representations via Inverse Spatiotemporal Modeling (PRISM). We aim to learn a compact representation that preserves information about both the actions underlying an observed transition and the resulting visual state. During representation learning, a bottleneck encoder compresses current and future visual features into a compact set of latent tokens. Inverse-dynamics supervision encourages these tokens to retain transition information informative of the underlying actions, while feature reconstruction encourages them to preserve future-state content, without requiring the full detail of the native visual representation. We then introduce MiniWAM, which separates learning what to represent about the future from learning how to predict it. First, PRISM learns to encode current--future visual transitions into compact targets through inverse-dynamics supervision and feature reconstruction. The representation encoder is then frozen, and MiniWAM is trained to jointly predict the resulting PRISM target and robot actions given the current observation. In this way, MiniWAM changes what the world model branch is trained to predict, rather than merely reducing the cost of predicting an otherwise unchanged visual future. PRISM is not tied to a particular visual feature space, because the bottleneck is learned downstream of the visual representation. We instantiate the framework with both generative WAN2.1 VAE features wan2025wan and discriminative DINOv3 features simeoni2025dinov3 . By replacing dense future representations with a compact set of latent tokens, PRISM reduces the number of future tokens by . Despite this substantial compression, MiniWAM consistently outperforms matched variants that directly predict the corresponding native future representations, while requiring substantially less training computation. These controlled comparisons show that the benefit does not arise simply from choosing a stronger visual encoder: replacing its dense future representation with the compact PRISM target improves the performance--efficiency trade-off. This performance--efficiency advantage is illustrated in Figure~ fig:headline . Empirically, MiniWAM reduces WAM training cost by up to 8 while outperforming native future-feature prediction across simulation benchmarks. A 0.25B MiniWAM is already competitive with WAMs built upon substantially larger pretrained video-generation backbones. Ablations show that adding inverse-dynamics supervision to reconstruction-only bottlenecks consistently improves performance across bottleneck capacities. These results suggest that strong world--action modeling does not require predicting the native visual future: compact learned representations can provide a stronger and substantially more efficient target for predictive co-training. Related Work World Models and World--Action Models for Robot Control. World models learn predictive representations of environment dynamics to support planning and policy learning, often in latent or pretrained feature spaces rather than pixel space NEURIPS2018_2de5d166, Hafner2020Dream,zhou2025dinowm . Building on this principle, recent methods increasingly integrate future prediction directly into policy training, giving rise to World Action Models (WAMs) that jointly model future states and robot actions kim2026cosmos,ye2026world,yuan2026fast . Using future prediction as a co-training objective, WAMs encourage the policy to capture structured environment dynamics while sharing information between world and action streams. This formulation has achieved strong manipulation performance, but typically requires predicting dense spatiotemporal visual representations, such as video-VAE latents, substantially increasing the cost of policy training. Efficient and Compact Future Modeling. Recent work improves WAM efficiency through architectural simplification and reduced future-modeling computation yuan2026fast,zhao2026faster,li2026efficient . A complementary line replaces dense future prediction with compact latent supervision, aligning or supervising policy-internal representations with features derived from future observations zheng2025flare,luo2026being,su2026world . These approaches show that predictive information can be represented more compactly than the original visual future, but typically retain native visual features as world-modeling targets or use compact representations primarily as internal policy states or conditioning signals. Concurrent work wang2026openwam shows that channel-wise compression of semantic prediction targets can yield strong world--action co-training performance. PRISM instead learns a control-relevant transition representation as the world-prediction target, jointly compressing its spatial and temporal dimensions to substantially reduce the number of predicted tokens and the cost of world–action co-training. Mini World Action Model with Predictive Representations sec:method Overview Given a current observation , a future observation window , and the corresponding action chunk , we seek a compact representation of the visual transition that can replace native future features as the predictive target of a World Action Model. title: Residual Modeling Closes the Regression and Generative Policy Gap in Robot Learning
summary: Learning from demonstration has enabled impressive robot behaviors. A common choice for policy learning is to use diffusion or flow matching (Flow-Policies), which often outperforms direct action regression trained with mean squared error (MSE-Policies). This gap is commonly attributed to multimodal demonstrations. We revisit this gap from the perspective of statistical modeling: how action-prediction residuals shape policy optimization. Our analysis of real-world robot demonstration data reveals substantial state-dependent variation in residual scales and heavier-than-Gaussian tails. While both MSE-Policies and Flow-Policies exhibit heavy-tailed action residuals, their training gradients behave differently: MSE allocates more gradient magnitude to observations with large action residuals, which hurts optimization. Motivated by these findings, we introduce heteroscedastic Student-t action regression (HT-Policies), which learns input-dependent residual scales and reduces the influence of heavy tails. HT-Policies predict action chunks with a single feed-forward pass and can reuse pretrained flow-matching-based policy networks as the backbone. Across four simulation benchmarks and real-robot evaluations, HT-Policies achieves success rates competitive with generative policy baselines, both when trained from scratch and from pretrained vision-language-action and world-action models, despite being faster in training and inference. Together, these findings shed light on the practical advantages of generative objectives in robot learning from demonstrations and offer an efficient direct-regression alternative for a range of architectures and tasks. Project page: https://the-labone.github.io/regression-policy-project/
full_text: Experiments and Analysis In Section~ sec:data-analysis , we have illustrated how a standard MSE-based--regression policy ( MSE-Policy ) fails to model state-dependent residuals and long tails in action learning. This failure leads to imbalanced gradients across state-action pairs with different estimated residuals, which in turn hurts model performance. In the following empirical evaluation, we focus on three questions. First, can the proposed heteroscedastic Student- policy ( HT-Policy ) address state-dependent residuals and long tails, as evaluated by its performance on robot manipulation tasks in both simulation and the real world (Section~ sec:evaluation-scratch )? Second, can we adapt pre-trained vision-language-action (VLA) and world-action (WAM) models to HT-Policy to fully leverage existing community efforts in generalized policy learning? Third, do the data likelihood (residual modeling) and gradient distributions of HT-Policies trained on real-world data support the observations and principles identified in Section~ sec:data-analysis ? Beyond their performance and general applicability, HT-Policies are a useful policy class for practitioners because they offer greater training and inference efficiency than generative policies, such as flow-matching--based policies ( Flow-Policies ), as shown in Section~ sec:evaluation-efficiency . We conclude this section with ablation studies of different robust-regression objectives and an analysis of the selection of . Furthermore, HT-Policies offer closed-form likelihood evaluation and efficient action sampling, making them well-suited for reinforcement-learning--based fine-tuning. We evaluate their exploration capability on an example task, Tool-Hang, in Appendix~ sec:appendix-exploration . Appendix~ sec:appendix-training provides additional training and evaluation details, and Appendix~ sec:appendix-loss-settings provides additional ablation results. Closing the Performance Gap When Training from Scratch sec:evaluation-scratch We first investigate whether HT-Policy's modeling of state-dependent and long-tail residuals improves robot manipulation performance when training policies from scratch. We compare HT-Policies with MSE-Policies, diffusion--based policies, and Flow-Policies. Simulation experiment setup. On RoboMimic~ robomimic2021 , we train U-Net and Transformer policies in both state-based and image-based settings following Diffusion Policy (DP)~ chi2023diffusionpolicy . On RoboCasa-GR1~ nvidia2025gr00tn1openfoundation , we train action decoders from scratch but using image features encoded by a frozen VLM backbone from GR00T N1.7 for the vision input. Appendix~ sec:appendix-gr1-scratch provides more model and training details. Table~ tab:rq1-performance summarizes the results. On RoboMimic, HT-Policies are on par with generative policies and substantially outperform MSE-based policies. On RoboCasa-GR1, HT-Policies outperform both MSE-Policies and Flow-Policies. Overall, HT-Policies are strong direct-regression algorithms for policy training from scratch. We provide per-task performance breakdowns in Appendix~ sec:appendix-dp and additional comparisons with MIP policies~ pan2026much on RoboMimic in Appendix~ sec:appendix-mip . Real-robot experiment setup. Furthermore, we evaluate different policies on three real-world manipulation tasks: Push-T, Peel-Note, and Insert-T (Figure~ fig:real-robot-eval ). Training and evaluation details are provided in Appendix~ sec:appendix-real-robot . On the real robot, HT-Policies largely close the performance gap between MSE-based and generative policies on all three tasks. The largest improvements occur on Push-T and Peel-Note, where MSE-Policies fail significantly. Overall, in both simulation and real-robot tasks, HT-Policies perform on par with generative policies when the action model is trained from scratch. These gains are achieved with a simple feed-forward-only policy, highlighting the importance and effectiveness of residual modeling. Fine-Tuning Pretrained Flow-Policies with HT Regression sec:evaluaiton-generality We next investigate whether HT-Policies can be fine-tuned from pretrained VLA and WAM models to leverage existing advances in generalized policy learning. Following the procedure described in Section~ sec:method , the only architectural change is the addition of a randomly initialized residual scale prediction head . We fine-tune the action predictor using the HT loss while retaining each model's original fine-tuning settings and hyperparameters. We show results on three models: ~ intelligence2025pi05visionlanguageactionmodelopenworld , GR00T N1.7~ nvidia2025gr00tn1openfoundation , and Cosmos 3~ nvidia2026cosmos3omnimodalworld , and on three benchmarks: LIBERO~ liu2023liberobenchmarkingknowledgetransfer , SIMPLER~ li24simpler, walke2023bridgedata, rt12022arxiv , and RoboCasa-GR1~ nvidia2025gr00tn1openfoundation . We evaluate each method across 10 evaluation seeds. These settings span VLA and WAM architectures and cover both fixed-arm and humanoid manipulation. We report the implementation details in Appendix~ sec:appendix-training . Shown in Table~ tab:rq2-performance , HT-Policies achieve higher success rates than MSE-Policies in all five settings, and outperform Flow-Policies in three of them. These results are obtained using fine-tuning recipes adopted directly from Flow-Policies, rather than specifically tuned for HT-Policies. The only tuned hyperparameter is the learning rate of the newly added scale prediction head, which is trained from scratch. We provide per-task performance break-downs in Appendices~ sec:appendix-libero-results , sec:appendix-gr1-results , and~ sec:appendix-cosmos-results . Residual Modeling, Gradient Allocation, and Policy Performance sec:evaluation-gradient The results above show that changing the residual model makes regression-based policies competitive with generative policies. To further close the theory-implementation gap, we examine the data likelihood and gradient distributions of policies trained on real-world data. This analysis tests whether the principles identified in Section~ sec:data-analysis regarding residual modeling and gradient allocation explain the observed performance gains. Gradient allocation across observations Figure~ fig:gradient-compare shows that the HT loss produces a more balanced allocation of gradients across observations: large-residual observations no longer dominate the gradients as they do under MSE. This allocation resembles that of low-noise flow-matching when . Appendix~ sec:appendix-gradient-stages extends this comparison to different training stages. r 0.40 fig:dist-quality-vs-sr Residual modeling and policy performance. Figure~ fig:dist-quality-vs-sr examines whether data likelihood under different residual models is correlated with policy performance on RoboCasa-GR1. Beyond MSE and HT, we include six alternative models, such as models trained with the Huber loss. Across all eight objectives, calibrated mean log-likelihood is strongly correlated with policy success rate (Spearman ; Pearson ). HT-Policies achieve substantially higher likelihood than the conventional Gaussian residual model from MSE-based policies, and the highest success rate. Modeling either heavy tails with a Student- distribution or state-dependent scales with a heteroscedastic Gaussian (HG) also improves likelihood and success over MSE, but neither matches HT, which incorporates both. Appendix~ sec:likelihood-calibration provides the evaluation details. Together, these findings support the principles that improved residual modeling and more balanced gradient allocation yield better policy performance. Training and Inference Efficiency sec:evaluation-efficiency A core advantage of regression policies for practitioners is their training and inference efficiency. We next evaluate whether HT-Policies retain this advantage while achieving strong task performance. Training efficiency. Shown in Figure~ fig:convergence , we compare the training progress of HT-Policies, MSE-Policies, and Flow-Policies in two training-from-scratch and two fine-tuning settings. In all four settings, HT-Policies reach strong task success with fewer training steps than Flow-Policies. Inference efficiency. HT-Policies require only a single feed-forward pass at inference. Table~ tab:inference-efficiency reports batch-size-one inference runtime on an NVIDIA RTX 5090 GPU. HT achieves higher end-to-end throughput than flow on all three models. Cosmos3-Nano shows the largest whole-model speedup of , with our HT-Policy replacing the 30-step sampling procedure of Flow-Policies. Appendix~ sec:appendix-efficiency provides additional implementation details and results on NVIDIA A800 GPUs. Ablation Studies sec:ablation r 0.65 fig:nu-sensitivity Ablation on the degrees of freedom . sec:rq-student-t-ablation In practice, we select in proportion to the action-chunk dimension , parameterizing it as . Figure~ fig:nu-sensitivity a shows that RoboCasa-GR1 performance peaks at an intermediate value of , favoring moderate downweighting of large residuals over either strong downweighting or the Gaussian limit. To evaluate this dimension-dependent choice across settings, Figure~ fig:nu-sensitivity b compares performance as a function of . RoboCasa-GR1, Bridge, and LIBERO all achieve their highest tested success rates at , supporting as a practical default across these settings. Appendix~ sec:appendix-nu-settings provides evaluation details. Comparison with alternative training objectives. Figure~ fig:dist-quality-vs-sr summarizes the comparison among HT-Policies and alternative robust-regression objectives by calibrated likelihood and performance; Appendix~ sec:residual-model-ablation defines these objectives (Table~ tab:app-loss-definitions ) and provides detailed results (Table~ tab:robust-loss-ablation ). Overall, HT-Policies achieve the best performance.

title: PLaW-VLA: Predictive Latent World Modeling for Vision-Language-Action Policies
comment: Accepted to the 10th Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL 2026)
summary: Learning to predict how the world evolves can provide vision-language-action (VLA) policies with predictive context for long-horizon control, but its effectiveness depends on what future representation is modeled and how it conditions action generation. We introduce PLaW-VLA, which models task-relevant future states in a pretrained prediction-oriented representation space, reducing the need to predict control-irrelevant visual details. Built on a Mixture-of-Transformers architecture, PLaW-VLA conditions action generation on observation history, current task semantics, and predicted future states through structured causal attention. Experiments show a +11.8 percentage-point (pp) gain over reactive policies on RoboTwin Hard Horizon III and a +1.77 pp gain over reconstruction-oriented latent prediction on zero-shot LIBERO-Plus, supporting improved long-horizon control and generalization under distribution shift, respectively. By avoiding low-level visual reconstruction, PLaW-VLA lowers the burden of future prediction, enabling a lightweight latent world model with parallel future prediction and about 1/19 the inference latency of generative world-action modeling at comparable policy performance.
full_text: Learning to predict how the world evolves can provide vision-language-action (VLA) policies with predictive context for long-horizon control, but its effectiveness depends on what future representation is modeled and how it conditions action generation. We introduce PLaW-VLA, which models task-relevant future states in a pretrained prediction-oriented representation space, reducing the need to predict control-irrelevant visual details. Built on a Mixture-of-Transformers architecture, PLaW-VLA conditions action generation on observation history, current task semantics, and predicted future states through structured causal attention. Experiments show a percentage-point (pp) gain over reactive policies on RoboTwin Hard Horizon~III and a pp gain over reconstruction-oriented latent prediction on zero-shot LIBERO-Plus, supporting improved long-horizon control and generalization under distribution shift, respectively. By avoiding low-level visual reconstruction, PLaW-VLA lowers the burden of future prediction, enabling a lightweight latent world model with parallel future prediction and about the inference latency of generative world--action modeling at comparable policy performance. Introduction Vision-language-action (VLA) models adapt pretrained vision-language representations to language-conditioned robot manipulation~ black2025pi_05,black2024pi_0,kim2024openvla,rt2,bjorck2025gr00t,kim2025fine . Long-horizon manipulation requires not only interpreting the current scene but also tracking how the task evolves across successive interactions. Under partial observability and execution perturbations, the current observation alone may be insufficient to infer the underlying task state. Effective long-horizon control therefore benefits from both modeling temporal context from observation history and anticipating future state evolution for action generation. Recent studies incorporate predictive representations and future modeling into VLA through future-representation alignment~ zheng2025flare,sun2026vla , visual feature fusion~ miao2026jepa , future-conditioned action generation~ cai2026internvla,lv2025f1,pai2025mimic , and joint world--action modeling~ zhu2025unified,shen2026videovla,ye2026world,bi2025motus,cen2025rynnvla,cen2025worldvla . This raises two key questions for control: what future representation should be predicted, and how should it condition action generation? Existing predictive targets derived from visual reconstruction or generation require modeling both task dynamics and appearance variations, even when the latter are irrelevant to control. This increases the prediction burden, while errors in these irrelevant components may propagate to action generation when the predicted future directly conditions the policy. We propose PLaW-VLA (Fig.~ fig:teaser ), a VLA framework that integrates predictive latent world modeling with action generation. Built on a Mixture-of-Transformers architecture, PLaW-VLA combines observation history, current task semantics, and predicted future latent states to generate continuous robot actions. The framework is designed around two key choices in future modeling for control. First, PLaW-VLA predicts task-relevant future latent states in a pretrained prediction-oriented representation space, emphasizing state transitions and interaction dynamics rather than low-level visual reconstruction. Second, these predicted future states directly condition the action model through structured causal attention, providing explicit predictive context for action generation. PLaW-VLA follows a three-stage video-to-robot training pipeline. Stage~I pretrains the latent world model on human and robot videos without action supervision, learning to predict visual dynamics in the representation space defined by the frozen encoder. Stage~II transfers these representations to robot control by introducing action-annotated robot trajectories and jointly optimizing future-state prediction and action generation, thereby aligning predictive dynamics with action-relevant behavior. Stage~III further adapts the resulting policy to the target task and robot embodiment. This training paradigm enables predictive knowledge acquired from large-scale videos to be reused for robot policy learning, providing a scalable path from generic visual dynamics to task-specific control. We evaluate PLaW-VLA on three simulation benchmarks and diverse real-world manipulation tasks. It outperforms by 11.8 percentage points on RoboTwin Hard Horizon~III and achieves 72.7 task-weighted success on zero-shot LIBERO-Plus, supporting long-horizon control and generalization under distribution shift. By modeling future dynamics in latent space rather than reconstructing low-level visual content, PLaW-VLA reduces the complexity of future prediction and enables a compact latent world model with parallel prediction, providing an effective trade-off between policy performance and inference efficiency. Related Work Vision-Language-Action Models. VLA models transfer pretrained visual and language representations to robot policies~ rt2,team2024octo,kim2024openvla,black2024pi_0,black2025pi_05,bjorck2025gr00t . Continuous action prediction~ kim2025fine,liang2025discrete , flow-based decoding~ black2024pi_0,black2025pi_05 , and action tokenization~ pertsch2025fast provide different interfaces between multimodal representations and robot actions. Complementary approaches augment policy context with memory~ shi2025memoryvla , spatial representations~ qu2025spatialvla , and hierarchical task reasoning~ zhao2025cot,huang2026thinkact . PLaW-VLA complements these directions by augmenting the policy with predicted future visual representations as additional context for action generation. World Models for Robot Control. World models have been increasingly incorporated into robot control by predicting future observations, latent states, or joint video-action trajectories. Visual-imagination approaches generate future images or videos and recover actions through inverse dynamics~ unipi_du2023learning,ko2024learning,tian2025predictive,zhou2024robodreamer . More recent methods jointly model future observations and actions through autoregressive formulations~ cen2025worldvla,cen2025rynnvla,li2026causal or video-action generative architectures~ zhu2025unified,shen2026videovla,cai2026internvla,lv2025f1,ye2026world . Motus~ bi2025motus unifies understanding, video generation, and action prediction within a Mixture-of-Transformers architecture, while mimic-video~ pai2025mimic conditions action generation on partially denoised video latents. These methods demonstrate the utility of future prediction for control, but most predictive targets are derived from observation reconstruction or generation objectives. In contrast, PLaW-VLA predicts future features in the space defined by a frozen V-JEPA~2 encoder~ assran2025v , using a prediction-trained representation space rather than a reconstruction-oriented target space. Predictive Representations for Policy Learning. Predictive representation learning provides an alternative to explicit observation generation by learning latent features that capture temporal structure. FLARE~ zheng2025flare aligns diffusion-policy features with embeddings of future observations, while VLA-JEPA~ sun2026vla learns latent action representations through future V-JEPA 2 feature prediction. JEPA-VLA~ miao2026jepa incorporates V-JEPA 2 visual representations into existing VLAs through feature fusion. These methods differ primarily in how predictive representations interact with policy learning: as auxiliary supervision, latent action representations, or visual features. PLaW-VLA instead predicts future representations from observation history and uses the predicted future state directly to condition action generation. It therefore combines a prediction-trained target space with explicit future-state conditioning for policy learning. Method sec:method Problem Formulation In this work, we formulate vision-language-action generation through predictive latent world modeling. Given a language instruction and visual observation history , the model first grounds the current scene into a semantic representation , predicts future latent states , and finally generates future actions . This formulation decomposes action generation into three causally ordered components, namely semantic grounding, latent-space prediction, and action decoding. Formally, we factorize the joint conditional distribution over scene semantics , future latent states , and future actions as: The vision-language model (VLM) grounds the language instruction in the current multimodal context and produces a task-relevant semantic representation . Conditioned on this grounded representation and the observation history, the latent world model (LWM) predicts future latents that summarize the anticipated evolution of the task-relevant world state. Finally, decodes future actions from the grounded semantics, historical latents, and predicted future latents. Model Architecture As illustrated in Fig.~ fig:framework , PLaW-VLA adopts a unified Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) architecture consisting of three causally ordered experts corresponding to the factorization in Eq.~ , including a vision-language expert for semantic grounding, a latent world model expert for predictive latent modeling, and an action expert for continuous action generation. Interactions among experts are regulated through structured causal attention that preserves the intended causal information flow. Vision-Language Model. We instantiate the vision-language expert from PaliGemma~ beyer2024paligemma , which provides strong multimodal understanding and language-conditioned visual grounding capabilities. The multi-view observation \(o_t\) and language instruction \(c\) are processed by the VLM expert to produce contextual embeddings \( _t\), which provide grounded semantic context for downstream predictive latent modeling and action generation. Latent World Model. Recent large-scale video generation models have demonstrated strong performance by generating future images or videos~ lv2025f1,cai2026internvla,cen2025rynnvla,ye2026world . In contrast, our approach performs future prediction in a compact latent representation space. The latent world model predicts future latent trajectories conditioned on historical observations and task context, without explicitly modeling low-level visual appearance. The observation history \(o_ t-H_o:t \) is first mapped into a compact visual representation space using a frozen pretrained encoder \(E\), producing latent states \(z_ t-H_o:t \). To perform future-state prediction, we introduce \(K\) learnable future queries \( _ 1:K \), where each query corresponds to one future prediction step. These future queries attend to both the historical latent trajectory and the contextual embeddings \( _t\) produced by the VLM, and jointly predict the corresponding future latent states through the latent world model predictor \(F_z\): r 0.35 Cross-expert attention. fig:causal_attention Action Model. The action expert models the policy \(p_a( _ t _t, _ t-H_o:t , _ >t )\) by decoding temporally extended action sequences conditioned on grounded semantic representations \( _t\), historical latents \( _ t-H_o:t \), and predicted future latents \( _ >t \). The predicted future latents provide predictive context that guides action generation over future interaction horizons. Causal Cross-Expert Attention. As shown in Fig.~ fig:causal_attention , PLaW-VLA adopts a structured causal attention pattern across the experts. The tokens \(P_i\), \(H_i\), \(F_i\), and \(A_i\) denote contextual, historical latent, future-query latent, and action-query tokens, respectively. This structured attention preserves information flow from semantic grounding to latent prediction and action decoding while preventing future information leakage and reducing cross-expert interference. title: GLIO2: A GPU-Parallelized Tightly-Coupled LiDAR-Inertial-GNSS System for Robust and Real-Time Global Localization and Mapping
summary: Globally consistent, real-time state estimation in large-scale, perceptually degraded environments is essential for autonomous vehicles and aerial robots, and requires fusing LiDAR, inertial, and GNSS measurements. Existing fusion methods, however, share a scan-to-map front-end with two failure modes. First, each scan is aligned to an incrementally built map that drifts under degeneracy, and once the estimate diverges the error is irrecoverable. Second, even without divergence, a registration biased by dynamic objects or wrong correspondences is propagated as a single pose constraint with an over-confident covariance, leaving its correspondences unavailable for GNSS to re-weight or relinearize. We propose GLIO2, a tightly-coupled LiDAR-Inertial-GNSS system whose GPU-parallel front-end jointly optimizes scan-to-multiscan LiDAR, IMU pre-integration, and raw GNSS measurements in a single sliding-window factor graph, sustaining real-time operation on edge hardware. A complementary offline back-end reuses the same cached factors to refine the entire trajectory in batch, completing the 30-min, 4.51-km UrbanNav Whampoa sequence in about 24 s. Across three public benchmarks (UrbanNav, MARS-LVIG, M3DGR) and self-collected UAV and vehicle data, GLIO2 attains the best overall accuracy among evaluated systems. On a 5.66-km bridge traversed at up to 96 km/h, where every competing baseline diverges under LiDAR degeneracy, it maintains 1.6 m horizontal accuracy. On an NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX, the full pipeline runs at about 25 Hz (39.60 ms per scan). The source code and datasets will be released.

Localization, Mapping, Sensor Fusion, Global Navigation Introduction sec:intro n autonomous vehicle in a dense urban canyon and a micro-aerial vehicle surveying open farmland face the same estimation problem: the state must be globally consistent over the whole mission, locally smooth at control rate, robust to sensor degradation, and computed in real time on the limited compute carried onboard. LiDAR, inertial measurement units (IMUs), and global navigation satellite systems (GNSS) each meet part of these demands and fail another. LiDAR-inertial odometry (LIO)~ fastlio2,glim,lio-sam exploits the rich structural information in point clouds to produce high-frequency, locally smooth, and locally accurate motion estimates together with dense 3D geometric maps. The IMU predicts inter-scan motion to deskew each scan and bridge the gaps between LiDAR frames, though it drifts rapidly when integrated alone. Relying primarily on local geometric constraints, however, LIO accumulates drift over long trajectories and degrades severely under geometric degeneracy (weak, repetitive, or insufficient structure such as open fields, long tunnels, and flat or sparsely featured scenes), where the registration loses observability along its under-constrained directions~ . GNSS, in contrast, provides drift-free absolute positioning in a globally referenced Earth-fixed frame, bounding the global error that LIO cannot~ GNSS_IMU_FGO_Welson . Yet its measurements arrive at only -- \,Hz and are corrupted by multipath, non-line-of-sight (NLOS) reception, and outright outages in the urban canyons, tunnels, and indoor spaces a robot must traverse, where a single contaminated observation can inject errors of tens of meters. The two modalities are thus complementary: GNSS anchors the estimate to an Earth-fixed frame and bounds the global drift that LIO accumulates, while LIO carries the estimate through GNSS outages and down-weights GNSS outliers with its more precise local geometry. Fusing LiDAR, IMU, and GNSS in a single tightly-coupled factor graph~ isam2 exploits this complementarity, jointly relinearizing the raw heterogeneous measurements as new information arrives~ glio,ligo,GNSS_IMU_FGO_Welson . Building such an estimator that is at once globally and locally consistent, robust under sensor degradation, and real-time on edge platforms, however, raises three central challenges. a) Front-end fragility: LiDAR--GNSS systems such as LIO-SAM~ lio-sam , LIGO~ ligo , GIL~ li2021gil , and GLIO~ glio all build their LiDAR estimate on a scan-to-map (S2M) front-end, which fuses past scans into a single deterministic map and aligns each new scan to it. In scenes such as a sea-crossing bridge, a flat open plain, or a UAV flying close to a repetitive high-rise facade, severe geometric degeneracy rapidly destabilizes this scan-to-map LiDAR localization, so the front-end can no longer produce a correct estimate; once it diverges, the back-end GNSS estimate cannot be recovered either. Even GLIO's offline scan-to-multiscan (S2MS) batch is insufficient, as it still requires a non-divergent front-end as its initial guess. The first challenge, then, is the inherent limitation of the front-end design adopted by these mainstream methods. b) Frozen, over-confident LiDAR: Mainstream S2M methods first reduce each scan to a fixed LiDAR constraint (a -DoF pose-with-covariance prior in LIGO~ ligo , a relative-pose factor in LIO-SAM~ lio-sam ) and fuse it with GNSS. In urban scenes, however, dynamic objects, passing traffic, and changing structure create wrong correspondences that bias this constraint. It then enters the fusion under an over-confident covariance that outweighs the GNSS correction, and because the past point clouds are never re-associated or relinearized, the bias is frozen into the trajectory rather than corrected. The second challenge is thus to admit LiDAR into the GNSS fusion as c) Real-time cost: the raw point residuals in one joint optimization, so that LiDAR and GNSS relinearize together. The price is computational. Each scan forms dense voxel correspondences against several keyframes, and every nonlinear iteration must recompute all correspondences, fused covariances, and Jacobians as the keyframe poses move. The third challenge is thus to sustain this dense, raw-domain joint optimization online, Motivated by these observations, we present GLIO2, a unified tightly-coupled LiDAR--Inertial--GNSS system. A GPU-parallel front-end fuses dense LiDAR, IMU, and raw GNSS in one real-time sliding-window graph, and an offline batch back-end refines the trajectory by reusing the same factors. The first two contributions respond to the three challenges; the third validates and releases the system. The contributions of this work are as follows. A unified online LiDAR--Inertial--GNSS front-end. GLIO2 fuses scan-to-multiscan LiDAR, raw double-differenced pseudorange and Doppler, and IMU pre-integration in a single real-time sliding-window graph (Sec.~ sec:system_overview ). The raw correspondences are re-associated and relinearized at every iteration, Tightly coupling both modalities on the raw measurements keeps the estimate robust to LiDAR degeneracy and to GNSS dropouts (Sec.~ sec:ablation ). Real-time onboard operation with a fast offline back-end. Validation and open-source release. On three public benchmarks (UrbanNav~ hsu2021urbannav , MARS-LVIG~ MARS-LVIG , M3DGR~ zhang2025towards ) and self-collected UAV and vehicle data, under both GNSS NLOS/multipath and LiDAR degeneracy, (Sec.~ sec:experiments ). A single-receiver variant runs without a base station (Appendix~ app:single_receiver ). The source code and self-collected datasets will be released. Related Work sec:related_work LiDAR Registration Paradigms subsec:lidar_factors Scan matching provides the geometric constraints in LiDAR odometry, and the way a scan is matched determines the form of constraint it produces and thus what LiDAR contributes to the joint estimator. (S2M) registration is adopted by most real-time LiDAR-inertial odometry (LIO) systems, which registers each new scan against an incrementally built reference map (e.g., a surfel or implicit-surface map~ deschaud2018imls,behley2018suma ) and produces a single absolute pose~ fastlio2,point-lio,lio-sam . Building on classical pairwise scan registration~ icp,loam , S2M is efficient and locally accurate. However, it treats the fused map as a fixed reference, so potentially erroneous earlier map points are never corrected by later scans, and each scan is summarized by one absolute pose rather than by its raw correspondences. (S2MS) registration instead keeps several keyframe poses as optimization variables and jointly refines them through relative constraints. The estimated poses update the world-frame geometry, while each keyframe's point cloud remains in its local frame. S2MS builds on the joint multi-scan alignment of Lu and Milios~ lu1997globally and nScan-matching~ nscan_matching , and modern formulations bring a distribution-to-distribution registration metric (GICP~ gicp , NDT~ biber2003ndt , and its voxelized form VGICP~ vgicp ) into a multi-scan factor graph. The main cost is computational: as the keyframe poses move, the correspondences, residuals, and Jacobians must be re-associated and relinearized for many scan pairs at every iteration, so dense S2MS has traditionally run at low rate or offline, as in the global LiDAR bundle adjustment of BALM~ liu2021balm and the GNSS-coupled global batch optimization of GLIO~ glio . Lightweight and GPU-accelerated formulations reduce this cost: FF-LINS~ fflins uses a frame-to-frame association on a solid-state LiDAR, while Koide et~al. apply GPU acceleration to dense factors for real-time LiDAR-inertial odometry~ koide2022globally and faster global mapping~ koide2021globally , an approach consolidated in GLIM~ glim . GNSS Observables subsec:gnss_observables A GNSS receiver outputs three raw observables, the pseudorange (PSR), the Doppler (DOP), and the carrier phase (CP). Prior work fuses these observables in different ways. The simplest is Single Point Positioning (SPP), which estimates an absolute position from a single receiver's pseudoranges, modeling the ionospheric and tropospheric delays and the satellite and receiver clock errors~ enge1994global . GVINS~ cao2022gvins , the raw-GNSS visual-inertial estimator of Liu et~al.~ liu2021rawgnssvio and gnssFGO~ zhang2024gnssfgo tightly couple raw pseudorange and Doppler, the Doppler providing a global velocity observation. Precise Point Positioning (PPP) applies precise orbit and clock products and estimates the receiver clock and tropospheric delay, removing the first-order ionosphere either by the ionosphere-free combination (GIL~ li2021gil ) or with external ionosphere maps (P3-LINS~ li2023p3-lins ). Differential methods instead suppress most of these errors directly: double-differencing (DD) the pseudorange against a reference station~ odijk2017differential cancels the satellite and receiver clock errors and largely removes the spatially correlated atmospheric delays over a short baseline, leaving meter-level constraints, as in GLIO~ glio . The carrier phase is far more precise but carries an integer ambiguity; the dominant strategy resolves the double-differenced ambiguity~ chang2005mlambda in a between-station/between-satellite formulation (Real-Time Kinematic, RTK), as in GLINS~ glins , GIVL-SLAM~ wang2024givl , and FGO-GIL~ li2023fgo , reaching centimeter accuracy. An alternative differences the carrier phase across epochs (Time-Differenced Carrier Phase, TD-CP); since the integer ambiguity is time-invariant, this differencing cancels it when no cycle slip occurs, leaving a smooth epoch-to-epoch motion constraint, as in LIGO~ ligo .
